TO BE SOLD BY AUCTION (subject to conditions which will he declared at the time of the Sale) by Mr. ALFRED CLIVE, at the Blue Bell, Horsemarket-street, on Wednesday, the 4th December, at 5 o'clock in the afternoon, the following Valuable SITES in Bridge-street, Buttermarket-street, Church- street, Knutsford-road and Liverpool-road, Warrington: LOT I.—A Plot of Freehold LAND on the west side of Bridge-street, between the premises belonging to Mr. T. J. Lee and Mr. J. Shaw, having a frontage to Bridge-street of about 21 feet 6 inches and containing about 262 square yards. LOT 2.—A Plot of Freehold LAND on the west side of Bridge-street, between the Feathers Hotel and the premises occupied by Messrs G and J Weaver, having a frontage to Bridge-street of about 26 feet G inches and containing about 223 square yards. LOT 3.—A Plot of Freehold LAND on the north-east side of Knutsford-road, formerly the site of the Mersey Bedstead Works, containing in the whole 2,031 square yards or thereabouts, with a Wharfage on the River Mersey of 136 feet 6inches, together with the buildings now standing thereon,subject to two rents of £7 2s. 4d. and £4 15s. per annum respectively. LOT 4.—A Plot of Freehold LAND, with the Two SHOPSgor WAREHOUSES, Nod. 13 and 15, Butter- market-street, having a frontage of 33 feet 6 inches and containing 256 square yards or thereabouts. freehold and partly dye of Liverpool-road, leaLsooThosi.d—, situate Plot oo fn LANDthe norptharatil adjoining Sankey Brook and formerly the site of the Chemical Works, containing in the whole 5,359 square yards or thereabouts. This lot will be sold subject to the yearly rents of £2l 6s. 6d., £l4 6s. 6d. and 10s. respectively and the covenants and conditions affecting the same. LOT 6.—A plot of LAND situate on the west side of Bridge-street, adjoining the Royal Court Hotel,having a frontage to Bridge-street of 21 feet 5 inches and con- taining about 209 square yards. This lot will be let on a imilding lease for a term of 999 years and will be sold subject to rights of light affecting the same but with the benefit of the party wall shown on the plan. LOT 7.—A Plot of LAND partly freehold and partly leasehold, but free from rent, situate at the corner of Church-street and Howley-lane, having a frontage to Church-street of 160 feet. to Howley-lane of 60 feet and to Greenall-street, of 67 feet, and containing 966 square yards or thereabouts. were,however, invading art at every turn, and he hoped lovers of art would do their utmost to expel them as quickly as possible. They were also invading music. They were asked So listen to some extraordinary things now—bangs, crashes and discords—and then they were told they had been listening to a beautiful, inspiring piece of music, from whiah the base relics of enedimval harmony had been absolutely cast out. They were being slightly invaded in the realm of literature also. Alderman BENNETT seconded the motion. He said the survival of that exhibition was a sort, of reply to the somewhat unsympathetic artist of whom Miss Broadbent spoke. The line he had accepted seemed to be the very least calculated to encourage the thing that was conspicuously absent from the old town. He was bound to admit that Warrington was not an artistic town. Love of the beautiful in Warrington seemed like the light of a candle in foul air ; it burned under difficulties. Having paid a tribute to the work of eminent Warringtou artists, Alderman Bennett said he had been frequently reproached by some of his friends in lamenting the state of things in Warrington and in the country generaUy, for venturing to doubt whether our industrial supremacy, of •vhich we' were so proud, was really a thing to be Iroud of at all. For what particular reason did we wish to be the workshop of the world ? John Bull seemed to think it was a glorious.thing to he the workshop of the world,but he (the speaker) doubted whether it was something to he proud of, because while it brought fabulous wealth and certain advantages, with the accumulation of wealth and the increasing manu- facturing success which accompanied it, we seemed to lose all those finer feelings and love of the more beauti- ful things in life which existed in England years ago, and which certainly existed among the great nations of the past. (Hear, hear, nd applause.) How to combine the two—to maintain our industrial supremacy, and at the same time to retain a love for the beautiful, which was much greater and nobler, was a Problem we had to face. One felt that the love of beauty was almost dead in Warrington, and it was therefore, a ratifying feature to find amid all its uncongenial surroundings that they were able to get exhibitions together and to find that the love of beauty still lived. (Applause.) He thought the time would come, though it was very slew in coming, when people would begin to believe that the life was more than meat, and that there Was something to live for besides gaining great wealth and indulging in the occasional excitement of football mat_hes.Af ter all the world Was a very beautiful world, though man never seemed to intrude on the scene without desolating and destroying that beauty. What did they want to do ? Was it possible by "this dirty river and under murky skies" to roar up the city beautiful ? He thought it was. It was only necessary to communicate their enthusiasm to others and gradually let the love of the beautiful percolate through the whole mass of the population, making people love teautiful things, so that they could not tolerate ugly and obnoxious surroundings. Once that love of beauty was created there would inevitably follow on the heels of it a determination to abolish squalor and sordidness which were the usual accompani- ments of life in industrial towns, making life in the great northern skies more pleasant and agreeable, and etch a life as any self-rest-entitle citizeu would not only tolerate, but enjoy. (Applause). 1 he motion was heartily carried.

div.head: ARTS AND CRAFTS.
div.p: ARTS AND CRAFTS.
EXHIBITION AT WARRINGTON.
THE DRAWBACKS OF INDUSTRIAL SUPREMACY.

Although there are not wanting those who declare that the love of the beautiful is well nigh extinct in Warrington, art has its little band of devotees in our midst hnd efforts are made to interest a wider public in idealistic pursuits by the holding of an annual exhibition. The examples of art and craftsmanship on view in Messrs Carter and Son's assembly room, Bridge-street, on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of this week were almost entirely contributed by local ladies and gentlemen. While the collection was not as varied in character as one might have wished—water colour paintings greatly predominated—there was much to indicate pain-- taking work, as well as undoubted talent, and the visitor could not fad to be favourably impressed. Six water colour pictures by Mr Oswald Garside, who has gained fame as an Academy exhibitor. and is doing roue's to maintain the old' traditions of the town in the realm of art, stood in a class by themselves. Mr Garside's sub- jects were all local, and one or two of them have pretensions to be regarded as beauty spots, but Mr Garside also enables us to see unsuspected charms in the commonplase. Perhaps his most affective picture was a view of Fiddler's Ferry, embracing the inn in the foreground, the sluggish water of the Mersey on which lazily floated one or two small craft, and a background of Halton Castle and the Cheshire hills. Mr Garside also showed a fine view from the west, of Winwick Church, characterised by bold outline and exquisite detail. Howley Lock presented an aspect of solitude, but there was the reminder of the ever- present industrialism in the shape of one of the mills which stands on the Mersey bank. Acker's-lane, Steckton Heath. was reproduced as it appears in the depth of an old-fashioned winter, a rsonderfully vivid touch being imparted by the shaft of light streaming on to the snow from the open door of a cottat,e. The old river led at Wilderspool and Dobby's lock, Latch- ford, were works of distinct beauty and merit. Special attention was also attracted by some typical Venetian and Chinese scenes and the entrance to a mosque at Smyrna, pointed in water colours by Mr V Rappini (London). The colours had a freshness and brightnees which harmonise well in subjects of this class, and the subtler atmospheric. effects were also successfully realized. Miss G Ridgway showed three portrait sketches and some original and creditable pieces of work under the the titles "Apple blossom," " Winter time," " The moat, Lyrnm Hall," and " Cock pits, Lymm Hail." Mr W N Hutchings had six rather striking paintings; including Helsby Hill and Arley Pool. Mr F J Barnish is to be complimented on ten fine architectural studies which called forth general admiration. The water colour "Early morning, Kinsale Harboour," by Miss Rose H Dakiu was of outstanding interest, the grey sky being repre- sented in a realistic, truly natural style which is FO seldom attained. The same exhibitor had also a portrait in oils of Mr. Alfi ed Dakin. One of the gems of the whole exhibition was Mr H. Woodier's " Wind and rain," a study of wild desolation very cleverly worked out, end he also showed an almost equally effective winter scene. Mr Arthur Hayward, a young artist (formerly of the Warrington Schcol of Art) sent several works which bear the mark of disiinct promise. They included "Low Tide," "Evening " "Summer Moon " and several examples of decorative art. Miss Cue stance 11. Broad- bent, whrse interest in the exhibition is beyond all praise, exhibited twelve water colour views, chiefly of places included in her recent visit to India, and the brilliance of Oriental colouring was finely reproduced. The scenes at Grappenhall and Latchford would, in our view, have gained in impressiveness by more delicate treatment. Miss Waring showed attractive studies of beauty spots on the Riviera. Mrs. Gerttude Pidduck had paintings of quaint places in Cornwall, but their peculiarly dull, greyish tints were not altogether satisfying. Mr D C Leigh sent an admirable series of black and white sketches and also a street scene in Rouen in water colours. In the crafts section, which was not so well filled as might have been expected, were beautiful spechiens of the products of native Indian industries lent by Miss Broadbent who also exhibited a lovely embroidered panel, designed and worked by herself. Other attractive features were :—Artistic candle shades by Miss Ridgway ; letter case in leather by Miss G Ryland@ ; paper knife in. hollywood and zy. lonite, brass belt buckle and specimens of wood- carving by Mr T Broadbent; needlework and embroidery by Miss Rylands (Massey Hall) and Mrs Broadbent; medallion by Miss Dakin. There was a good attendance at the opening of the exhibition by Mrs Edelsten on Tuesday afternoon. Miss BROADBENT presided and pointed out that nearly all the exhibitors were local ladies and gentle- men. She had no need to mention Mr Oswald Garside, whose beautiful work was known to them all, but she would call attention to the youngest exhibitor (Mr Arthur Haywatd), whose work sire considered was clever and original. She bed written to one well-known artist to try and enlist his sympatny and interest, but he had replied that he had severed his connection with Warrington. He had no pleasant memories of the place, and he understood that art was quite extinct there. However' he was glad to hear that there was still a flicker. Miss Broadtent urged that they should try to fan that flicker into a steady flame and do their utmost to keep up the best traditions of the town. Mrs EDLESTEN said she was sadly aware that she had not accomplished anything in the realm of art to justify her selection to open the exhibition, The extent of her technical skill was perhaps the ability to diaw a pig with her eyes shut. !Laughter.) But fortunately art required a public, not necessatily gifted with the power of expression, but possessing the seeing eye and the appreciative mind. Those who were gathered together that day, whether they had the gift 01 execution or not were united in their love for the beautiful. (Elear,hear.) They could not all be artists,but they could all cultivate the appreciation of beauty and to see the beauty of any- thing they must look at it and notice it. Most of them would remember the fascinating little story in "Even- ing's At Home" of "Eyes and no Eyes"—the two boys who went fur the same walk; one found it so extremely dull and monotonous, while to the other it was full of beauty and interest. The bird in the hedge, the wild flower on the common, the curious stone lathe quarry— all these were lost upon the boy with no eyes. There was no doubt that the true artist saw what was hidden from the ordinary mortal and he set it forth in colour and in form, and said to the ordinary mortal "Now look" and he looked and saw this time, because his attention had been drawn to it. It was wonderful how a good sketch of anything sent one back to the reality itself with a new appreciation of it. To those who had the great advantage of living in the country, Nature presented at all seasons of the year endless wide studies and slight sketches. But even those who saw those beautiful but familiar objects every day did not always appreciate their charms. She had met people who did not know one tree from another, and that not only in winter but when they were clothed in their infinite variety of leaves. Anyone so unobservant missed a very great deal of the beauty of the world and then there stepped in the artist, lending his mind out, and opened our eyes for us. If in the country art was desirable and educative, how much more in the town—in a town like Warrington dear old smoky Warrington. We did get Turneresque effects eometimes of smoke rolling across a sunset sky —she had seen very beautiful ones often 'near Bank Quay Station—but as arule there was not much that the eye rested on with pleasure in the "long unlovely streets." She did not forget that the Beautiful War- rington Society was trying to remedy this and that many were earnestly labouring for the adornment of the town. The work exhibited in that room embodied the yearning of Warrington's sons and daughters for the beautiful She felt sure that they would not find on those walls any of those extraordinary pictures resembling jigsaw puzzles -(laughter) -which they could only painfully, partially elucidate with the aid of a catalogue, where " Afternoon tea in the garden might equally well be a " Sketch in the Balkans " oounr nt hge t 0t o 0i 10ent v etraabel ew—i with a tat ng 60 rt, eh re)r—a rap leaarrleyd. (Laughter)—or where a lady who had unfortunately left htoe rb et eeantduerae vs rme em shouldbe bees seasy. handicapped ghoul-like apparition. (Laughter.) One i true artistnsrros amongi es. D e theyool erne wondered what Ruskin would have said to those iknagletihdaot the ee mo general commanding his troops, not an old lady carried off her feet by the mob ? There was one axiom of the great master which they might do well to remember, as they gazed on these problem pictures, and that was " Never force yourself to admire anything when you are not in the humour."But she was sure that afternoon they were in the humour to admire, to praise and to appreciate. The exhibitors were their own fellow townsmen and women. Many of their names were "familiar in our mouths as household words."Thev were proud of them. They thanked them for the pleasure e and the education that they would give thern,and it wr a with a profound sense of he privilege which had been conferred upon her that she wished that exhibition every success. (Applause). Canon STEVENSON, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs Edelsten, said be was glad to hear that there we re not in the exhibition any of those particular eflortsof art to which Mrs Edelsten had referred and which we generally known by the name of " post impressioniseti," though what that phrase meant he had no idea. retic;y

div.head: St John's Presbyterian Guild.
div.p: St John's Presbyterian Guild.

The above Society met on Monday evening, Mr R Nlungall, presiding. The paper for the evening was " Missions to Ancient Civilizations" by Mr Robinson. Dealing principally with China, the speaker sketched out the conditions of the people under Confucianism and Buddhism and spoke in nigh terms of the work done by missionaries in the foreign field, in enriching the lives and bettering the conditions of the natives generally. There was a good discussion and the ques- tion of Foreign Missions from many points of view added interest to the evening.

Church Lads' Brigade. The" coming of age " of the Warrington battalion of the Church Lads' Brigade was celebrated on Sunday afterno.n by a special service at St Paul's Church. Under the command of Colonel Appleton, the battalion fell in near the Cannons at Arpley, and marched to the Town Hall via Bridge-street, Rylands-street, and Winmarleigh-street. They were to have been joined by the Mayor, but he was unavoidably absent, and his place was taken by Alderman Smethurst. They tben marched to St Paul's Church via Sankey-street, Horse- ma,ket-street and Bewsey-street. The clergy present at the service in addition to the Vicar and the Rev E E Peters, were the Revs Canon Willis, O C Briggs, J Collins and T Vickers. The special preacher was the Rev. F. F. Komlosy, of Newton-le-Willows, mho took for his text the words " A good soldier of Jesus Christ." He urged them to interpret the letters C.L.B. as meaning qualities that were dear to them all—cleanliress, loyalty and bravery., On assembling outside the Church, Alderman Smethurst presented to Lance-Corporal Unsworth a watch and chain, kindly given by Mr. Henry Ashton, a good friend of the U.L.8., for the smartest lad on parade at one of the weekly drills a week previous.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S A. Society.

A successful meeting on Sunday was presided over by Mr J Himsworth, who spoke upon "Seeing Visions.' Rev T T James M.A. of Sheffield. gave the address, his subject being "Bit of blue." We had all sorts of men around us, some who could more readily see the cloud and gloom than the beautiful blue sky. Some said the days past were better than the present. But when history was carefully looked at it would convince us , that the present was an improvement on previous generations 100 years ago. Children had to rise early and work eight hours per day. At that time they were taken by their parents to see public executions. Then long terms of imprisonment were inflicted for compara- tively small debts. These methods did not exist now, child life was protected and there WBS more humane punishment for miner offences. Let the blue or bright side of our naturo have its perfect work and our own lives would be made brighter, and other lives cheered and helped. Let us get our inspiration from the great bright side giver, ever trying to take sunshine where-I ever we went. Mr William Booth sang in his usua effective style" Sun of my soul," Mr Payton presided at the organ, Mr C Cotton read the lesson and Mr Hirusvvorth led the prayer. Three new members received a hearty welcome.

div.head: Rev. T. T. James at Wycliffe Congregational Church. _ ._ _ _
div.p: The Rev. T. T. James at Wycliffe Congregational Church. _ ._ _ _

The Rev T T—Ja—mes, M A., of Wycliffe Chapel, Sheffield, again occupied the pulpit at Wycliffe Congre- ptional Church on hunday, and aiso visited the Sunday School and the P.S.A. in the afternoon, delivering short addresses at each. Speaking specially to the children at the forenoon service be told the fairy story of the fir tree, and drew the least's that none were of too small account to do some good to those around. "Unite my heart to fear Thy name " (Psalms lxxs., 11) were the words chosen for the morning discourse. Referring to the interpretation which was some- times put upon the word fears he said they must not attach the idea of fright, horror or dread, for no one who had seen tbe light and knowledge of the glory of God in Jesus Christ could imagine God as being of such a nature as to make him horrified or terror-stricken by His presence. God was a being whose companionship and friendship and counsel were open to everyone. It was true He saw our sins and punished us, but the punishment of God was the fruit of His changeless love to purge our hearts and make us clean. The text was a petitiop of the Psalmist that he was ready to allow God to claim the whole of his life, and the preacher urged his hearers to consecrate their lives to God's will and purpose in all the activities of life.

Preaching to a large congregation at night on the words" There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water," he sai4 the incident was one of the most familiar of the Bible stories. Christ recognised that body and soul acted and re-acted on one another. The shame of the great cry and bcrden of poverty in our midst was not that it robbed man of the bread which periebeth but that it robbed him of the bread of life itself. Christ put upun each individual soul an infinite value cf eternal worth. We had to recover that belief and make it our own. It was difficult in an age when we thought in the mass to believe that not only had each individual something to do with the inspiration of a better future that was to be, but that every unit and every individual in the process had a definite and eternal value that could not disappear. Only in that faith could the gospel bring enthusiasm that lasted and endured. That had been the secret through all the story of the Gospel's history and it was this belief in the eternal value of the indi- vidual soul which had inspired many men to make great sacrifices. Mr W Booth sang as a solo" Sun of my soul."

div.p: " SANKEY-STREET PARADING A DISGRACE."

" Home making is the woman's privilege" said Miss Florence Edmill (organising secretary for higher , education for Stretford), in an address to the girls of Fairfield and Trinity Branch Technical Schools at the annual distribution of prizes and certificates at the Gymnasium on Wednesday evening. In a practical and homely address Miqs Edgill urged the girls not to be carried away by the craze for amusements but to equip themselves with all the details of domestic training so that their homes might be pleasant places to dwell in. Mrs C Jackson Holmes (a member of the Warrington Education Committee) presided, and amongst others present were :—Mr and Mrs Holman Kingdon, Miss Bibby (superintendent of Trinity school), Miss Ewatt (superintendent of Fairfield school), Mr J Moore Murray (director of education), and Mr R B Roberts (assistant overseer).

Mrs. HOLMES impressed upon the girls to show their appreciation of all the advantages they enjoyed nowadays, by obtaining leave of their parents to carry out in a practical way the course of household lessons they had been receiving. If they were granted leave to undertake to provide and prepare the daily meals for their parents, they would be fitting themselves, in a proper way, for their own future in life, for depend upon it, there would be a great deal of domestic work wanted from each of them sooner or later, if they were to have ham)/ and well-ordered homes, in whatever station of life they might be placed. Of course, those remarks included the weekly washing aud sewing. Let each girl take a pride in being able to do things well, in living a noble life,and in being a practical example of all that was lovely and well-ordered in life. (Applause). Miss EDGILL assured the girls of her intense interest in the career of all girls—no matter how or where situated. They had left their childhood behind. Their minds had been carefully cultivated and tended by their parents and teachers—just as a garden needed caring for if good results were wanted. Much preparation was necessary for the seeds of knowledge which were planted day by day until the time came when they left the day school. Then, in her opinion, their real education began. (Hear, hear.) Like the leaves, they were • just beginning to unfold. They bad just arrived at a stage when they might be interested in something, and, unless they at once continued the good work com- menced in the day school, they were turned out into the world with unripe judgment, unreal views of life, insufficient knowledge, and their brain, which had only begun to bud, would slowly wither, or narrow, or become a blank. " All this,' continued Miss Edgill "sounds rather awful, but it is absolutely true that if you do not go forward you are bound to go bsckward, None of you want this to happen ; rather I feel sure do you desire to make good use of the faculties with which ou have been endowed and to derive the greatest possible benefit from the advantages by which you are sorrounded. Very great care and thought have been exercised by the committee and their director in providing facilities for your further education. Good schools—well equipped for the work which has to be done—capable, earnest,enthusiastic teachers, thoroughly qualified to give tbe required instructiou,and more than that, ready, I feel sure to help and advise if only you will take your difficulties to them. Some of you will, I know. have difficulties to overcome in order to attend regularly an punctually. Personally I have a great admiration for the girls who, after a hard day's work, turn into school two or three even- ings a week instead of

LOITERING ABOUT THE STREET or going to some place of entertainment night after night. Such girls must be possessed of strong will and sound judgmen t and are worthy of all praise.(Applause.) I am not suggesting for one moment that recreation and healthy amusements are to be ruled out of the programme. As a matter of fact, something of the kind is practically essential to the complete life, but dont overdo it girls; that is where the mischief comes in,and above all, do not get into the habit of being unable to spend a.quiet evening happily at home." (Applause) Continuing she said she eas not going to presume to advise them as to the course of their studies: those who understood t heir ciromaistances and their needs were always at hand to give them helpful advice. If they had to turn out into the world as wage earners they would naturally feel the need of fitting themselves for whatever branch of work they decided to undertake. They called that the bread and butter side of education —very necessary, though apt to get a bit wearisome at times. Apart from the monetary value of their increas- ing knowledge, however, she was firmly convinced that the cultivation of their minds would make their hearts more tender and a woman's heart ought to be tender, "Do not be selfish in your studies," Miss Edgill went on "but learn all you possibly can, so that not only will you be able honourably to make your own may in the world if necessary but that you may have the power, as far as in you lies, to help others, to thoroughly under- stand the world you live in, to broaden your minds, enlarge your sympathies, and brighten your outlook upon life, and so become a credit to your sex and a valuable member ef the community. Is this ton much to ask, girls? It won't come all at once you know, but you are none of you too young to make a start, and we only have to live one moment at a time. You must remember that the girls of the present are the women of the future—physical fitness and moral character are essential considerations and there is an obvious duty before every one of you. You ought to know what is in you, what you can do,

and care for, what you are lit for. Therefore, girls, Ca refully consider these points and prepare yourselves for the future, for, married or single, every woman can and ought to be a home maker. You cannot attach too much importance to this. DOME MAKING in the true sense of the word is the woman's privilege a wonderful privilege, and we are none of us so for- bearing, Po gentle, so kind, so altoget her attractive that we can afford to neglect the practical ways and means of getting on comfortably and well with one another. You know quite well how much more respect you have for the woman who keeps herseli neat and clear) than for the one who is always slovenly and dirty. you are much more comfortable in a tidy room than art untidy one. A well-cooked meal, however simpler tastefully served, is much more nourishing and appetis- ing than badly cooked food put on the table anyhow s and a happy, sunshiny face with manners to match is' much pleasanter to go home to than a woebegone countenance and nagging ways. Therefore it behoves us to equip ourselves very thoroughly with all the details of domestic training so that our homes may be very pleasant places to dwell in, and that we ourselves may find pleasure and happiness in the work involved. (Applause.) So I sun going to put in a special plea for your attendance at the domestic classes. I have not said all this to you, girls, without thought and experience behind the thought. For nearly twenty years I have been working amongst the girls and boys in the evening schools, an I claim to know something of their little ways and big difficulties, and I tell you girls that you have a tremendous power for good if only yon will exercise the will. Set up. high standard and live up to it. Boys as well as girls will follow ; they don't like being left behind. So long as you are without a definite aim as to what you are going to attempt in life, so long must the rest beginning of your career be postporied, and some people put this decision off for so long that they have not left themselves time to gain even a small prize. Now all this means work, but the meaning of life 19 work, and our share is just a humble detail of the gl'ea Plan. If undertake,. in the right spirit, such work brings joy and the duty of service, in which I have a firm faith, whether in the schoolroom, the workroom, the office or the home, can be sanctified by knowledge. Therefore, girls, again I beg of you to lose no opportunity ef making yourselves of real value in the world and of living up to the highest ideals of womanhood:, (Applause.) I Mr HOLMAN ICINGDON, in proposing a vote of tharike I to Mrs Holmes and Miss Edgill, said the students must I bear in mind that all the knowledge and education theY got at school was to fit therm for a better life after- I wards. People very often failed to draw a clear dis- tinction between knowledge and education. Knowledge consisted largely in having a mass of facts at their disposal, but that was not education. Education we° knowing where to find the knowledge and how to apply, it when they had acquired it. Mr J MOORE MURRAY seconded. Ho Rpponled to the parents to give their daughters a chance of arPlYing the domestio knowledge gained at the school by allow- ing them to cook meals end to assist in the mending and other household duties. Then they would have at?. idea of what they were able to do and—wha:: was more important—the girls would he preparin& themselves for the time, which would come perhaPS sooner than the parents thought, when they would ba.v.e, to use their knowledge in homes of their own. NV" regard to over-doing pleasure, he did not wish tao lecture the girls but he would make an appeal to the on one point The state of SANKEY-STREET ON SUNDAY NIGHT was a digrace to Warrington—and that disgrace so; caused mostly by young people under the age ), twenty, who aimlessly paraded backwards and forwarfo; jostling each other. There was no real fun or pleas' a in such conduct. They were doing themselves no gd and the time would come when they would regret How much better would it be on da-k nights to sPe. their time in the companionship of good books, to _ learning something of the world outside their trto' homes. instead of aimless wandering which often lea something worse. also. The vote was heartily passed and each lady syss the recipient of a handsome bouquet.

div.head: NOTES BY " MUST."
div.p: NOTES BY " MUST."

The Warrington men have been having a quiet time, Witt' the last two Saturday matches postponed through Lancashire and Yorkshire cup ties, and they should return to the fray to-day with eagerness. Their opponents will be Wakefield Trinity—the first visitors of the season from the broad-acred county. Wakefield have always given the Wirepullers a good game, and will probably prove a tough proposition to-day .Last season they were not in Warrington's League fixture list, but the two teams met in the N.U. Cup, and Trinity had the honour of giving the Wirepullers their quietus after playing six matches in three rounds. At Warrington the score was a try each— Trinity equa ising in the last minute, and at Belle Vue the Wirepullers went down 10-5.

Wakefield are still one of Yorkshire's best teams, and in the League they are treading on the heels of the leaders. Their record is better than Warrington's but for all that I expect the Wirepullers to win. The •on'y weak spot which causes anxiety is forward where Warringt n are rather light to tackle Yorkshire scrummagers. But if they will pack and heel like they did in the second half at St. Helens there should be no doubt of the result. Warrington have a some- what damaged home record to repair.

The Warrington team will be :—Jolley, full back ; Brooks, Dickenson, Tranter and Mclntyre, three- quarters ; Rushton and Nicholas, half backs; G Thomas, It Thomas, Cheaters, Fearnley, Skelhorn and Cox, forwards.

Renw ick has resumed training and hopes to turn out in the match of the season next Saturday, when the undefeated Huddersfield team are due at Wilderspool By the way, the Warrington men are now training two nights a week—Tuesday and 'Thursday.

During the week Warrington have signed on J Manchester, a wing three-quarter from Sr. Helens aged 19, and brother to the ct. Helens forward. Young Manchester was anxious for a trial with the Wirepullers and will shortly turn out for the "A " team.

The Wakefield team has been selected 118 follows: Laud, full back ; Goodison, Lynch, Poynton and Quarinby, tdree-quarters ; Newbould and Slater, half- backs; Walton, Burton, Kershaw, Taylor, Beattie and 'Crossland, forwards.

This week the "A " team has an open date. Last Saturday they broke their poor combination record at tome by trouncing the smart Wigan Highfielders. When the latter were two tries up in the first ten minutes, the match looked like proving another local -fiasco. But Dickenson was in the side and he pulled the men together in such effective style that by half time they had taken the lead by 10-6. Thereafter, they played brilliant football and won by the big score of 6 goals, 7 tries, 33 points to 6 points. Highfield were a man short most of the second half but they were a beaten team before the mishap.

I doubt whether the result would have been the earn° but for Dickenson's inspiring leadership and fine football. George is a flower of the ever- lasting type, and is qualifying for a bumper benefit later in the season. But the "A " team lads showed that they could play football. If the forwards 'would always perform as manfully, and the backs stick to the passing game as they did on Saturday, they would need a lot of beating. Young Alec Brown played a great game at scrummage half, and should develop into a class player before many months go by. On the right wing Davies played an excellent trial game, and would have been among the scorers, but for Jordan's propensity to wander towards the centre. div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION N.A. CENTRE.

Owing to it being the last week-end for weighing in en Saturday, Sunday last saw mt,,e members venture out than usual. But they made no headway with the SPecimen list, the general opinion being "off feed," although the local rods were well prepared with all Classes of bait—worm, maggot, feeders, bread, paste,and even stone, stick and gravel baits. The fish were ruasters of the situation and beyond one or two members taking a decent fry nothing of any consequence was done, the hest being a gudgeon of loz 12drs, caught by tr C Ashton. As all weights finish being registered for 1912 with the end of the month, next week we hope to print all the winners of set prizes and specials. Norton was tried by four or five locals, but nothing Vas caught beyond one or two small ones. Now those Who have registered fish from here for specials can rest content. Although the cornpetion has been keen, it has teen fairly open all the season. The Gowy was visited but here again tbe fish beat the angler, but this is the great facination of this stream as it is the most difficult water round Warring- Ofl anglers have to be above the average to fish it. vTa have known local anglers to go week after week Without returning with a scale and then bring off their -greatest catch, so the novice who fails at this water need not despair. Some of our oldest members admit that they even yet have a deal to learn when fishing the Gowy. Chester was also visited, but as DO reports are to oßud we take it there was not much done. Long Barn had a few shop men on Thursday after- noon and the best from here were four roach,the largest "Sing about 3,10z5. tr"o glancing over the weighing in board one notes that the records fall below last season's with the ‘"oeption of roach and perch. The other winners are the Poorest lot for several years. , The Northern Anglers' general meeting takes place -to-day and the report will appear in next week's issue. A.S.

div.head: RUNCORN OUTCLASSED AT WIGAN.
div.p: RUNCORN OUTCLASSED AT WIGAN.

Dest;iielit-e-fe:a that the Wigan team was not it full strength, the Runcorn representatives were outclassed at Central Park, where about 8,000 persons assembled. The disparity was more observable in the latter stages, when the Wiganers amassed a substantial number of points, and repeatedly penetrated the defence by exceeding clever play. Bradley, who was prominent throughout the encounter, opened the scoring, and prior to the interval Ramsdale and Seeling also regis- tered tries, two of the goal kicks, taken by Francis, being successful. As the only response was a gos.l from a penalty kick by Richardson, Runcorn were in arrears at the interval by 13 points to 2. Immediately after the resumption, Walford crossed the visitors' line, and then Richardson garnered Runcorn's remaining points, again as the result of a goal from a penalty. Wigan, however, forged ahead, Carwen adding three tries, Bradley two, and Coldrick and Silcock one each,Francis lauding a couple of altditional goals. Result :—Wigan 4 goals and 11 tries (41 points), Runcorn 2 goals (4 points). ST. HELENS' FINE FINISH AGAINST THE

div.head: RANGERS.
div.p: RANGERS.

This league game attract'eT;Crowd of 8,000 specta- tors to the St Helens' ground. In the opening half the Broughton backs passed and Craven crossed, Davidson failing. Continuing to be aggressors' Barnes picked up in front of the St. Helens' posts and dropped a goal. Shortly afterwards Barton broke away, and kicking past Danson enabled Manchester to score, Turtill improving. Immediately upon resuming the Broughton forwards burst away and Roberts scored for Barlow to goal. Changing ends St Helens were penalised, and Davidson put on a goal for Broughton, who were all over the home team until the last ten minutes, of the game, whoa they foolishly adopted defensive tactics, which suited the " Saints" and enabled the diminutive Richardson to run over twice in succession, Barton and Latin. improving his tries. In the last minute of the game Greenwood forced his way over the line for 'rurtill to improve. Result :—St Helens. 4 goals 4 tries (20 points), Broughton Rangers, 3 goal 2 tries (12 points). .L.AIJ.i.Y'S BENEFIT—WIDNES BEAT LEIGH.

At Widnes, before 2,000 spectators. The match was Bet apart for the benefit of Lally, who nits been a member of the Widnes team for ckse on a dozen years. In the first half Higgins crossed the line following a cross-kick by Redmond. Weak play on the part of Keegan and Roberts let in S Aspey, and a very bad mull by Davies enabled Reid to score a third try. Some clever passing early in the second portion ended in Redmond scoring a try, which Dainteth improved. A fine dribble by Taylor ended in a fifth try, and then Moon scored under the post from a pass by Dainteth. Both were improved. ln the last minute Cartwright scored an unimproved try for Leigh. Result:—Widnes 3 goals 6 tries (24 points), Leigh 1 try (3 points). Teams and officials :
_ Widnes—Jones, back ; Redmond, Lally, Taylor, and Hainteth, three-quarter backs ; aloon and J O'Garra half backs ; G Aspey, S Aspey, Lloyd, Reid, H O'Garra, forwards.

Leigh—Davies, back ; Keegan, Roberts, T Johnson, and S Johnson, three-quarter backs ; Yates and Cain, half backs; Woods, Lowe, Lee, Barton, Cartwright, and Marsh, forwards. Referee, A Hestford, Broughton. Touch judges, A Cross, St Helens, and W 0 Johnson, Salford.

div.head: COMBINATION.
div.p: THE COMBINATION.

WARRINGTON "A " V. WIGAN HI Girl lELD.—The smart Wigan Hightleld team were the visitors to Warrington on Saturday, a crowd of over 3,000 assembling. The visitors started in brilliant style, and in the first ten minutes Land and Hart scored tries on either wing. No goals were kicked. The Warring- ton men then rallied and after a powerful run by Dickenson, Clare raced round the posts for Critchley to improve. The home forwards showed any amount of dash and kept in the Highfisld quarter. Brown broke away cleverly and after passing and repassing with Davies he scored a smart try, which Critchley again converted. Half-time: Warringtn " A," 10 points : Wigan Hightleld, 6 points. Early in the second half, Atherton, one of the Highfield halves, was hurt and had to retire from the game. The locals were now playing brilliant football, and fine combination resulted in Dickenson twice racing through the defence. Before the close, Arnold, Gibbs, and I-Termer all scored, and Critchley kicked four goals. Final : Warrington, 6 goals, 7 tries (33 points) ; Wigan Highileld, 2 tries (six points).
FRIENDLY MATCHES. RY LANDS' RECS v. DITION RECS.

Ryland& journeyed to Ditton with a weak team on Saturday, but had no difficulty in securing a victory. The visitors, although & man short, did most of the pressing in the Brat half, and from a pass by Potter, Griffiths scored, Leah kicking the goal. Half-time arrived with the score five points in favour of the visitors. The second half provided a bustling game with the forwards, neither side being able to score, the game ending in a victory for Rylancts' by five points to nil.

BROADHEATII V. LYMM.

At Navigatio;;;O;cl,—Ait-rln-cl;a-m--, 'o-ri—aturday. After fast play J Pearson opened the score for the home team. Aroused by this reverse, Lymm opened out the game and commendable efforts were made by Barber, Owen and Leigh. Hinde at fullback for Lymm repeatedly pulled up the home forwards. Broadheath were penal- ised and Owen scored a goal. Half-time :One goal each. On resuming good work by Clare (left-half) for Lymm gave Barber an opportunity. He got away in capital style and transferred to Leigh at the right moment for the latter to score a capital goal. Pearson being help- less to save. At the other end Peacock just put over the bar, whilst Walker missed a fine opportunity of equalizing through rashness. In the closing stages Broadheath fought desperately to get on an equal foot- ing, but made the mistake of playing too close a game. A well-fought game ended with the score Lymm, two goals ; Broadheath,

OUGHTRINOTON AMATEURS V. BARTON VILLA. At Ileatley on Saturday. At the end of 10 minutes Gresty opened the score for the Amateurs. Pardoe brought off many fine saves in the visitors' goal and was ably assisted by his backs. Half-time: Oughtrington Amateurs, one; Barnton Villa none. In the second half, Barnton were quickly away and within five minutes Alcock equalised the scores, whilst within a minute or two Bert Leicester gave them the lead. Encouraged by their success the Barnton for- wards played brilliantly and were continually harassing the home defence Lees, the visiting centre-forward, in addition to keeping the forwards going in capital style, performed the hat ttick before the close of the game. As the homesters could only reply once in this half (Gr. stv), they were easily defeated with the score —Barnton Villa, five ; Oughtrington Amateurs, two.
WIDNES AND DISTRICT ALLIANCE. WIDNES ATHLETIC V GREAT SANKEY.

These teams met, with unbroken records, at Widnes on Saturday. The locals took up the running after the home goal had experienced a narrow escape. The Athletic forced a corner, which ended disae,rously. The ball was not fully cleared and P Walton lying well up scored their first goal. Haying gained the lead the locals pr?ssed strongly; and A Brown scored a second from a melee in the goalmoutft. Sankey, however, made ground on the right, and T Cook had a fast drive charged down. Although in arrears the visitors played up in the pluckiest fashion and E Forster had hard lines with a shot which just passed outside. A penalty was awarded to the Athletic, from which J Hayes scored with a fast low shot. Interval : Widnes Athletic 3, Great Sankey O. Resuming, the visitors were the first to get away, but could not adapt them- selves to the narrow ground. The Athletic forced two corners, which were cleared. Sankey pressed continu- ally, only to be repulsed by the home defence. T Cook was robbed as he was about to shoot, and T Whitfield just missed from a free kick for hands. In the last ten minutes it was miraculous how the home goal escaped downfall. Result : Widnes Athletic 3, Great Sankey,O. MOBBERLEY V. OUGHTRINGTON PARK. At Mobberley, on Saturday. div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

SANKEY LADIES v. LYMM ROYAL LADIES. Played at sankey on Saturday. The home team showed good Orrin on the attack from the start, and were leading 3-0 at half time. In the second half Sankey continued to overplay the visitors ,:nd added two more goals before the game was abandoned 17 minutes from" time " owing to an injury to one of the Lymm ladies. The scorers for Sankey were Miss Davenport (2) and Miss Dodds (3.) Final : Sankey 5 goals; Lymm nil.
MIXED HOCKEY MATCH. CROSFIELD'S v. MISS BROADBENT'S XI

The match was played OD Crosfield's ground last Saturday in dull weather. For the firs t ten minutes Miss Broadbent's eleven pressed without result, then Crosfields assumed the offensive and scored two goals in rapid succession, the result of splendid shots by Lythgoe and Dickson, after some good dribbling. The game now became very even, attacks being made on each goal. Half-time arrived however without further score.On resuming Crosfields again took up the offensive and made repeated incursions into their opponents terri- tory. Bloomer scored three goals during these attacks, assisted by some excellent work by the home forwards. Miss Broadbent's eleven made futile attempts to wipe out some of the deficit, but Crosfield's defence proved most reliable. The last goal was an excellent one, scored by Miss Jackson, and the whistle sounded for time with the score of C nil in favour of Crosfields. The great feature of the game was the brilliant goal keeping by Mellor of Crosfields. He made some splendid saves and proved a veritable tower of strength. Miss Broadbent also played a clever game and was one of the hardest workers on the field. The play on the whole was much more even than the score suggests. Crosfields, however, seized their oppor- tunities, and scored when possible. A return match has been arranged to be played later in the season. 1 Crosfields are at home to-day to Heaton Park. The team is as follows :—Goal, A Mellor ; backs, H Ranch E Paget ; halfs, J Evans, J H Harrison, A flodson ; forwards, A B Lythgoe, T A Dean, A C Bloomer, B T Dickson, W Heywood. LATCHFORD v. ALDERLEY EDGE. The First Eleven were defeated at Alderley Edge by 3-0 after a great game. They had to play up the slope to begin with, and although doing a good amount of attacking failed to score. Alderley scored through F Tvveedale. Wright stopped several nasty shots also. The Latchford inside left was then accidentally injured and practically took no further part in the game. On changing round the visitors with the advantage of the slope kept up a continuous attack on the home goal. The midfield play of all the team was the best seen this season but the forwards, notable Travis and Pearson, had the hardest possikle luck in not scoring. Alderley scored a goal just on time. The game was a very fast one. For Latchford Knight played a superb game at left half and was the best half on the field. He had to mark Twesdale who is a slippery customer. Isherwood and Fletcher also did very well against Armstrong, the Cheshire outside left, who, with F Platt, makes a formidable wing. The Second team beat Alderley Edge "A" by 6-2. The play in the opening half was pretty even but Alderley were behind in the scoring at half time and were kept on the defensive for a big part of the game afterwards. The Alderley fullbacks, goal-keeper and centre-half had a warm time of it but they played very steadily and were the best of the side, the forwards being overplayed by the Latchford halves. The Latch- ford forwards played with delightful vim and were dangerous near goal. Minards signalised his reappear- ance by scoring three times and Marsden on his second game for the club also scored three goals and should be a decided acquisition. Eccles played another sound game at right back and was backed up strongly by Binhl and Dixon.

div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
(By PEDo.)

D N Gaussen, a freshman, running at Oxford for the University against Highgate Harriers covered the 7 miles 600 yards course in 40min. 3 4-5 secs, the previous being 40min. 14secs by C 13:Porter. Result of the team rare Oxferd : 1,4, 5,7, 9-26 points ; Highgate : 2, 6,8,10-29. NVarrington A.C. decided the third test of their points competition over a 54 miles course and Vose dominated the position throughout. Result: C Vose 10, A Cresson 9, J Nurse 8, F Sbadwell 7, 'W Walters 6, Hanson, 5,1 Watson 4, T Turton 3, N Stafford 2, S Siddall 1 ; G Wak, field end J Hayes just missed getting in the count and H Woods, F Price, F Colbourne and J Sankey were close up. H Holbrook, F Antrobus and W Bolton were included in the field of 23 but they preferred to take matters easily until they are fitter. The novices shewed good form in maintaining a sub- stantial measure of Improvement.

div.head: ST! HELENS- LEAGUE AT RUNCORN. . _ .
div.p: ST! HELENS- LEAGUE AT RUNCORN. . _ .

Nearly, 1,000 spectators witnessed a race between about 100 runners from the Tally Ho club's head- quarters at the Pleasure Grounds, Runcorn Hill. A good trail was laid through the Park, over a distance of about 71 miles, and although Sutton were an easy first for team honours many thrilling finishes were seen. J smart (Sutton) end W Wharton (ktavenhead) fought a great finish in which the former just won, and a similar tussle between A Ferrell (Runcorn) and E Harrison (Sutton) resulted in favour of the local man. E Barnes and J Gavaghan ;both of Sacred Heart) had a friendly set to before the Sutton pack hrrived with two locals 'in hot pursuit. Mr Shaw sen. acted as starter and it is safe to assume that greater interest will now be taken in the doings of the Runcorn Tally Ho. Result : 1, Sutton (J Smart 1, E Harrison 4, W Burrows J Morris 8, L Tearle 9, D Brown 10), 39 points ; 2 gacred Heart. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY NOVEMBER 30, 1912.

The negotiations MR LLOYD between the Chancellor GEORGE AND THE of the Exchequer and DOCTORS. the representatives of the British Medical Association are still proceeding. There is reason to believe that they will be brought to a satisfactory conclusion, though not without a most vexatious and inconvenient delay. If Mr Lloyd George were in as peremptory a mood as the doctors' repre- sentatives, all further negotiation would come speedily to an end. Fortunately he is a man of extraordinary patience, and with a strong desire to find a satisfactory and, as nearly as possible, a permanent solution of a problem of great gravity which has been complicated in what we cannot help believ- ing to be a most unworthy manner by political considerations. The British Medical Association seems to have sent its repre- sentatives to the Treasury not to make an amicabl arrangement, but to put forward further demands, which, even if they were accepted, could not be voted upon by the medical profession by the time at which the Insurance Act comes into operation. The Chancellor of the Exchequer must feel that a pistol is being held at his head. The Insurance Act presents the bulk of the medical men of the country with a great opportunity of making a really vast improvement in their position, and they are making the most of it, suffering themselves to be led, not by those who are most interested in a favourable and speedy settlement, but in the main by men whose Practice will not be affected by the Insurance Act one way or another. Dr Esmond, M.P., who is taking a sort of Plebiscite on his own account, has earnestly asked the profession not to let itself be influ- enced by personal and political consider- ations. There is reason to believe that this appeal would be responded to readily enough but for the impracticable attitude taken up by the doctors' trade union. So far as present indications go, quite as many . medical men as are necessary to the efficient , 'working of the Insurance Act would accept 'lr Lloyd George's terms if they were free to make their own choice in the matter Indeed, the situation is one that must seem most satisfactory to medical men who have

been contracting with Friendly Societies on terms which, on the average represent less than 4s. per head. It is calculated by experi- enced members of the profession who do not happen to be opponents of the Government, on the only figures available, that the terms of the CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER will give an income of £6OO a year to doctors working under the Insurance Act.. We do not say that this is too much, but it is surely sufficient. In almost all cases there will be in addition to practice under the Act a large amount of practice for fees. Taken all round the proposals of Mr. LLOYD GEORGE will at least double the incomes of poor practitioners Surely the offer is one that should be immedi- ately grasped at instead of haggled over in a spirit of hostility to the Government and under the belief that a change of Govern- ment must soon take place, and that a Tory Government would offer better terms than the Administration that is now in power. In the first place, there is not the slightest prob- ability that a Tory Government would offer better terms. It would not be in a position to do anything of the kind. Hopes based on that expectation are pure delusion. But what ground is there tor supposing that soon or even for years to come, there will be a change of Government? One of the speakers at the National Liberal Federation meetings at Nottingham said that if the Tory party adheres to its Tariff Reform proposals, it is not likely to return to office for twenty-five years. That seems to us to be a quite reason- able forecast. It is with the present Govern- ment that the doctors will have to make Iterms and the sooner they adopt a rew onable attitude the better for themselves and their profession.
Mr. Crosfield has made SIR EDWARD some /pertinent obser- CARSON'S VISIT. vations in another

column on the visit to- day of Sir Edward Carson—notorious now as the leader of the " rebellion" in Ireland which changed into a comedy circus, and a participator in the House of Com- mons riot which a Conservative paper likened to the "methods of the pot-house brawler." It is quite conceivable that Sir Edward Carson may take an opportunity this evening of trying to throw dust into the eyes of the Warrington electors. He will doubtless feel that some explanation of his outrageous flouting of King and Commons is demanded of him, and what more likely than that he will refer again to the "monstrous character" of the Govern- ment's proposals, and suggest boldly' that this is sufficient reason and justi- fication for all that has occurred? Such cheap pretensions can be easily dis- posed of. Mr. Asquith's great speech at Nottingham tore into tatters the Tory pretence that the Liberal Government had concealed from the electors the intention of the Government to introduce and pass under the provisions of the Parliament Bill, should the electors give a mandate for that Bill to be placed on the statute-book, a measure of Home Rule for Ireland. Such a pretence could only be honestly put forward by those who had forgotten the pointed declarations of Tory( leaders at the last General Election, which assured the voters that Mr Asquith had made the intention of the Government "quite clear." Indeed, not one but two opportuni- ties have been !given to the country to throw out a'Liberal Government, if they wished to do so in order to prevent Home Rule being passed, since Mr. Asquith announced in 1909 that the Government held itself free to intro- duce legislation for giving Ireland control of her own domestic business if and when the obstructive powers of the House of Lords had been removed. It appears to us timely to remind Sir Edward Carson of facts like these,
The ignorant Tariff JUMPING THE Reformer is always TARIFF WALL. told that Protection

will create employment here by keeping out foreign goods. Our Consul-General says (page 9 of the 1910-11 report) that the Protective tariff has not kept foreign goods out of France: "The Frexch Press is quite alarmed at this invasion of France by foreign , manufactured articles, and points out that the value of this class of goods has increased 100 per cent. during the last ten years, whereas French similar exports have gone up by about 43 per cent. The figures of the last five years, 1907-11, are even m9re striking. They show that the increase of manu- factured imports in that period reached a total value of some £16,440,000 as compared with a rise of only £4,160,000 for French similar exports. These facts are causing much comment here, and a certain amount of anxiety at the apparent inability of French manufacturers to hold their own in France or to export as success- fully as before in respect of certain classes of articles."

The Consul-General also points out that in France, as in Great Britain, Government stocks have fallen, because the public is transferring its investments to commercial and industrial undertakings "yielding a more remunerative rate of interest." So that what Protectionists in this country blame Free Trade for is actually happening in France under Protection.

div.head: SCAFFOLDING FATALITY. WORKMAN KILLED AND FOUR INJURED.
div.p: SCAFFOLDING FATALITY. WORKMAN KILLED AND FOUR INJURED.

A singular accident, resulting in the death of one workman and injuries to four others, occurred at the works of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., Warrington, on Thursday morning. The men, who were employes of Messrs. E. Forshaw and Son., Ltd., engineers and contractors, Warrington, were engaged in the erection of a huge tank in the oil manufacturing department on the Cheshire side of the Mersey. They were working on a scaffolding constructed inside the tank(lsyds. in diameter and 33ft in height), when the wooden structure suddenly collapsed and they were thfown to the bottom of the tank. The ambulance corps in connect:on with the firm of Messrs Crosfield were quickly summoned to the scene and rendered first aid to the injured workmen, who were afterwards conveyed to the Infirmaryswhere it was found that two of the men were in a more serious condition than their comrades. The names of the men detained in the institution were : Henry Kettle, 33, Lai.ra-street (injuries to head). Thomas Melia, 20, Victoria-street (injuries to the arm and head). Kettle succumbed to his injuries at 3.30 yesterday afternoon. The other injured vrorlmen were : Charh s Finch, 7, Wellington-street Harry Dean, 20, Victoria-street William Hilson, 84, Ellesmere-street These are suffering fr,.m cuts and bruises, and after receiving attention went home.

div.head: SNAPSHOT AMONG THE RUINS YESTERDAY.
div.p: A SNAPSHOT AMONG THE RUINS YESTERDAY.

Damage estimated at about .E 3,000 was caused by a disastrous fire which broke out at the chemical works of Messrs. H. D. Pochin and Co., Ltd., manufacturing. chemists, Bank Quay, on Thursday evening, The works are situated in an area surrounded by other valuable works properties and these were in imminent danger. The credit for confining the outbreak to the works of Messrs. Pochin is entirely due to the prompt action of the Combined fire brigades of Warrington and Messrs. Crosfields', and they are to be congratulated on a remarkable save. The fire originated in the drying hearth which adjoins the coopers' workshop. The flames were first noticed by a workman namea Joseph Johnson, who resides at 2, Quay Fold. At first the outbreak was only of small proportions and Johnson succeeded in extinguishing the flames with buckets of water. A few minutes later the fire again burned and was again subdued. Johnson left the works to inform themanager, Mr. Farrington, and onh is return he found the coopers' workshop enveloped in flames. Communication was at once sent to the Fire Station and the brigade under Superintendent Turner arrived promptly on the scene. In the meantime the brigade of Messrs. Crosfields' had put in an appearance. About this time the fire had secured a firm hold of the coopers' shop and the alum department, and the flames shot up to a great height. After a short and sharp conflict, the combined brigades got the fire under control. The works are undergoing repairs and re-organisation, but the new part escaped the fury of the flames. Large crowds gathered in the vicinity, but good order was kept by the police, under the supervision of the Chief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls.) The damage is covered by insurance.

The feeling has been growing in the town that young children are being too readily taken and admitted to the various places of evening entertainment, and as a result of representations the Watch Committees has resolved:—

That the Proprietors of all premises in the Borough licensed for public perform- ances, be informed that in the opinion of this Committee it is undesirable that children of tender years should be admitted to any evening performances unless such children are in the charge of an adult person. • •

Stockton Heathens- have often realised ' with bitterness what it means to be outside the Borough. For one thing it costs a half- penny more to get home. Now, we see, another injustice is to be perpetrated at their expense. • The Tramways Committe has resolved: That a new clock be provided at the Latchford terminus, and that the old clock there be removed and repaired, and fixed at Stockton Heath terminus" We know that old clock. It has an unpleasant propensity for making the tram depart just one minute b3fore time (your time). The new Latchford clock has a pleasant open face, a pea-green body, and no such objectionable traits of character. We really feel sorry for the Heathens. They are face to face with the problem of: How to be happy though hurried

_ * * * The women of France are being urged to make an organised attack upon the drinking habits of the nation—an evil from which in its consequences, they and the children are the greatest sufferers. The movement has been initiated by the French "League against Alcoholism" with the two-fold object of, inducing the Chambers to limit the number of licensed premises, and to impose restrictions on the liquor traffic. According to the League, there is one public house for every 82 persons—men, women, and children —but many of them are also general shops, In France as in other countries, "the trade" possesses great political influence, and Parlia- ment has been chary of interfering with it, but the whole subject is bouud to figure largely in the report of the Commission on depopulation, and this may compel the French Government to act. Another evil which is prevalent in France as elsewhere, is the effect of the medicated wine business in spreading drinkirg habits among women. These preparations enter the house without question, in the guise of medicine, but they are intoxicants, and ultimately not infre- quently lead to drinking for drinking's sake.

King Kars= kums to-day. All hail ! All ale !! _

* - The Tory Party has once more bought The Flag. Union Jacks could be had for a half- penny each this week. As cheap as telegrams to Harold in Ulster ! * * Yesterday, in preparation for the monstre open-air demonstration of loyalty to King Carson, the ground was being strewn with ashes. We understand that the sackcl6th is coming from Bolton.

There should certainly be some interest in Sir Edward Carson's visit. He is not one of the men you would pass without notice even in a crowd. Of late he has loomed very large. Did he not have a semi-Royal reception as leader of the " rebellion " ih Ireland? Was he not the father of the precious solemn covenant, signed in blood, which twice invoked the Deity and sounded very terrible, but committed the signatories to nothing? And did he not recently take a foremost part in the disgraceful brawl in the House of Commons? Why, he actually said "there shall be no more business in this House," and, as usual, it was not so. - *

* * He is a great fire-eater is King Carson. At Belfast on September 27th he was received with the National Anthem, and presented with a flag which was carried at the Battle of the Boyne. Nothing could have been devised to more thoroughly fire the martial ardour of" the King." Accepting the flag, he said: " I will bold it until we have killed the conspiracy that confronts us." N.B.—Two days later the flag was returned •to its owner, who lives in England

* * - * But we must turn to higher authority for a description of King Carson in his sublimest moment. The Daily Mail reverently and eloquently describes the closing scenes on the memorable day when the Covenant was signed: "The hour v, as at hand when Sir Edward Carson must take his leave. He bad dined at the Ulster Club with the Lord Mayor, and while be dined the people watched and waited, singing songs of patriotism. When at last their leader stepped upon the balcony forty thousand faces turned towards him, uplifted and radiant under the glare of electric lights. The people had come to say not' Good-bye' but God-speed.' As Sir Edward Carson stood there, his tall figure and Pale, ielentless face stamped on the darkness by a flood of brilliance, there rose about him the deep, round roar of the populace. it grew and grew until one _mighty. yell seemed to rend the skies.

He raised hislan-d-and the tempest ceased." The Daily Mail gives us one more glimpse of the scene where the hero would finally take his rest. "Sir Edward Carson's cabin was decorated with roses and smilax and over his pillow was spread a Union Jack." Poor old Union Jack! * * Monday will see the recurrence of what seems lestined to be the annual orgie of the local Conservative Party. Another hot-pot supper is announced and the announcement at once recalls to mind the awful occurrence at the hot-pot a year ago, when a Tory Town Councillor was obliged to shout" Stop the beer," in order to secure a hearing for the speakers. We can hardly expect the same gentleman to perform such signal service on Monday evening. Indeed, it is reported that any guest of the evening deemed liable to so far forget himself next week, will be allowed a sufficiency of hot-pot and then be muzzled! Due decorum must be assured at any cost. • *

Quite a lot of good --solid Conservative cash must .have changed hands last Saturday. Warrington Tories were confident of the overthrow of the Free Trade champion in Bolton. New hats, and odds of three to one, were wagered galore. In the Conservative I Club, speakers awaited the triumph at the Poll with shouts of gladness trembling on their lips. The faithful reporter of the party paper was there too, note book in hand, and pencil ready whetted. We are told that nice blue bills recording the downfall of the Government were ready printed. All that was required were the great and glorious figures. When they came there was a silence that could be felt for some distance round Sankey-street. A great attraction has been secured for the Royal Court Theatre on Wednesday, Thursday, Fsiday and Saturday evenings of next week, and matinee on Thursday, in the form of the famous Lancashire drama by Stanley Boughton entitled " Hindle Wakes," produced by Miss Borniman. Few plays of recent years have been re) much discussed. " Bindle Wakes" is the play, that the Vice-Chancellor I banned the other week at Oickird thereby arousing a storm of controversy which is still running, and it has been freely discussed in the newspaper and in the pulpit for the last few months: the criticisms being both favourable and adverse. "Hindle Wakes" makes a special appeal to a Lancashire audience. It is a domestic drama of Lancashire life with intensely human cbaracteriz ation, a delightful flow of humour and a problem in propriety which gives one "furiously to think." The success of the play both in London and the Provinces has been phenomenal, and Warringtttn people will welcome such an early opportunity of seeing it in their midst. The play is not a lengthy one and will be produced twice nightly, 7 and 9, at popular prices.

_ The Ogden Lectures.

That the popular lectures arranged by the Museum Committee in co-operation with the Ogden Trustees are highly appreciated by the public was evidentffrom the large attendance at the second of the present series which was given by Mr J E Phythianj in the Masonic Hall, 80ld-street, on Saturday evening. Mr J Upson, who presided, commented upon this gratify- ing fact and said it had alsosome to the knowledge of the committee that the lectures had given an impetus to some who had attended them to adopt a course of study upon the lines the lectures had indicated. (Applause). Mr Phythian's subject was "Old Castles of England and Wales," and illustrated with beautiful limelight views, it proved most interesting. He pointed out that the Normans on their invasions of this country in lOW built castles in order to keep the English in subjec- tion. At first they erected artificial mounds of earth, and later stone castles. Those buildings were used by the nobles to subjugate the people and to facilitate warfare among themselves. As time went on and the King became the central authority and much more powerful than the nobles, the castles were no longer of use. The invention of guopowder also made the castles useless. It was a peculiar thing that the first fortifications in the country were earthworks, and we had gone back again to earthworks. Commenting upon the association of the castles with fighting, the lecturer said be disliked war, both in theory and practice and he should be pleated it the whole world would disarm to-morrow, and let them get on with serious business. (Applause.) Just as changes in our own land had made castlea for the most part entirely out of date, se he thought changes over a wider area would make fighting tools of all descrip- tions out of date some time in the future.

The Mayoress. On Sunday the Mayoress of Warrington (Mrs. Arnold Nield) gave birth to twins—both boys. The interesting news quickly spread throughout the town for in consequence of the happy event the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) had to cancel an engagement to attend a church parade in connection with the local battalion of St. Paul's Church and sent his apologies, along with an explanation of the cause, to the Rev. W. Bracecamp. Mrs. Nield's medical attendant was Dr. Bower, of Stretton, an old friend of the family. The Mayoress was married to Mr. Arnold Nield, son of the late Councillor Nield, last January, and rublic esteem of the parties found expression in the large congregation attending the ceremony and the many handsome presents— including one from the Town Council—of whigh they were the recipients. By the grace and tact with3which she has supported her father in his multifarious duties, the Mayoress has earned the thanks and regard of all sections of the community, and hearty congratulations have been extended to Mr. and Mrs. Nield and the Mayor on this week's interesting event. We are pleased to learn that mother and children are doing exceedingly well. It is appropriate to recall that when the late Alderman John Edward Wright was Mayor a son was born to him while be was attending divine service at the Parish Church on Mayor Sunday, Dr Joseph the present Mayor being in attendance on the mother. Last Sunday afternoon Dr Joseph had arranged to be present at a service at St Paul's Church, but felt it to be his duty to absent himself in the circumstances. Beethoven Recital. The members of the Bold street Wesley Guild spent a pleasant and profitable evening on Monday, when Mr Frank Hickman gave a lecture on " Beethoven " which was illustrated by selections from the works of the great master. The Rev II Williamson presided over a good attendance. Mr Hickman said that however musically regarded, Beethoven stood alone, towering prominently, and of all the periods created by musicians, Beethoven's was the greatest. He was the mighty tone poet, the great hearted and big-souled man for whom the world waited. As a player he showed wonderful ability, and but for the deafness with which he was afflicted later in life he would probably, to the end of his life, have been an. expert in this \ direction. Stirred as if by sheer desperation through his deafness, he launched forth score after score of ever-increasing magnitude and splendour. His music was broad and majestic and required to be treated in that way, and unless the interpretation was soulful, justice could not be done to it. The flippant and mechanical could never convey the full meaning of the great works, neither could the indifferent listener understand or discern the beauty and purity of the outpouring of his soul. Between the musical realist and the musical sentimentalist there was constant warfare. At that time it was Beethoven against Rossini. The Italian made them senti- mentalize, the German made them feel. The senti- ment of the one gave the emotional conception of artificial joy or suffering, the natural feeling of the other gave the emotional conception which belonged to real joy or suffering. Beethoven's soul was in his music and his woik could have only one effect upon all—that of making men and women better and nobler. (Applause). The musical items were highly appreciated Mrs Margaret Booth sang in artistic style " Die Ehre Gottes aus der Natur" and " Au die Hoffnung." She was also heard to great advantage in " Lochnagar " and" Sally in our alley," two old airs arranged by Beethoven, and "Ah Perfido." Miss Clarice Newell gave further evidence of her abilities as a pianist in her interpretation of the " Sonata pathetique." Mrs Haviour and Miss Newell gave Sonata No 5 as a duet for violin and piano, for which they were heartily applauded. Mrs Haviour (violin), Mrs Bouchier (violoncello) and Miss Parkinson (piano) played two trios with taste and skill.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH
CRAIK. PATHETIC CIRCUMSTANCES.

Pathetic circumstances attend the death of Mr. Joseph Craik (eldest brother of Councillor J. G. Craik) who is renaembered in Warrington as the proprietor of the Wharf Meadow Mill, which was burnt down many years ago. For a considerable time Mr. Craik, who was 73 years of age, had lived in retire- ment at Balmoral-road, South Shore, Blackpool. His youngest daughter was married at South Shore Church three years ago to Mr. Harvey Brown, and lizte :touple took up their residence in Virginia, U.S.A. Each summer Mrs brown has visited her father at Blackpool and her many relatives at Warrington. Last Saturday the sad news was received by cablegram of her sudden death. To her father the intimaton came as a severe blow and be had been much distressed ever since. Councillor Craik (Warrington), wrote condoling with him in his loss and yesterday morning he had a reply addressed in Mr Joseph Craik's own handwriting. White on his way to town with a letter in his pocket, Councillor Craik was banded a telegram announcing that his brother had passed away the previous night. Death must have occurred almost immediately after address- ing the letter to Warrington. The late Mr Craik was well-known in Warrington; He appeared to have enjoyed robust health until he learned of his daughter's death. The funeral will take place at. Warrington.
