PICTURE PALACE MANAGER'S EMBEZZLEMENT What the procecuting solicitor described as a case of 1. insufferable meanness " was investigated at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, before Councillor Henry Roberts (chairman) and other magistrates when George Horton, picture palace manager, tierners-street, Leicester, pleaded guilty to having embezzled £l, the money of Andrews' Picture Palace Con pany, Wilders- pool Causeway. Mr WI! J Jenkins for Mr Fit Roberts), prosecuted and S Steel appeared for the prisoner. Mr. Jenkins explained that the prisoner was employed by the company in June 1911, as manager of the picture palace at Warrington at a salary of £2 per week. He made such progress with the business that his salary was increased to £2 ss. Part of his duty was to pay the servants of the company. On one occasion, in respect of which he WPA charged, he acted in a mean and most wicked way. The film operator went for a fortnight's holicay. and a man named Griffin was brought in as a relief hand. He should have been paid £2, but the prisoner got him to sign a blank wagesheet. paid him £1 and then filled in the sheet for £2, retaining £1 for himself. There a ere other charges which could have been preferred against the prisoner. The case he had outlined represented the kind of insufferable meanness of which the prisoner had been guilty, because he not only robbed his employers, but poorer persons than himself.

Mr Steel said he was instructed that the prisoner began with a salary of 355. per week. H,4 raised the takings from an average of .£2O to £7O per week, and whilst he was at the picture palace he was the means of making a prcflt of something like £2,000. He had some differences with the company's travelling inspector, and there were interviews with Mr Andrews, who offered him a position in London. Eventually Mr Andrews expressed himself as prepared to overlook some irregularities and offered prisoner a position in London.

Mr Jenkins said a plea of guilty had been put in, and if the line of defence, as suggested by Mr Steel, was continued he should prefer other charges. Mr Steel said be did not wish to provoke the prosecution, but there were circumstances which he could mention to minimize the offence. He had for one thing incurred expenses in the way of increasing business—expenses which he could not legitimately charge to his employers. Then for three months he was down with rheumatism. He had a situation to go to and he hoped the Bench would deal with the case so as not to interfere with his future prospects. The Chief Constable said prisoner had previously been convicted of illegally pawning a length of fllm at Leicester.
Horton was fined £lO and costs (213 17s. in all), with the option of a month's imprisonment.

-UNREGISTERED MONEY LENDER FINED AT WARRINGTON. " A wretched business by which the poor are ground down" was the comment of the Chairman (C mncillor H. Roberts) al- the Warrington Police Court on, Tues- day, when the first prosecution promoted by the local police against an unregistered money lender was heard. The defendant was Mary Ann Bate, a small shopkeeper ' 'carrying business at 32, Ilaydock-street, and she pleaded not guilty to the charge of having acted as a money-lender without being licensed.—Mr Steel repre- sented the tefendant.

The Chief Constable said the defendant had been in the habit of lending money to different persons every week. In some cases interest at the rate of 866 per -cent per annum had been charged, and in other cases, at the rate of 433 per cent per annum. Chief Inspector Williamson informed defendant that compl4nts had been receired that she was acting as a moneylender. TShe denied it, and in reply to further questions she said she did not keep any books for the alleged money- lending or for purchases made by customers. The ,evidence was laid before the Attorney-General who directed that the prosecution should be taken. Mrs Richardson, wife of William Richardson, 38 Haydock-street, said she had been dealing with the defendant for about twelve years and had frequently borrowed small sums of money from her. She had paid interest at the rate of one penny per week in the shilling and had kept an account of her money lending , transactions on pieces of paper which she produced. I In answer to Mr Steel, the witness denied the segges• tion that she fixed the rate of intereet herself by offer- ing to repay the defendant in even money. Further questioned witnesa said she had mentioned the case to a lady from the Guild of Help, but denied that the reason was because she was not on friendly terms with Mrs Bate. . . .
_ Were you not in want of groceries at the time the Guild of Help lady came ? —Yea And was it not in consequence of the help she was -going to give you that you mentioned about Mrs Bate? —No sir.

_ Have you not male out those papers since you were visited by tha lady from the Guild of Help ?—No sir. Margaret Roberts, wife of Joseph Cornelius Roberts, 90, Haydook-street, said that just before the coal strike she borrowed money from the defendant and was charged 2d in the shilling per week as interest for the loans. She had not been oealing with her in any other way and had Lev-r purchased groceries from her. . . . . .

Mr Steel submitted that the defendant had been a good friend to people living in Ilaydock-street. She had acted innocently, and had had no knowledge that it was necessary to be registered. That was the first prosecution of its kind in Warrington, end it would 1)4 no doubt a good and sufficient warning not only to Mrs Bate but to other people. She had acted in ignorance and had never thought for a moment she was carrying on business as a money-lender. The Chairman characterised the offence as an exceed- ingly grave one, and said persons convicted were liable to a penalty not exceeding £lOO or three months' imprisonment At the same time, as that was the first .charge of its kind, they hoped their decision would act as a warning and they would put a atop to some extent to a wretched business by which the poor were ground as they were hardly ground in any other way. They bad had instances that morning of interest being paid at the rate of 850 per cent by poor people. They could not help saying that it was in its effect as bad as betting, and the people who got Into the unfortunate position of debtors could never get free except in some extraordinarily happy circumstances. In the circum- stances they had decidel to fine the defendant .£lO and costs (£l2 6s in all),with the alternative of one month's imprisonment.

MONDAY—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst and Bolton, Messrs S Wright, W Furness, G Pilling, W Roberts and T Locker. A BAD CIIARACTER.—Patrick Richard Moran, who had 51 previous convictions, was charged with loitering at the rear of 2. St Austin't-lane,with intent to commit a felony.—He pleaded not guilty.—Mark Harold Holt, a'postman, 174, Knutsford-road, said that he was at his father's house, 2, St Austin's-labe, on Saturday night when he heard someone at the back of the premises. He rushed out and found the prisoner on the step. He asked Moran what he was doing, and the prisoner replied : " I am a Scotland Yard detective." He recognized the prisoner as the man he caught in the yard the previous night. Moran was in the yard a fort- night prior to that, lie detained him and sent frr the police.—Constable Rowles said that when he charged Moran the prisoner replied : " I reserve my defence." —Moran said that the yard adjoined his lodgings, and he could not pass the window without being seen.—fle was sent to gaol for a month

A WIFE'S BROKEN RlBS.—Thomas Kearns, of Gaud ,'s-walk, was again reruauded for a week, on a charge of having caused grievous bodily harm to his wife by kicking her.—Dr Lowe said the woman was still in the Infirmary suffering am-a several broken ribs Signs of internal injurieswere also showing themselves THURSDAY.—Before Mr A J Jolley (in the chair), Messrs W Roberts J Upson and Dr Naden. FACTORY ACT PROSECUTIONS.—Messrs W and A Ashton, builders, were summoned at the instance of the H.M. Inspector of Factories for failing to report an accident, to Fred Rigby, an employee, and were fined 9s 6cl and costs-20s in all. A further charge of failing to maintain a fence on a planing machine which it was alleged was dangerous, was also preferred. The Inspector explained that a guard was provided but that it was not in position when the machine was working. Mr WH 3 Jenkins contended that the emyloyees had been warned by Mr Ashton to use the guard when the machinery was in motion. A workman named Ravens. croft admitted in reply to Mr Jenkins that he h turned the guard deliberately out of position, but it was contrary to the master's instructions. A floe of ss. Gd. and Hs. 6d.costs was imposed. MOTC,R PROSECUTION.—Eugene Hughes, 3, Baxter- street, Standish, was summoned for driving a motor car at a speed dangerous to the public on the 3rd of November. Inspector Stuart saw the defendant driving along Winwick-road at a speed of 15 to 20 miles an hour. The Chief Constable said he would consent to the case being dismissed on payment of costs. From inquiries they had ascertained that the defendant was a most. careful driver. This course was adopted by the Bench.

div.head: Mr. Henry Herbert's Visit.
div.p: Mr. Henry Herbert's Visit.

The visit of Mr. Henry Herbert with the Benson Shakespearean Company is one of the events of the season in local theatrical circles: Mr Herbert and his wife (Miss Gladys Vanderzee) have won more than local popularity, and the excellence of their stage pro- ductions is always well up to the best Benson rstandard. In Warrington there is iiievitably a fine reception for the company, hod this week each performance has been attended by large and appreciative audiences. (Joe of the features of the week s repertoire has been an interesting departure from Shakespeare. Mr. Herbert staging for the first time in Warrington that fine romantic play "If I were King," by the late Justin Hunti McCarthy. The play was presented on Wednesday and Friday evenings to crowded houses, and had a most enthusiastic recep- tion. Romance, poetry, humour and trageoy are artistically woven around a strong, if fantastid story. The hero is one Francois Villon, ballad singer, master of arts, aud roystering wine-bibber in the period of Louis XI. Villon has more good qualities than bad, and in his worst days even he is beloved by the cut-purse, light-loving habitues of a low-class Parisian tavern. Here we first make his acquaintance. Half-drunk and half-famished he reels into the crowded tavern and decl tinge a satirical lampoon on "Louis-do-naught," ending with roseate predictions of what he would do "If I were King," As it happens, King Louis (incognito) is one of the strangely mixed crowd in the Fir Cone Tavern. He appreciates the jest and the jester, but before he can intervene e‘entra move rapidly. The Lady Katherine de Vancelles (worshipped and sonneted from afar) enters and seeks out our hero. He is to prove his devotion on the body of her persecutor, Thibaut d'Aussigny, Grand Constaale of France and a traitor to boot. Opportunely enough, the villain also makes the tavern his objective and is soon engaged in a quarrel by the artful Villon. A fight a la lantern and sword follows, and the noble- man falls. Enter the guards in force, Villon captured, summary execution threatened, until Louis emerges from his dark corner and intervenes. One of the King's whimsical fancies has taken possession of his miud and he causes Villon to be drugged, shaved, perfumed and accoutred as Grand Constable of France. He awakes amid sumptuous surroundings, and after woLder has given place to realization, he proceeds to play the part in knightly style. Luis sardonically informs him that be has a week to" make good ; " unless he wins the fair Lady Katherine in that short time he shall hang as a rogue and thief. But there is some of the stuff in Villon of which heroes are made. In seven days he restores the popularity of the monarch, pacifies the soldiers and defeats the proud Burgundian at the gates of Paris. He even wins the love of his lady, but goaded by the King and his own conscience, at the eleventh hour lie avows his identity as Villon the poet and rascal. My Lady is furious at the deception and throws her lover over. The King smiles the smile of one who fancies him- self the arbiter of fate, and the last act sees Francois at the gallows. But so sad a fate is averted by the nobility and sacrifice of Katherine, and the play ends 'on a joyful note. Mr Herbert found a most congenial role as Francois Villon. Be pave a fine characterisation if the devil-may-care scribbler in the first act, and showed us a complete metamor- phosis later. We liked him even better as Grand Constable—the many sided character of Villon. alternately humorist, poet, and hero being exemplified with a skill and delicacy worthy of all praise Miss Vanderzee was charming as the Lady Katherine, and though the part makes no great demand on her knowii capabilities, she made Villon's deity a real, living presentment. The capital role of Louis XI. was magnificently played by Mr John Cairns, who showed us the weak, crafty, sardonic ruler to the life. His acting was a delightful piece of histrionic crafts- manship. Among a large number of minor characters all well-played, the artistic and spontaneous work of Miss Thea Johnson, as Haguette du Hamel, "the Abbess," was specially noteworthy. We might add that the four acts were splendidly mounted, while the handling of the crowds was a tribute to the skilled stage management. "If I were King" is a play which Mr Herbert and his company should be slow to relinquish. P

div.head: SOCIALISM AT CAIRO STREET CHAPEL.
div.p: SOCIALISM AT CAIRO STREET CHAPEL.

Sir,—There is in your to-day's issue a letter under the above heading which I feel bound to notice. Those who know me and my work at Cairo-street Chapel will see at once that" A Comrade" has got a totally wrong impression both of my special sermons aid of the talks which took place after each of them. The word " Socialism " should never be used without full definition ; in my sermons I Dever used it at all. In the meetings held after the sermons many and varied things were said by different people. All that I myself said amounted to this, that, if a man feels discontent with things as they are, he must find his own way of fostering discontent ; for that he might require inspiration, and such inspiration should be religious and idealistic, and ought to be found in a place of worship. As far as Cairo-street Chapel itself is concerned, its fundamental purpose is religious,and my own foremost interest in life is religion. As "A Comrade has not grasped my point of view, I should be pleased to have an opportunity of talking with him on the matter, if he would make himself known to me.— Yours truly. Nov. 23rd, 1912. STANLEY A. MELLOR. 31, Wilson Patten-street.

Sr,—l should like further to supplement "Comrade's" letter to you last week, but first of all should like to express a few words of admiration for his brilliant discrimination, his magnificent perspicacity, his scrupulous sense of honesty, justice and fair play. . .

He seems' to be able to discern thoughts of Dr. Mellor's that are yet unspoken : "turning the guns of the enemy against themselves; " such, by his inverted commas, he states to be the words of the rev. gentle- man. They have not been voiced by the Dr. yet. (What an illuminati "Comrade" must be). _.

Then again "Look at Trade Unions, those have been quite captured by them." Despite the fact that in many instances 1 rade Unionism is diametrically opposed to Socialism and that most of its leaders are not Socialists, there can exist no doubt in the minds of persons of so high an order of intelligence as '" Comrade "that Trade Unionism and Socialism are one and the same thing. Though Dr. Mellor's first and foremost interest in life is the preaching and practice of a true religion, devoid of cant, sham, hypocrisy and humbug, anyone who cares to wear a pair of green spectacles can see he is a thorough paced reactionary Socialist."

In conclusion let me add a word of warning to your correspondent. If be wishes to remain as high and broad-minded as be seems to be, it would be as well to keep away from Cairo-street. Dr. Mellor will most certainly extend his vision or hypnotise him with the truth. Yours truly,

div.head: , ANOTHER COMRADE. Warrington, November 25th, 1912.
div.p: , ANOTHER COMRADE. Warrington, November 25th, 1912.

Sir,—Having read "Comrade's" letter in your issue of the 23rd, re Socialism preached in the Cairo-street Chapel, I came to the conclusion that he had adopted the wrong "nom de plume," Be ought to have signed himself " Anti-Socialist " ; it would have been more correct and certainly more honest. As I understand the word " Comrade," it is gener- ally applied to a person who stands by his fellows through thick and thin. Judging from the tone of the whole letter, I should say that he would be just as likely to do a thing of that sort as he would be to fly up to the moon. He E eem s too much concerned about the employing class to consider his fellow-men. He evidently attended the after-meeting on November lith, and I believe he voiced his opinions at that meeting, judging from one portion of his letter, but he must certainly have only attended on that one occasion, or he would not have been so ready to rush into the Press with so small a fund of superficial knowledge. Had he attended the whole series of sermons he would, I feel sure, have been inspired by the sincerity of the preacher, arid would have had a clear conception of the ideal running through the whole series

I boi e "Comrade " will Come to Cairo-street and hear more, and lam sure he will have the narrow- mindedness removed from his nature. He does not need to concern himself about the Trades Unions being captured by the Socialists. I, being an active trades unionist for m re than twenty sears, have no fears from that quarter. What we have to fear and watch more closely, is the subtle methods being employed to undei mine trades unions by the party to which I think "Comrade " belongs, viz , the Anti- .. Socialist and Anti-Trades Unionist Party

We are having a demonstration of their friendship in Grand Committee of the [louse of Commons on the Trades Union Bill, which they are trying by all means in their power to wreck. They are most solicitous for the welfare of trades unions ; they never lose an opportunity to curtail their activit;ea. TRADES UNIONIST-

Sir,—The outstanding feature of the letter of "A, Comrade," which appeared in your issue of Saturday last, is its ut.becoming cynicism To those of your readers who have actual knowledge of Dr Mellor's religious ideals and also of the traditions of Cairo- street Chapel, the letter in question must have given cause for regret.

By oblique hints, your correspondent is most pains- taking in identifying Dr Mellor with Socialism. Now "Socialism,", of all terms in the English languag is perhaps one of the most abused and most vaguely applied. Usually, a "Socialist "is a man who does not hold one's own played-out, but respectable.political views. No doubt, in this sense, Dr Mellor would not greatly object to being labelled a Socialist. But.why label him at all ? Be comes amongst us with the avowed object of preaching the gospel. When he Sees, As all two-eyed men see, that the existing order of living negates the finest aspirations of the human soul, what can he in sincerity do but condemn it ? By pursuing this course, is he of necessity paving the way to " Socialism " (whatever that may mean) ? Surely there may be a better mode of life that does n t inevitably depend for its existence upon any partLcular political "jam-" Your correspondent suggests that Cairo-street Chapel is an institution " which the Socialists might press into the service for the spread of socialistic knowledge."; and further, that, having regard to the line of religious activity which Dr. Mellor is pursuing, " It only remains for the Socialist to come forward with his programme." So far as any particular brand of "Socialism "claims to show the way to the realisa- tion of the Kingdom of Heaven, "A Comrade "may rest assured that it will be fairly tested by the members of that institution, including the pastor. One thing is ceitain, it will be neither rejected nor accepted because of the label it bears. Any institu- tion which falls short of this ideal is necessarily in a state of decomposition, or at least of paralysis. Your correspondent speaks of "the securing of existing institutions for (socialistic) propaganda work." There is no prospect of Socialists, as such, "securing " Cairo-street Chapel. if, however, the I outcome of a true and unfettered religion is to produce S cialists, so much the better for Socialism. But it is not as adherents of any particular " jam" that men and women will find Cairo-stret Chapel a possible religious home. It is a free church, and can endure only by an emphatic recognition of the common life that unites men and women of all shades of religious and social conviction.—Yours truly, • A COMRADE'S NEIGHBOUR. Warringtou, 25th November, 1912. Sir,—ln these days of rapid progress when the ideal state is BO near, in which class and p ,verty and sick- ness will be unknown, honour and brotherly love will prevail and work will be a labour of love, it is gratify- ing to observe the great efforts of Cairo-street Chapel in this unselfish cause, so well mixed up with its religious devotions. " Comrade " last week gave some excellent advice and it seems to me be would make an excellent leader. But I am concerned more with the religious aspect. Christ said His Kingdom was a spiritual kingdom and most of the clergy and ministers seem to act on this absurd view, but He did not anticipate, obviously, the dreadful feudal condi- tions under which we live, when people rush to the theatres and picture shows to escape the brutal land- lords and to drown their misery. There is no doubt Christ is becoming out of date, because it is recorded of Him when requested by a man "Speak to my brother that he divide the inherit- ance with me" that he sternly answered "Who made me a judge and divider among you? therefore beware of covetousness." Of course he was quite mistaken. No doubt a quarter of an hour's discussion with
Victor Grayson or Dr Mellor would have convinced him of his error.
But the great cause must go on and religion can do much if understood in the light of the great ideal.

One great feature seldom —referred to— in this con- nection is that there will be no prisons and asylums with' their hosts of attendants. The former poor unfortunates who did not distinguish between meum and tudm will not take then what they already own; while the latter who merely hold very extreme views on specific subjects will have their fancies directed into right channels and will be principally engaged in advocating the great ideals which still lie beyond us All is economy and efficiency. Even some of the great parks such as Tatton and Dunham will not, be obliterated though many may have feared they will be. For it will be always necessary to hold up to the people some illustration of the feudal tyranny and oppression of the past and thus they will be preserved as we preserve fossils and old furniture. And the best and most self denying of our leaders will reside there as being best able to stand the strain of the surround- ings and to receive the salutations of sleek cap tipping servants, who, in like measure will possess special qualities for demonstrating present day serfdom in the presence of the overlord. In the meantime we have to wait with the desolation of abomination all about us.
Dr. Mellor should take his courage in both bands and declare a revolution at once. The time is ripe ! Yours truly,

div.head: ROBESPIERRE.
div.p: ROBESPIERRE.
TORY ATTEMPTS TO KILL TRADE UNIONS.

Sir,—May I draw your readers' attention to the Tory (and particularly to Lord Wolmer's) attempts to destroy and cripple trade unions. Lord Wolmer has repeatedly moved amendments which, if carried, would fundamentally destroy the power of trade unions to collective bargain on behalf of the workers and his latest attempt should be known to all the electors in the industrial constituency which he represents. Lord Wolmer has put down an amend- ment that would render all contracts, between a trade union and its members, tiable to a court of law and this would completely destroy the provision of the Act of 1871 which expressly relieved such contracts from liability. He also wishes to make use of the provident funds by the Unions in case of a strike, a criminal offence. Mr Harold Smith, M.P. professes to believe in Trades Unions yet he repeatedly supports Lord Wolmer both in the !House of Commons and in the Newton Division. It will be interesting to reconcile this attitude with his expressed friendly views when speaking to Trade Union deputations. In conclusion if the Trades and Labour Council ever required to be alert it is now. The Tory attack on Trade Unions decided the Bolton election and if the workmen of Newton and Warrington desire the vital safeguarding of their rights and wages Mr Harold Smith and Lord Wollner will have to be defeated at
their next attempt to represent the workers of these two constituencies.—Yours &c. TRADES COUNCIL.

div.head: RIGHTS OF ANIMALS.
div.p: THE RIGHTS OF ANIMALS.

Sir,— I hope your readers will observe how the anti- vivisectionists who wrote in your last issue, wriggle when faced with a concrete problem of public health. The illuminaiiug and expert advice of Miss Kidd and Mr. O'Callaghan on polluted milk would no doubt be very helpful to the Commission at present sitting to deal with this very problem. lfir O'Callaghan's advice is simple--boil the milk. Miss Kidd would inspect the dairies. She regards bacteriology as a fad, and if such a thing as tubercul.ms milk exists, well it is probably harmless ; and this in spite of the Royal Commission on Tuberculosis which decided, so far as this country was concerned, that a large amount of tuberculous disease in children was directly due to tuberculous milk. It is logical and consistent for the anti-vivisectionists to deny the whole science of bacteriology because that science is largely built upon animal experiments. By doing so the anti-vivisec- tionists take their proper place among the flat earth theorists and similar sec's based on the vagaries of the human intellect.

These sects if kept withim limits perform a useful service to society. They employ a certain number of people and add to the variety of life, but their chief function is to make the more orthodox examine the grounds of their beliefs and prove their contentions, The greatest set vice the anti-vivisectionists have done to the commnnity is to bring the Research Defence Scciety into existence. This society will have little difficulty in convincing normal-minded people that the experimental method in the medical sciences must continue, and in performing this duty it will incident- ally perform another, equally important, namely, the education of the public in the methods and results of modern medical research. It will thus act as an intermediary between the scientist and the laity, and so give the latter such knowledge as may be acted on with confidence.

In the matter of tuberculous milk the public should understand that the guinea-pig is specially susceptible to tuberculosis, and is on that account used as a test. In cases of gross pollution a speedy result is obtained by direct microscopical examination of the milk, but in other cases where the tubercle baccilli are more sparsely distributed thr ughout the milk, the only available test is the animal test. Ido not think the Warrington public are likely to give up this test at the bidding of the anti-vivisectionists, when it alone stands between them and the recognition of tubercu- lous milk, and the animals are used for experimental purposes according to their special characteristics. Thus apes and monkeys are used to elucidate problems of the nervous system, dogs for problems of digestion, rats and mice for problems of cancer. It must always be remembered that with the exception of inoculation experiments, all experiments are carried cut under anwsthetics by skilled operators, and thus resemble surgical operations. . . .

'fie implication conveyed by the passage which Mr O'Callaghan quotes from an address by Sir Fredelick Troves at Birmingham has been repudiated by Sir Frederick again and aga:n. The passage is torn from its context and used to convey a meaning different from what was contended. This is a favourite method of misrepresentation with people of weak arguments. Personally lam willing to make them a present of it, for Sir Frederick Treves experience with the inteatines of dogs bears the same relation to the achievements of animal experimenta- tion that the flattening of the earth's poles does to its rotundity. To a flat earth theorist anyone admitting the flattening of the poles is at once hailed as a sup- porter of the ' cause. —Yours faithfully. JOHN MANSON.

div.head: 8, Wiionarleigh-street, Warriogton. Not. 25th 1914. – ENGLISH CHURCH UNION AND ROMANISM.
div.p: 8, Wiionarleigh-street, Warriogton. Not. 25th 1914. - ENGLISH CHURCH UNION AND ROMANISM.

gir,—Permit me space to make some necessary observations with regard to the annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the English Church Union, held last week. Whatever my views may be on the con- troversy which is rending the Church of England in twain, I give the speakers credit for plain outspoken- ness, and I am glad that so full a report of their speeches has been given, for surely the people of Warrington can never again charge Protestant Church- men with exaggeration of the condition of the Estab- lished Church. I am aware that some sincere Christians think it a pity that I am so uncompromis- ingly Protestant, but I venture to believe they will now acknowledge there is just cause, and urgent need, for the stand I take. The speech of the Rev W J Stanton I will pass over entirely as being the least objectionable, merely observing that his remarks on the Divorce Commission report deserve careful perusal But the speeches of the Rev R J Brockman, and the Rev Canon Willis, contain and express most openly, and clearly, the misrepresenta- tions of the High Chutch party. It is nauseating to see the constant UEO made of the word "Catholic." i Of course the implication s that Protestantism is not Catholic, and that all Protestant Evangelical vicars and curates are outside the borders of the Catholic Church. Yet the Church of England clearly defines her meaning of the word, thus : " Ye shall pray for Christ's Holy Catholic Church, that is for the whole congregation of Chri-tian people dispersed throughout the world." (Canon 55, 1662.) All who love the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity are members of Christ's Ho!y Catholic Church, what- ever branch of Christ's Church they belong to. If a great deal less was said about the" Church Tradition" and " Catholicity " and more about the efficacy of the sh‘d blood of Christ for the cleansing of the hearts from sin, it would be more to the credit of those who are constantly talking about and longing for, so-called Catholic worship. It is, of course, obvious that members of the E.C.U. have no " desire to be reckoned with the followers of the Reformation," for the Reformers protested against the very doctrines that it is now their avowed design to re-introduce; and, alas ! have re-introduced in thousands of our

national churches ; but is it not a little inconsistent of Mr. Brockman to charge Protestantism with helping converts to the Church of Rome? The Church of Rome herself will bear me out when I deliberately charge the E.C.U. of making converts to the Roman Church. The R.C. " Tablet " declared :—" We con- sider Ritualism to be indirectly the most powerful propaganda for the Church (Papal) which England has yet seen." And the number of secessions to Rome of Ritualistic Anglican clergy, confirms the truth of the statyment. To further prove that Mr. Brockman is at fault, I suggest a very simple test. Let those who are interested attend a service, say at the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth's church in Lovely-lane, and also attend a service at my Own church in Bold-street, it would soon be evident which of us is helping the Homeward movement. Further, he charges Protestantism with falsifying history and cites as his authorities "Roman Catholic Controversialists." Now, it is easy to make a sweeping statement, but quite another thing to prove it, and Mr Brockman knows full well that the falsification of hist,ry is charged against the Ritualistic party, which is self-confessedly a Rornanizing party. 'l'he late Rev Dr .Boultbee, a true son of the Church of England, made use of such words as "that dark history of fraud," "audacious clumsy forgery," " most audacious fabrications," in connection with the falsi- fying of history by the Church in the Middle Ages. But the subject is too vast for discussion here ; I mention it so that your readers may know that history is not against, but overwhelmingly for, Protestantism. With regard to the Rev Canon Willis, we now know from his own lips that he " desires re-union with the Church of Rome, on right terms, from the bottom of his heart." By "right terms" I suppose he means full recognition of Anglican Orders, for it is Rome's refusal to admit the validity of our Orders which keeps a large number of the Anglican clergy from at once openly acknowledging The Papacy. To desire re-union with the Church of Rome is to be 'totally at variance with the canons and authoritative teaching of the Church of England, and those who desire re-union are directly responsible f..,r the present sad condition of our National Church, and partly so for the popular cry for Disestablishment.—Yours,

div.p: WILLIAM T. JAYE. Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church, Bold-street, November 27th, 1912.
POLITICS OF THE HOME.
MR. A. H. CROSFIELD'S ADDRESS TO WOMEN LIBERALS.
TORIES AND REVOLUTION.
Miss Crosfield on Welsh Disestabilshment

At the invitation of Mrs P H Brown, the Women's Liberal Association held a successful organizing meeting at Netherfield, Orford Green, on Tuesday afternoon. There was a good attendance to welcome Mr and Mrs A H Crosfield and Miss Crosfield. Amongst those present were : Mesdames Osborne, Locker, Lindley, Halliveell, Hill, Delaney, Bunch, Mason and Miss Booth. Encouraging speeches were delivered by Mr and Mrs Crosfield, Miss Crosfield and others. The meeting was keenly enthusi- astic and goes to show that when the next General Election comes round the Liberal Women of Orford will have to be reckoned with.
Mrs Crosfield, in a brief address, urged women to take a keen interest in pplitics which, in these days, so closely concerned their home life.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD ON THE POLITICS OF THE HOME.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD ON THE POLITICS OF THE HOME.

Mr Crosfield said he was very glad to have that opportunity to offer his warmest congratulations to Mrs Brown, and all the ladies present on the work they were doing to help to strengthen the Liberal and pro- gressive cause in that part of Warrington. (Applause). Mrs Crosfield in her speech had referred to the great influence the work of the Liberal party had upon the home life of the nation, in which women were so specially concerned. It was just for that very reason that he felt that, however busy they might be with other absorbing duties, every minute of the time given to supporting the Liberal policy of modern social reform was indeed time well spent in support of the best of good causes. (Hear, hear.) The poet, Burns had written

div.head: "To make a happy fireside cline For weans and wife,
div.p: "To make a happy fireside cline For weans and wife,

That's the true pathos and sublime 0' human life." (Applause.) And besides what the inmates of the home themselves could do the striking fact we had all to realise was that Parliament could do, 3es, and since the Liberals came in in 1906 had done, a great deal to help to make " the happy fireside cline." The

POLITICS OF THE HOME really included the general well being of all in it, their health, their standard of living, the education of the children, the wages and terms of work of the father (and in some cases of the mother), and so on. "Take" said Mr Crostleld, "the simple fact that 950,090 old folk are receiving old age pensions—(applause)—and just think of the difference that has made these last three years in sa many thousands of homes, not only in those of tbe old folk themselves but in those of their sons and daughters, whose families in so very many cases bad formerly been making sacrifices in order to help the old folk." That Act bad brought comfort and relief and had shed a little sunshine into the closing years of life on a vast scale throughout the country. "Is the Insurance Act" continued Mr Crosfield, "one whit less beneficent or less far-reaching in its power for good? On the contrary, like the truly blessed Old Age Pensions Act, it is another

MONUMENTAL WORK OF SOCIAL REFORM which will safeguard not scores, not hundreds, not thousands, but tens of thousands of homes in old England from the cruelty of circumstances and the undeserved disaster that would otherwise have over- taken them. (Applause.) There are instances where the Insurance Act may with advantage be amended. Certainly. Why not? What better 'arty of putting on the finishing touches than by giving it a practical trial? But, ladies, don't let the trees shut out the wood ; don't let us lose our sense of proportion, or allow these minor amendments to prevent us recognizing what I magnificent piece of statesmanship the Insurance Act is as it stands." (Applause.) And that fact was recog nised not by the Liberals alone, but by Liberals am Conservatives alike when this great measure was first introduced into the House of Commons. The more pitiful then, these wretched attempts, which the Tor: Party had made all over the country to manufacture little bit of political capital out of it ; the more sordi( the false coin which all over the country they had put into circulation in their efforts to mislead people about the Act. (Hear, hear.) Well, that sort of thing might go on for a few months, but the Tories and Tariff Reformers who bad played that low down game would rue it afterwards. Let them wait till men and women in their hour of need were sharing in the benefits of this Act all over the country, and see whether the Tory party would continue their

- CAMPAIGN OF DEFAMATION. Not much. (Laughter.) We should find them singing a different tune then. (Laughter.) It would not be long before this Insurance Act was recognised as the finest piece of constructive social reform in our political history, and he would not except even the invaluable Pensions Act itself. " Let us say, friends," continued Mr Crosfield " they will both stand together as part of the noble edifice we are rearing, based on the solid foundation of Free Trade. And let us safe- guard that foundation, for of all things in the world of politics it is Free Trade in which you are most specially and vitally interested, and the chief issues it raises for the women of England are, after all, simple enough and clear enough, especially now the Tariff Reforme,s have

div.head: TARRY ANOTHER FATAL PLUNGE
div.p: TARRY ANOTHER FATAL PLUNGE

and committed themselver-t-T,o-di;;;Ca;;;;:12-at will fall not only on your beef and mutton, your bread and cheese, your butter and eggs, and other food of that kind, but upon boots and stioes,and shirts and stockings, on all kinds of clothing and on all sorts of things that are wanted for the home—curtains, or tablecloths, the table itself, an extra chair or two, whenever these are wanted, instead of buying at the naturally lowest price you will have to pay an artificially increased price. is it any wonder then that Conservatives are shaky enough themselves over these taxes on food and cloth- ing, and we see even Lord Lansdowne himself trying to do a sum that Mr Chamberlain could never work out ? And so they are now again trying to persuade you that it doesn't matter about having to pay more for bread and meat and dairy produce, because you will have to pay so much less for tea and coffee, and cocoa and sugar. Veil, now, ladies, may I quote you a figure or two from a calculation that has been made-by Mr Cbiozza Money, one of our leading statisticians. Ile has calculated that if these FOOD TAXES were put on according to the scheme Mr Chamberlain proposed in 1903, the consumers of the nation—that is to say, yourselves—would between you pay £18,000,000 extra per year, and of that £18,000,000 less than one half would find its way to the Government's coffers, more than half would be pocketed by private indivi- duals. That you see is because only what comes in from foreign countries, or from the Colonies and is taxed when it comes in, produces revenue for the Government. But all that we use of tea, sugar, coffee and cocoa comes from abroad and therefore all the taxes on those articles go to make revenue for the 'country. These taxes Mr hiozza Money reckons at a little over £10,000,000, so that if the whole of that were abolished the government would lose a couple of millions per annum and you, the consumers, would lose £8,000,000. But there is another very important con- sideration we must not overlook. While you keep the Liberal party in office you will see these taxes on tea,

sugar, coffee and cocoa being gradually reduced without taxation being put on other most indispensable nrticles of food and clothing.rherefore, ladies, your Free Trade case is impregnable and I trust you will give time to consider it and master the facts, and male them known in tho town. (Hear, hear.) Then the Protectionists will not have a leg to stand upon—(laughter)---and having made sure of our foundations we may proceed with the splendid work of modern constructive Liberalism." (Cheers). Subsequently, before leaving, Mr Crosfield said he had apiece of interesting news to give them.

BIRRELL was coming to address a mass meeting in the Parr Hall on February 15th. (Applause). "Yes," went on Mr Crosfield, "and he will come to defend that system of self-government which has teen the very making of the British Empire—(hear, hear)—and that orderly progress which is in striking contrast to the sheer hooliganism preached by some people. Now of course the nation as a whole is vitally interested in the maintenance of orderly progress, but the women of England are even more interested in preserving that than the men,—(bear hear)—because they suffer soonest and suffer most from disorder and anarchy. So when you read of Mr Boner Law countenancing a faction of violent Irish fanatics in one corner of Ireland and giving them encourage- ment that leads to acts that are nothing less than criminal, I hope you will make a note of it. And when the Tories in the House of Commons threaten to smash the Parliamentary machine—("shame")—the machine that gives us our Old Age Pensions scheme and our Insurance Act ; and when Sir Edward Carson threatens that no more work shall be done in thie Parliament—("shame")—lhope you will make a note of that too. The Tory party, ladies, has faillen far indeed when those who once upon a time claimed to be a party of Law and Order now do their very best to knock law and order on the head." (Hear, bear). Mr Crosfleld again warmly congratulated the members of the 'War- rington Women's Liberal Association on their activitYt and Mr a Crosfield, Miss Crosfield and he were very heartily cheered when they left the mee MISS CROSFIELD ON WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT. Miss CROsFIELD also gave a short address, arid referrrd to moral courage in which women had never been found deficient. They could all nail their colours to the mast Right thinking produced public opiniofl. and they could do their share in helping public opinione if they would educate themselves by reading pamphlete and good newspapers on political que-tions of the day, and discussing them with their menfolk. Whatever the Government's enemies accused them of, they could not say they had been lazy. Mini Crosfield instanced the great tasks which the Liberals had under- taken since they were returned to power in 1906—the Education Bill, the Licensing Bill, both thrown out by the Lords, and the famous budget of Mr Lloyd George which first introduced the new principle of id in the tax on undeveloped land, and on which the Liberals had again to go to the country. The country ratified it ; then came the Parliament Act, and then Old Age Pensions, and now the Insurance Act. Before them still lay the great steps of Home Rule, Welsh Disestablishment and the Electoral Reform Bill. As she came from Wales, she thought a few words on Disestablishment might interest them. Whet did Establishment mean? It. meant that the State maintained the Church in a position of privilege and set it up over other religious bodies in Wales. Now, if the majority of the Welsh people belonged to the Church, this State patronage might be more justifiable. But what were tbe figures ? The number of worshippers in any given sect wag arrived at by taking the number of communicante. There were 138,000 in the Church, 533,000 in the three big Nonconformist bodies, divided as thus: Calvanistio Methodists 186,000, Congregationalists 168000. Baptiste 133,000: so that as they saw, the Calvanistio Methodists alone outnumbered the Established Church by nearly e T quarter. o put it another way, out of a population hi Wales of 1,727,000 of five years of age and upwards, 1,032,000 belonged to the four leading Nonconformist denominations. Yet it was calculated that Noncon- formists paid two-thirds of the upkeep of the Estab- lished Church. This was chiefly on account of tithes. Now tithes brought in a little history. Ihey were originally granted by the State for the use of the National Church. The Established Church was set up in Wales by the Normans in 1115, but the Christian Church in Wales was far more ancient. Miss Crosfield outlined the early missionary work in Wales and pointed out that the old Celtic Church differed itS several points of observance and doctrine from the Church which looked to Rome as its head- quarters. However, the Normans set up the Established t.hurch and compelled the great landowners to eel tithe to it, as being the National Church of the country. But the Welsh had never looked upon the English. Church as national. It had always been an alien io their land, and if they read over the history of tbe 180 800 years, it had generally been unsympathetic to tbe ideals of the nation. Its Bishops were almost alwa3l Englishmen, set up from Westminster, and hen° in glove with the English policy rather than with the ideals and wishes of the Welsh peoPle• There had been a steady demand for Disestablish ent 30 years in Parliament and for 100 years in the natifor on; Thirty-four M.P.'s were returned from Wales and 3t. were for Disestablishment. The moment a Chun"' ceased to be a National Church, it had no right to keeP the national funds. These, as she had shown, were the S tithes and other moneys accruing which the State long ago granted to the National Church. But in no instance would endowments by private persons be touched, the title deeds of which went back about 300 yeer: That was, of course, the private property of the Chore The tithe money would, it was suggested, go to winos' tion, cottage hospitals, trained nurses for the Poro; institutes, libraries' and generally to help the sick,l .t , halt and the maimed in life. Surely that was the practice, side of cur Lord's teaching. (Applause.) If 14"; conformists could support their own religion why ee„ the Churchpeople ? There would then he comPletf religious equality,the sense:of injustice and favouritise" would be removed, and the friendly relationsbil between the Anglican and the Free Churches, avid,, she was glad to say were far better than of yore, woo" be increased. (Applause).

div.head: WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
ITS 2a-Oth ANNIVERSARY

In the course of researches which have been necessary in the preparation of these articles a number of Warrington documents have been discovered, and the information contained in them, while perhaps not of the first importance,is much too good to withhold from those who are interested in the War- nogton of the past. We propose, therefore, to quote them in one or two supplementary chapters giving such clues to their meaning as we are able. We return in our story to the period of the Restoration with its suspicions and Upheavals, and the ejectment of ministers in 1662. The Lord Lieutenant of the County Upon whom fell the burden of maintaining law and order was Lord Derby of Knowsley. At his right hand, probably as Deputy- Lieut., was that zealous loyalist Sir Roger tradshaigh, of Haigh Hall, Wigan, a most active justice of the peace, and doubtless in his own eyes, a man of iibmense importance in the State. By a most happy fortune one of Sir Roger's letter books, which enshrines quite a mass of typical documents of the Period, has recently become accessible. The letters reveal the worthy knight as living a life of high activity. He is con- cerned with the training of the militia, the Object being the suppression of disorder. He is receiving, too, day by day, information • concerning two sections of the community Upon whom suspicion most rests and from Whom trouble is obviously anticipated ; Cromwells old soldiers and the Phanatickes, A term which included Anabaptists, Fifth Monarchy Men and the much-misunderstood • Quakers.

DAYS OF HIGH TENSION. High Royalists like Sir Roger were at a r' tension and their watchfulness against rebellion led to suspicion and enquiries of ;• an extraordinary kind. The letters contain " accounts of " desperate designs," none of which are too trivial for Sir Roger to ' investigate. Before the operation of the Act of Uniformity he is warned upon 'high authority"that the presbyterians have arranged a fierce and general " ryseing" from Which bloodshed may be anticipated. With Such reports pressing in upon him the keen royalist is constantly ordering searches to be - Made for arms and other evidences of plots. The following letter, which relates to Warrington,will serve to show what trifling platters were reported upon as suspicious in ,0 that disturbed time. Sir.—Calling at Warrington and upon enquiry I understand the Phanatickes have their frequent k, meetings here. Ilarvy of the " Eagle and child" had a silver trumpett brought unto him within these three days by Gerrard, Ford of Wigan, the Penterer, whom you may Please to send for and make further enquiry! These things I could not but make known° unto you, as alsce.—Your affectionate Brother and Servant, OEI FREY SIIAKERLEY. Warrington, March sth 1663. F, TO SIR ROGER BRADSITAIGII, hr. HAIGH. Sir Roger makes enquiry and adds a note: Gerrard Ford confesseth to have delivered the 1- Trumpet and that he received it publiquely of one Taylor in Stafford and delivered it publiquely. THE FIRST LASH OF THE LAW. The earliest matter of any serious import Which touches Warrington people appearsl under date January 1662-3. Unexpectedlyl We gain some light upon the imprisonment of Robert Yates to whom allusion has been made in these articles. Henry Newcombe Wrote in his journal: Mr. Yates and several good people of Warrington were carried to Prison yesterday, (Jan. 10th 1662-3). He does hint however give us any knowledge of the charge upon which they were convicted. It seems almost certain from the records of Sir Roger Bradshaigh that Yates was convicted, along with others, for the holding of a religious meeting at Sankey Bridges. Here are the notes of the examination: Richard Nicholls (examined) denyeth all. Parson Yates of Warrington denyeth that he was at Sankey Budges or any heare out of Towre the filth of Jan. instant (1662-3) or that bee suspecteth any one to have soe much malice against him as to informe anything but truth concerning hirn. Richard Worrall deposeth to the same effect. John Naylor denyeth all and that hee was out of Warrington any way upon the sth instant. Robert Tuchet deposeth to the same Efft Richard Nicholas denyeth that he knoweth George Barrow the informer. Yates doth deny

the same. There is nothing to show whether a con- viction resulted, but the fact that Robert Yates told Henry Newcombe the story of his imprisonment on February 4th,he haying just been released, suggests that the ejected rector took thus early his first measure of ouffering under the Uniformity Act. ALARUMS AND IMAGINARY PLOTS. That he was carefully watched is revealed In the next entry that refers to Warrington People. It dates a year later,in March 1663-4. In that month certain anonymous letters Were received by Mr. Mosley, of Manchester, Inaking accusation against the Presbyterians eq Lancashire and the West Riding. One of the letters contained what appears to have ecen a Nonconformist memorial complaining Of the prevalent crimes, superstitions,Popery etc. The deputy Lieutenant of Lancashire con- %idered the letters but attached no importance to them because honourable names like that Of Lord Delamere were mixed up with the gubious ones. The Yorkshire Authorities regarded them more seriously. In one of Itese letters the following are alleged to be Chiefest Engagers" in the plot in Lanca- Ithire and Cheshire. "In Cheshire ; Mr Eaton and Mr Brurtor both professing Preachers of the race of Presbitry and Independency who (Simeon and Levy-like) where Bretherne in Cruelty and Rebellion one." "In Lancashire ; Mr Jolly, Mr Yates, Mr Newcurn, Mr Anger, Mr Harrison, Mr Hirt* Mr Johns all pretending Levies calling to the office of Ministers ; Mr Ditchfield arid Sergeant Will Booth both liveing in Warrington." , The Conventicle and Five Mile Act 13rought fresh discontent to the Noncon- [lo.rrnists, and the high-strung knight makes imself exceedingly busy in his search for Sedition and his close scrutiny of "persons of P,llanaticke Principalls." In August 1655 141, e Militia are ordered to be in readiness ; ;trict watch is kept over leading Noncon- 19rmists and many are placed in a suspected tti,St as persons to be searched for arms. ll:here is also "a particuler of persons fit to secured " i.e., arrested, among whom are John Masey of Warrington, late servant to 2,0 late Traytor Lockyer, Blood, Newton. Isoe Ditchfeild of YVarrington." o Orders made by the Deputy Lieutenants 1,11 September 16th 1665 show that arrests been made. Among them John Ditch- ,:!eld of Warrington is taken, but he is released upon single security for the good uehayiour and to appeare."

div.head: LOCAL PERSECUTIONS.
div.p: LOCAL PERSECUTIONS.

Taking Lancashire as a whole there was little resolute persecution of Nonconformists on religious grounds during the unhappy years that followed the ejection. Sir Roger Bradshaigh stands out as an exception. He is hostile to Nonconformity and his attitude draws to him discreditors and accusers from far and near. In August, 1665, Peter Legh of Bruch makes a raid upon a conventicle in Woolston and hurries off the preacher, who " denyed to give his name" to his uncle Sir Henry Sclater. In due course the matter comes to Sir Roger. This unlawful gathering was held in the house of Richard Davice and the following are taken :

Hugh Haslope, Wan ington, apothecary. John Seadon of Bui ton Wood, Threatened to Rescue if taken without Warrant under hand : nd scale. John Barrow, Ralph Earlom' both linen websters, Thomas Holland, Thomas Holland wife, John Sadon wife, Margaret Spruse, Elie Pruse, Jane Murey of Warrington, widow. Another woman who I knowe not. A male boy whom I knowe not. The number being with the speaker 13.

Two months later in October 1665 two persons, Mr. Tomlinson and Cudbert Hand who "both of them live in the house commonly called Captain Cubane's house att a place called Causey Bridges in Burton Wood" are reported as " P.hanatiques "and one is convicted.

In September 1666 Sir Roger is facing a new•difficulty of which there is an irritating instance at Warrington. Writing in that month to his fellow justices he points out that one cause of the failure to supress Non- conformity lay in the fact that the people were opposed to the persecution, and elected constables who were sympathetic to the conventiclers and who instead of trying to capture them gave warning to them when their meetings were suspected. With a soul full of zeal for his monarch and the uphold- ing of the laws of the realm he wrote an interesting letter dated from Warrington on September 18th, 1666:

Gentlemen,—ln my vtay to Londot upon ISth inst. at Warrington I melt with several] informations of conventiels frequently held in that Towne but none punctual;y proved, the constables of this Towne being generally Ellected of tbo same stamps, As by the informations of one Thomas Hall one of the constables owne con- fession upon oath may spears. Which I take to bo so clears that bee was knoweing of the Fact and neglective in his duty that I thought fitt to bind him to good behaviour and before ',tat, wishing° you to take speciall notice of the xaminations se aa to lay particuler rnarke upon him to deterr other Constable from the like neglect. S, e begging your pardon for this ttoble, being urged to it by my duty to his Majestie I rest.— Your most faithful servant,
ROGER BRADSHAIGII.

Upon the same day he had held an" Infor- mation " at Warrington at which Serjeant John Willson and Lieutenant John Grims- ditch stated that " they had informed the constable that a conventickle was being held in the house of Richard Nicholls, Chandler. " "Theconstable told them to stay where they were until he came back and on his return said he had spoken to the said Nicholls who promised that the people should depart and that they were going away when he came from thence."

Thomas Hall, who served his fellows in the capacity of grocer as well as constable,for the crime of leniency towards the Dissenters was charged by the Justices to " be of good behaviour and to appear next sessions to answer what shall be objected." A delightful little comedy may be found here by those who are skilled in reading between the lines. The Sergeant and Lieu- tenant, quivering with zeal for Church and State, break in upon the quiet of the grocer's shop to tell the Constable that the Dissenters are holding a meeting. They show a dis- position to go and assist him in the break-up, but he insists that they shall stay where they are and be comfortable. Without show- ing any signs of haste, the constable, himself possibly a secret frequenter of conventicles, walks downto the tallow chandlers and comes back with the very tame story that the people are going to be told to go home. Sir Roger might well be angry and ask his fellow-justices to make an example of him.

div.head: AUDACIOUS TALLOW CHANDLER.
div.p: THE AUDACIOUS TALLOW CHANDLER.
With such an indulgent constable it is not to be wondered at that conventicles went on as before.
Under date April 15th, 1667, Lieutenant Grimsditch is again playing the part of informer and appears at the residence of Sir Roger for that purpose. This is how the " Information" is worded:

The said John Gritnsditch upon his oath slyth that upon Sunday the 14th inst, this informer seeing severall persons goeicg it.to the house of one Richard Nicholls of Warrington Chandlor (a palace where Conventicles and unlawful! meetings are usually held), and suspecting the like occation and having an Order for apprehending of persons soe mett, acquainted the Constable of the said Towne with the same, requireing him to give his assistance for the apprehending of the said persons. And accordingly repayreinge to the House and demanding etterarce, or to know who was theare and upon what occation, the said Richard Nicholls came to the inside of the doro ; and the said John Giimsditch acquainting him with his warrants,the said Richard Nicholls said he neither cared for him nor his Warrant unlesse a Justice of the Peace weare theare present, and denyde to open the door or declare who was in his house; though this informer saw above twelve persons goe into the said hou3e as he veryly beleves, and further sayth not,
JohN GRIM SDI Tcll.

Between " conventicklers " as impudent I as Richard Nicholls the tallow chandler and loyal knights like Sir Roger there was bound sometime to be a crash. Such audacity on the part of the Noncon- formists was not to be tolerated. The matter was brought to the notice. of Lord Arlington —possibly by Bradshaigh himself—who wrote to Lord Derby a?, Lord Lieutenant ordering him to make. strickt enquiry " and " put the Lawe in execution for the suppressing of such meetings." But Lord Derby found no pleasure in persecuting the Nonconformists. When Bradshaigh complained that con ven ticles were held at St. Helens, quite near to his residence, he replied that if he must enforce laws against the Presbyterians he must with equal severity enforce them against the Papists, whom Sir Roger shielded. In the present instance he allowed twelve days to elapse and then did no more than send a copy of the letter to Bradshaigh. With a Lord Lieutenant so delightfully indifferent the Warrington " Conventicklers" went on in comparative peace.
A. M.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 30, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 30, 1912.
JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

marks but ano'her step in the direction now indicated The woman clerk is de,tiued to increase ; the ma'e clerk to decrease. And so forth and so on. We have the lady dentist and the lady barber; and Liverpool has lately produced a lady engineer. The lady jobbing gardener has done so well that it is evident she has come to stay. I think it was only last week that the arrival of the lady chauffeur was aurae to ced, though the lady aviator has been at work for sometime. To harp back for a moment upon a previ us subject, I read a while ago that among the well-paid professions now open to women that of dis- pensing is rapidly increasing in popularity. This ie no doubt due primarily to the readiness with which a fully-quaLfied wcman-chemist finds employment But the work is pleasant and interesting, and not arduous The Pharmaceutical Society, to whose activitie a I have had occasion to sllude in a former paragraph, I ave done ra.uch to clear the way by xtending t women exactly the same privileges as are enjoyed by men. For the information of any youthful reader of this c, lumn who may be personally a'tracted by the reference, it is added that a good general education is needed in order to pass the preliminary examination, after which comes an apprenticeship of aree years with a registered chemist, followed by a course of leesons either at the School of Pharmacy or some rimiliar est iblishment. Then the student is called upon to pass the final examination of the Pharmaceutical Society. But to my main argument. As c, ntem- poraries have already obs,rved, one by one tie out- posts of masculinity have been carried by assault. Women have invaded the university, the laboratory, the surgery. N, t only have they bi come indispensable to the commercial ofliae, they have threatened Parlia- ment itself. The tilliard room is no longer sacred from their intrusion, the smoke-room has lost its terrors for them, and they refuse to be banished from post-prandial gatherings—orgies is no longer the word for them—at which, it is whispered, , he cigarettc-b x is passed round indiscrimin- ately. What refuge is there left for man ? Said I not well that he is destined ere very long , to remain at home and mind the baby what time Lis wife alternates between some outside business and her club? As for the occnpirion mentioned at the outset, rent collee ting is a comparatively new work for women (one of the rex tells us), but they are very an crs-ful in it. It is almoot universally the wome!, who pay the not in the homes of the poor, and they nrefe r a woman collector. They underetand that she must be firm about getting the money, but they are 4retly solaced for parting with it by a :sympathetic Nord or two and a I, ind'y manner. That sounds all ight, but I should just like to add that Borne of us

would prefer a little more of the " sympathetic word" and the " kindly mariner" on the pArt, say, of the " hello' girls at the telephone or the fema!e clerks at our post offices up and down the maintry.

div.head: GREAT UNPAID.
div.p: THE GREAT UNPAID.

What a magical and coveted fax is the " J.P." to which the Rev. A. M. Mitchell incidentally referred at the last meeting of the Board of Guardians ! What tales any experienced journalist could unfold as to what goes on behind the scenes between aspirants after this especial distinction and persons of influence who are expect,:cl to help them to attain it in return for political services! There is a good deal of the mean and pitiful about it all. At the same time there is often considerab'e difference between newly-fledged magi 4 ate's exaggei ated estimate) of the honour which he has obtained and the ordinary man in the street's opinion fit. I have known one of the former label his own luggage quite conspicuously with it and I dare say he was surprised %%hen acquaii tances who noted it on the railway s'ation platform did not seem greatly impressed in his favour. As a matter of fact, it was the cause of much hilari y at lis expi.nse not unmingled with contempt for such snobbery. Then there are those who by reason of their presiding over some local adtninistratic e body are entitled for the time being to a seat on the Bench and the exercise cf cer:ain other magisterial functions—but, then, they are not really J.P.'s,

COURTESY TITLES. What I naNin is that, unlike the Simon Pure, they are not on the Commission of the Peace, and so long as their names are not wriiten in that particular book of life, they are Justices of the Peace but temporary, and if we put to their names the initials in question they owe the concession to the courtesy of the public. That sort of thing is c-aistantly done, and applies pretty well all rcuod. A clergyman here and there may, strictly speaking, be perpetual curate rr incumbent, but with the bulk of us, all are vicars nowadays, and only a pedantic purist or a very extreme stickler for ecclesiastical precision cares anything about fine-drawn distinctions as to such matters. In the same way, we address every medical man as " Do:.tor " without ever thinking of enquiring into hi 3 xact qualificalions. Ile may be , or, what i 3 tome likely. just M.B ,CM ;to matter—to the hyirian ho is M.D. This is common every day xpouienco, and nobody ever dreamt of making a griev,nee of it. And so we are in the habi• of 311ing a eifzen " J P." as long as he retains thi chairmanship of the Cm ell that gives him the iighi to act in a judicial capacity ; and yet the heavens de not fall !

CHEMIST AND DRUGGIST. The carelessness cc good-natured indifference of which I have written may conceivably be carried too far. Too seldom do we ever t die the troub'e to discriminate between the fully-qualified chemist and the mere retailer of drugs who, if he has ever made the attempt, has been unable to pass the necessary ' examinations. Naturally, the genuine chemist, who has acquired his triumph over the severe tests now-a- days very properly imposed, has little patience with the thoughtless and unobservant people who fail to discriminate and constantly describe as chemists persons who are simply salesmen at a drug store, and who, s far from being able to make up a physician's prescription, are even forbidden by law to deal in any mixture for internal use containing poison. The rights of the chemists are jealous'y guarded by the Pharmaceutical Society, a rel I haie known many a sharp lesson administered by their representatives ia districts in which I have lived. In one of these the local secretary was peculiarly smart and keen. Whenever be fou, d one who was not a qualified chemist venturing beyond the legal limit, he promptly wrote offering the (ffn nder the choice between immediate summons before the magistrates, will public exposure and its inev.table consequences, and a private subscription of .V. 5 to his society's fund. One after another, he thus caught in turn every unqualified person in the locality posing as a chemist, and each was glad to pay the 3:5 rather than face the Court ordeal and its concomitants ; indeed, in at least one instance, one unwary tradesman who was twice caught tripping submitted on each occasion to be thus " bled. ' STANDARD BREAD. When the craze for the so-called standard bread referred to in last week's " Nub's " was at its height, I interviewed three more or lees interested persons respecting it, and the results were curious. The first was a doctor of advanced years and considerable local reputation, and I found him particularly enthusiastic. He was actually munching some of the new bread as he entered the surgery, and insisted on my sampling it there and then. From what he said to me, I could only infer that as for him and his house, they would eat only standard bread thenceforth to the end of their earthly pilgrimage. Next a baker in whose hearing I had spoken favourably of a certain much-advertised brown bread held up for my admira- tion a specimen of tie own " standard " loaf, and proceeded to compare it with the one I had praised— greatly to the latter's detriment and the exaltation of his own, perhaps it were needless to add. Finally, 1, got into the company of a few most interesting individuals who were intimately concerned in the milling industry, and I gathered that the "standard bread 'boom had proved one of the most profitable to themselves tbat they had ever known, as it had enabled them easily to sell at something like fancy prices immenso quantities of otherwise. worthless stuff. Owing to the house-wife's insistence upon a regular supply of the finest white flour, this supposedly inferior stuff, which had come to be regarded as refuse in a sense, had accumulated on their hands to such an extent as to constitute a serious embarrassment. Then came the " Daily Mail " t, the rescus ; the nswspaper boom saved the situation—nay, it not only created a market for what had long been looked upon as hopeless stock, but it enabled at least a proportion of j yful speculators to realise fortunes by means of what had been contemptuously described as " sweepings." But what about my baker's confident comj arisen anti my doctor's glowing eulogy? SHOCKING. A frivolous reader of the " Examiner" came to me with a copy of last week's issue open at th et account , of the fire at the C; apel House in Thelwall-lane, and propounded unto me this enigma : '• When did the ! fender blush ? For a moment I feared that something had affected him in the upper st ry, but I was soon satisfied that he was quite normal. "It's a conumdrumm you know," explained he; when did the fender blush?" Not being c'ever at conundrums , I gave it up forthwith ; and the wretch shamelessly supplied the startling answer : " When the clothes fell off the maiden !" Then turning to Mr E England's ; extraordinary rhetorical feats at the Debating Society's ' meeting, he tried on me a painfully brand new j ke ; about " England " being "England still," but, like Buuyan's pilgrim, I put my fingers in my ears and fled, lest my self-restraint should prove unequal to the ) strain, and I should do him an injury. MAN'S INESCAPABLE DOOM. Yes, it is bound to come. A few generations more shall roll and a few more changes come and " the ' hand that rocks the cradle" will be the man's hand, I and it won't " rule the world " either. Labourer _Rewarded. for Saving. a Lady's_Life:

A young labourer, Alexander Dries, sgewel 21. of Parliament-street, Ditto°, near Widnes, who helped to rescue par.songers from the turning coaches of the train which came to disaster at Ditton Junction on Septem- ber 17, has been rewarded by an elderly lady at South- port with £lOO for saving her life. Davies s rya that on the Light of the accident, as he was having his tee, he heard a shout that there sv.s a train on the line. "There was a young lady standing by one of the carriages, and when she saw me she shouted, Come and help mfmother."fh, re was an elderly lady in the compartment, and ate seemed too done up to help herself. I went; in by the duo., and as f opened it the flames came in after me and the teatriage was filled with smoke. I helped to get the lady to stand up, but she seemed to have given up all hope of getting out. the said, Let me stay whete I am. Do let me stay.' I said, ' It's no use, missus, you'll have to corne out of this.' The smoke was too thick to stay in any longer, and the flowers on tbo lady's bat began to burn, 60 I tried to lift her through the other d or. That was the hardest part of the job, but I got her out on the line and helped her along to the platform, where she was taken to the waiting room. When I went t aok.to see if there were any net re people in the coach was all in flames." When Mrs Sbarp,who was burned ab ut the bands and arms and had a fLot °unshed, recovered, she instructed a Widnes gentlemen to ascertain the identity of the young man who bad saved her from a terrible death. There were several claimants, but all of them failed to repeat the conversation which took place in the bt.rning carriage. Eventually, Davies was asked to visit Mrs SlL:rp at Southport. The remark, "It's no use, missile', you'll have to come out of this" at once satisfied the lady. Asked if he intended doing anything with the money, Davies said, "No I'm just leaving it there until ym wanting it. I'm in good work as a labourer."

THE lIARDY TEA PLANT. We all know a little about the tea plant, but there are things about it which we may like to learn. We know of course that what we call tea consists of the leaves of a plant that grows in China and Ceylon. We know too that it is carefully and plentifully cultivated.

If left to itself it would grow into a tree eighteen or twenty feet high, but in the plantation it is not allowed to grow higher than three or four feet. A peculiarity is that it flourishes in its foliage all the year round. There is no special season for pick- ing the leaves; they may be plucked at any time.

The plant is cultivated for three or even four or five years before it is touched and then for two years or so the leaves are gathered every week. After this, all its branches are chopped off and it has a period of rest. The fresh branches grow very quickly and within two or three months the hardy little shrub is again ready to submit to the constant plucking for two or three years. Yet another curious thing which we western people do not know about the tea plant is that the various parts of the shrub give leaves of varying value. The bottom branches give the poorest quality and the top ones are the best. The special names given to tea do not describe the places it comes from but the parts of the tree from which it is gathered, certain branches being called by given names. The choice buds from the tips of the topmost branches the Chinese will not al:ow to be exported. They keep them for their own use and won't let profane people in Europe get a taste of them.

ROYAL ALBERT INSTITUTION LANCASTER. Forthcoming Concert. The subscriptions for the past year for the Warring- ton district of the above institution being only half those of previous years. it has been thought advisable to give a concert in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening, January 30th, to make up tbe deficit. The institution is for the feeble minded of the Northern counties and is supported by voluntary contributions. There are five children from the Warrington district at present undergoing training there. The concert, organised by Miss Mary Cornell, will be promoted by the Ladies Association, Warrington Branch, of which Mrs Aylmer Frost is President. The names of those on the committee are i—Mrs H R Armitage, Mrs Darwall, Mrs J Davies, Mrs Eddowes, Mrs Lisbon, Miss Morris, Mrs Charlton Parr Mrs Rylands, Mrs Shepherd-Cross, Mrs Watkin, Mrs Johnson and Miss Eddowes being joint hon. secretaries. The Royal Albert Institute which was founded in 1864, is not a lunatic asylum but a training home for feeble minded. The results of training are shown by the following statistics. Since the opening of the Institution in December, 1879, there have been admitted 3,193 patients, of whom over 700 are still in residence. Out of every hundred of those who have passed through the Institution 81 have been more or lees improved, many to such an extent as to be able to maintain themselves after leav- ing. Besides the school instruction, training is given In a great variety of useful occupations. The boys are taught tailoring, shoemaking, basket-making, brush- making, mat making, joinery and cabinet making, wood carving, printing, and baking, and there are excellent means of out-door employment and training in farm and garden work. The girls are trained in needle work, housework, and simple laundry work. The mainten- ance of such an Institution, is naturally no light task, the annual expenditure now amounting to about £25,000. To meet this expenditure the only fixed, and certain item of income is the interest derived from the Endowment Fund which now amounts 10 £9,410 a year the remainder having to be made up by subscriptions donations and payments for patients, so that the Institution was established and is maintained by volun- tary support. It receives no aid from grants and is the only Institution of the kind in the northern counties which admits free patients.
