div.head: RAILWAY SMASH AT DITTON.
div.p: RAILWAY SMASH AT DITTON.
Narrow Escapes.

Only a miracle prevented a repetition on Monday night of the horrible scenes witnessed at Ditton Junction, near Widnes, on September 17th, when 15 people sere killed and 42 injured in a railway smash. The 5.5 express from Liverpool to Chester, the train concerned, is one of the fast trains of the North-Western Railway Company, and only stops at Runcorn after leaving Liverpool. The tram consisted of an engine (driven by James Speed, of Chester) with a tender, and eight coaches containing about one hundred passengers. All went well till Ditton signal-box was reached, and the train took the points on Ditton Bank. The engine was going at a foir speed, when the axle of the tender suddenly snapped. The tender left the line,and careered for two hundred yards, 'tearing the metals up, and hurl- ing them in every direction. It finished by falling fifteen feet into the gully below. Fortunately the couplings connecting it to the carriages and engine broke, or fearful loss of life must inevitably have occurred. Every one of the eight coaches was derailed, and thrown higgledy-piggledy corers the metals, end fully two hundred yards of sleepers were reduced to rnatchwood. The noise brought a crowd of helpers from the village. One of the staff of the Broughton Copper Works close' by was standing at the time of the accident a hundred yards away. He heard a loud rapping noise, and saw the engise part from the tender and run on some hundred yards. The tender then left the first coach, and after running in a crippled way with a wheel off toppled over the embankment. The recent smash was fresh in his mind, and he and others from the office hurried in alarm to do what they could. Dr Jerome Murphy, of Runcorn, who did much for the injured passengers on September 17, also appeared ready to give his services again within a few minutes of the accident. Many of the passengers had got out as soon as they could, and there was a general confusion for some minutes until the assurances of the guard and other officials helped every one to realize that the accident was no worse. It was not, however, until all had been gathered on the station that it was found how singularly fortunate the escape had been. Many women were unnerved for the time. One who was very dis- tressed said that her husband's coffin was in the guard's van, and it was at once carried out to a waiting-room. The excitement, however, soon Quietened down. Most of the passengers told very much the same experi- ence. They felt a jolt and .waited in alarm as the train bumped over the permanent way until it came to a stop. In some cases a window broke, and in the more crowded carriages—there were a number of excursion parties returning to North Wales from Liverpool—one or two were thrown against the others on the other side. They all feared that a serious accident might be happening to other coaches, and were all relieved when they found that that was not so. After it was found on the station that no one needed medical treatment they were all sent forward by a elow train through War- rington, which arrived in Widnes from Liverpool, and reached Chester about two hours late. The traffic along the line was of course suspended. But breakdown gangs soon arrived and set to work. By ten o'clock all but two of the derailed coaches had been got back on the lines, and it was anticipated that it would not take many hours before the lines were relaid.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 30, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 30, 1912.
WOMEN LIBERALS,
SUCCESSFUL SOCIAL IN ST. JOHN'S
WARD.
MR. AND MRS. A. H. CROSFIELD AND THE BOLTON VICTORY.

The satisfaction felt by all sections of the pro- gressive forces at the magnificent victory for Liberalism in the Bolton by-election is shared by the members of the Warrington Women's Liberal Associa- tion who, at another of their series of ward socials on Monday evening, hailed with enthusiasm the speakers' references to this signal evidence of the Lancashire workers' loyalty to the causes of Free Trade and social reform. There is no more active section of the War- rington Liberal forces than the women's organization and the gatherings held from time to time in the various wards do much to maintain the interest of the workers. Monday evening's social, which was for members and friends in St. John's Ward, was one of the most successful ever held. About 350 sat down to tea, which was followed by the usual concert, inter- spersed with sreeches. Excellent arrangements had been made by the ward captain (Mrs Roberts), the members of the committee and the hon. sem-wary of the aFsociation s Edmund Osborne). A hearty welcome was extended to Mr and Mrs A H Crosfield and Miss Crcsfield who are keenly interested in the efforts of the association. Amongst those present, in addition to the officials and members of the committee, were Councillor James Shaw, Councillor J Skelland, Mr W Fielden (Todmorden), Mr P Delaney and Mr E Hughes. An interesting musical programme was sub- mitted and every item was well received. Mrs PII Brown gave a couple of songs, in pleasing style ; Mt Stubbs displayed talent as a pianist ; lr Fielden delighted the audience with humorous songs and Mr S AuLland was, as usual, highly popular in his comic sketches and concertina solos.

Mrs. CROSFIELD, in an introductory speech, said they had every reason to be in a jubilant frame of mind. (Applause.) In the first place, the meeting was a splen- d:d ore. She hid ou several occasions been present at gatherings in that room Lut the attendance that even- ing excelled all previous records in that respect. They had now a Literal representative of St John's Ward— (applause)—and she was delighted to take that oppor- tunity of congratulating Councillor Shaw on his great and magnificent victory. Further, they as Liberals had additional rearon to be elated at the

SUCCESS ACHIEVED BY THEIR PARTY IN THE BOLTON By-ELECTION. (Loud applause.) They all knew what the result ef the election would be—they expected a Liberal victory because they knew that people of common-sense would support the causes of Free Trade and progress—but they did not expect such a fine majority. (A VOICE : " A better cue next time.") Let them hope the better one would be in Warrington. (Applause.) Mrs Croefleld then emphasised the fact that politics, in some aspects, concerned women even moro deeply than men, for modern legislation terded more and more to affect home life. Women could look at such questieus with a more practical eye than the men and they should be grateful to the Government for introducing measures which must conduce to home comfort and happiness in a far greater degree than the work of any previous Government. They had passed Bills referring to health, the standard of living, the education of the children and the wages of the workers. Mr Boner Law had declared hitemlf absolutely in favour of the introduction, at the earliest opportunity, of tariff reform—that war, the taxation of fcod, clotling and all the necessities of the home. As Liberda they had to light as hard as possible against the Protectionist propaganda and explain to their tariff reform friends all that Free Trade meant and how much the happiness of the home and of the child'en was bound up with the maintenance of that system. The Government had also done a great deal to combat the evil of sweating, from which the women especially suffered, for it was they who were often over-worked and nnderpaid. Another measure which touched women very closely was the

INSURANCE ACT. Of course, a great many people had run it down. At the outset, when the Conservatives thought people would immediately understand and appreciate it and that it would he a great success, they were all speaking in favour it. lAter when they saw that people did not quite realise the benefits which the measure would confer and were inclined to find fault with its details, they turned their backs on it and raid " This Insurance Bill is the worst thing that could possibly have happened." (Laughter.) One striking example of that Tolle face was their member's brother, Mr. F. E. Smith. (Laughter.) Perhaps they did not like to hear her calling Mr. Harold Smith their member—(laughter)— she did not care to hear herself using the word; but, under the present circumstances, that was his title. They hoped it would not be for long. (Laughter.) Mr F. E. smith was one of the first to declare himself strongly in favour of the Insurance Bill, but as soon as he saw the trend of events was not quite what he had expected, he turned right-about lace and began to criticise and condemn the Bill. When the benefits were in actual operation, the Conservatives would doubt- less change their tune again, and be only too anxious to claim some of the credit for the Bill. (Hear, hear.) The worst thing that could happen to a household was unemployment following upon the illness of the breadwinner—in fact it often led to the breaking-vp of the home. Such unfortunate events were robbed of much of their terror by the Insurance Act which would place the worker in a position of comparative security. John Bright had I declared : "The nation in every country dwells in the cottage and, unless the light of your constitution can shine there, unless the beauty of your legislation and the excellence of your statesmanship are impressed there on the feeling and condition of the people, rely upon it you have yet to learn the duties of government. The other side undoubtedly had 3et to learn those duties, but she ventured to state that the Liberal Government had impressed its influence on the feeling and condition of the people and had caused the light of its legislation to shine in the bumble homes of our land. (Applause.) 'there had been a
GRILVF DEAL OF ROWDYISM IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

lately, under the leadership of Mr. Boner Law. The people of Belfast were also .being incited to rebellion by leaders of the Opposition. They kolieved, however, that the _people were much too sensible to listen to such counsels, but at the same time it must be remembered that the women were the first to suffer when law and order were broken and anarchy reigned in their place. Did those members who had been behaving like unruly school boys in the House imagine that they would create any impression, but that of disgust? Did they think they could force Mr Asquith and the Government to resign by springing a little surprise on the House ? Of course not. Mr Asquith and his colleagues had many measures to pass for the welfare of the people and they were going to remain in office until they had placed them on the statute book. (Applause.) A few school boy tricks would not frighten them into resignation, (Applause.) At the same time, she would impress upon the Liberal women of War- rington that they must be prepared for any emergency. They must have their weapons burnished and not allow themselves to be taken by surprise. She did not think the time of trial was near—in fact she was sure it was not—but a good soldier was always watching and sentries must be continually on guard. (Applause.) Mr W FIELDEN than gave a short but telling topical address, enlivened with a fund of humorous stories. He said it was one of the most promising signs of the times that women were taking an intelligent interest in politics ; theyf were realizing that those people who looked out for themselves heel a much better chsnce than those who were indifferent to what was going on around them. Women had suffered for their lack of interest in politics in the past and he was glad that their outlook was now widening. In Mr Lloyd George —(applause)—they had a man who had lived the humble life of the working people and who realized the hardships and drawbacks to which they were subjected. He bad, therefore, come to the conclusion that too much was made of the man who did not want much help and too little of the man who really needed it. having set to work to counteract that inequality, who could tell where his efforts would finish ? The legislation of to-day, and that which was promised for the next few years, was not in the interests of the squire and the parson and their friends, but of the mass of the people who earned the wealth of the country and who deserved help the most. (Applause). Councillor JAMES SHAW referred to his recent victory in St. John's Ward and took the opportunity of refuting some of the mis-statements circulated by Iris opponents. He denied that there was issued, along with his poll-card, an announcement in connection with Evangelical services at Brick-street Mission, of " a shilling tea for sixpence." His asser- tion that, before entering the Council, he had interested himself in bribging the question of the lighting of the ward before the Council, bad also been ridiculed. As a mat ter of fact, the day after his defeat at the previous election, he wrote the Town Clerk calling attention to the had lighting of John-street and pointing out that it was the chief means of access from many streets to Horseruarketestreet. He felt highly honoured thlt he had been chosen to represent the ward, particularly as he understood it was about fourteen years since St John's had a Liberal Councillor*

IF cutting his teeth makes your child fretful, get a Stccdman's Powder for him. Thio medicine contains no poison or narcotic, but relieves feverish heat and preserves a healthy state of the constitution.

He had been placed on the Cemetery, Sanitary, Health, Rivers and Bridges Committees, and be had alreredy attended about twelve meetings. if he continued like that, he would have a very good record, and he believed his opponents would have a great difficulty in ousting him. (Applause.) He felt the work of a Town Coun- cillor was almost a sacred duty. Although the duties of a member of Parliament took primary rank, Parliament deputed to the municipal authorities ' the administration of important measures. He believed that if the laws already in force were thoroughly administered, there would be a great improvement in our municipal life. (Applause.) Councillor Shaw concluded by reading a letter he had received from Mr A H Crosfteld after his election, stating : "The town ass whole, without distinction of party, is to be congratulated on your election to the Council, but recognizing, as we all must, to how large an extent party politics do enter into municipal elections, how great a triumph your splendid victory has been for the Literal and progressive party and also for yourself." (Applause). Mr. A. H. CROSS IEL D, who hail a great reception, said be agreed that they as Liberals hal very good reason to be in good feather. The victory won by his old friend Councillor Shaw, in St. John's Ward, was a red letter event in the history of the party in War- rington. (Applause.) Then there had been a pretty ignilicaut triumph at Bolton, where they bad given their opponents something like the knock-out. (Applause.) He attached even greater importance to that result in view of the fact that the tariff reformers had been so plainly showing

div.head: CLOVEN 1100.-P OP PROTECTION.
div.p: THE CLOVEN 1100.-P OP PROTECTION.

They were unmasked now. There had been a lot of beating about the bush and many attempts to obscure the issue, but they had now come out into the open. The Bolton election was the fist which had followed the declaration made by the tariff reformers in Londoli that they were going to stick to their plan of putting taxes on food and all the articles that entered most essentially into tho lives of the people who lived in the humble Lorces of Britain. Liberals and progressives maintained that that was an evil and wiclei policy. (Hear, hear.) Ile knew how many questions in these modern times were affecting women quite as ;much as men, but even including old age pensions and the Insurance Act, the question which, above all others, concerned the women, was that of Free Trade. It might have its complicated sides, but fundamentally it was just a question of whether in England, with our teeming industrial population, we were to have the right to buy those articles which were necessary to existence at the natural price, or whether we were to hal e an art:tidally enhanced price placed upon them. When one considered that in the vast majority of cases it was the wife who had to see that the ends were made to meet week by week, he did not

div.head: KNUTSFORD DIVISION LIBERALS.
div.p: KNUTSFORD DIVISION LIBERALS.

Mr. Needham at Whaley Bridge. Mr. C. I'. Needham, M.P. for South-West Manchester, and Mr. Oliver, Liberal :candidate for the Knutsford division, visited Whaley Bridge on Saturday evening and addressed a public meeting there. Mr. Needham M.P., in advocating Mr. Oliver's candidature, said the Conservatives now threatened to make drastic amendments in the Insurance Act, but they did not vote against it on the third reading in the House of COITIMODs. They controlled the House of Lords, but there the Insurance Act was passed without a division. All this was done because it was seen there was party capital to be made for the Unionists during the waiting period. He hoped there would soon be an agreement with the doctors. The great aim of the Insurance Act was to improve the health of the country, and he bad no doubt that that would be achieved. Referring to the Old Age Pensions Act and the election at Bolton, the speaker pointed out that in Bolton alone there was a diminution of 586 persons in receipt of out-relief as compared with the period before the passing of the Act, and that to pay these people would require a rate of 91. or 101 in the pound. Thtse two measures would enormously relieve the poor-rate of the country, and they would be able to extend these beneficent measures by the natural growth of the revenue which was tappei by the Budget of 1909. They would have to fight Tariff " Reform "again, but he had no doubt as to the result of any election in this part of tha country fought on the Tariff question. On the question of Home Rule the Unionists spoke with two voices. When they wanted to alarm an audience in this country they said the proposed Irish Parliament would have almost the powers of a sovereign state, but when they talked to the Irish Nltionalists they said the powers wore not large nor wide enough. It was being said from house to house, but not cn the plat- form, that the Irish Parliament would pass legislation to persecute Catholics, but Sir Edward Carson said he certainly had never said so.

div.head: USES OF ESPERANTO.
div.p: THE USES OF ESPERANTO.

Mr H B Mudie, president of the British Ezzperanto Association, gave a lecture at the Manchester Grammar School on Saturday afternoon on " What Esperanto can do for you." Mr Mudie said that the ordinary traveller the advantage of Esperanto was that it abolished frontiers, and found him friends everywhere ; or the man of science the scientific literato in Esperanto wi uld have that universal currency that was so much needed in science ; and for the commercial traveller, that it inter-nationalised all markets. Mr Mudie men- tioned the fact that the British and Foreign Bible Society had consented to do the Bible into Esperanto, and that this Esperanto version would appear on the Ist of December.

div.head: WELBECK ABBEY.
div.p: WELBECK ABBEY.

The King and Queen have this week been on a vi.sit to the Duke and Duchess of Port- land at Welbeck Abbey. This ie his Majesty's first visit since his acceseion. The last crowned heads to occupy the State apartments were the late King Edward and

Queen Alexandra. Welbeek is one of the most splendid seats in England. The King has been occupied mainly in shooting over the splendid game preserves of the Welbeck estate. The Queen has paid visits to the chief places of interest in the district.

wonder at the rplendid rally to Liberalism amongst the women of War' ington—(applause)— because be could not imagine how any thoughtful, responsible woman could hesitate one minute between baying as cheaply as it was possible to buy under natural conditions and entering upon a reign of dearness and scarcity. Look- ing at all the signs of the times, they would agree that the Prime Minister was quite justified in his state- ment that in the political garden to-day there was

div.head: NO SICKLIER- PLANT
div.p: NO SICKLIER- PLANT

than tariff reform.: (Hear, hear.) They had learnt a little during the nine years since the raging, tearing propaganda was started. They remembered some of the prophecies with which the tariff reformers tried to bamboozle the people of Lancashire and Yorkshire into abandoning Free Tra e. They were told first of all that we were going to lose cur over-sea trade—that gigantic export (redo which found a livelihood for so many hundreds of homes in Warrington alone. They had seen what that prediction was worth—how the figures had mounted up until we were now far past the 1,000 millions of over-sea trade per annum. (Applause.) He could remember the time when that limit was looked to as a kind of landmark that we might possibly reach some time, but we had exceeded it. (Applause.) He could give heaps of examples of the realer s, ignorant, stupid talk of the tariff reformers, but of all the astounding statements that were made surely, to us in Lancashire, the threat that if we did not havetariff reform cotton would go " was about the most ridiculous. (Applause.) Cotton had indeed gone, in one sense, and was still going to all the ends of the earth—a trade built up under Free Trade and which was the envy of every industrial nation in the world— (applau9e)—as well as the supporter of the homes and well-being of hundreds of thousands of people in the C3unty Palatine. (Applause.) A further prophecy as that without tariff reform we could not maintain a united Empire. It w.:s no exaggeration to say that the Empire was never more united than at the present day, and the feeling of kinsmauship and patriotism which pervaded it was stronger than at any other period of our history. (Applause.) Another fact which made one suspicious of tariff reformers was that after nine years of propaganda they were not, in the slightest degree, able to agree among themselves. Not one of them could define tariff reform—in fact they seemed to be in a state of bewilderment on the subject. On the one hand they repeatedly told us that we must be prepared to mako sacrifices to maintain the unity of the Empire, while in the next breath they tried to commend Tariff Reform as remarkably good business. If the solidarity of the Empire 'did depend upon sacrifice, he was sure the vast majority of &Webers would be prepared to make it. But we had got a united Empire and if ue were going to introduce into the Imperial household money matters and set up a system of haggling and bargaining betueen the different sections, he could think of nothing more calculated to sow the seeds of discord while at the same time com- pelling our people to pay through the nose for every- thing on the score of promoting concord. Tariff Reform in many respects resembled the

div.head: CHEAP JACK CURE
div.p: CHEAP JACK CURE

which was supposed to be a remedy for everything and very often killed the person who took it. It was nauseous to see wealthy people meeting together to dice at £l,ofo per head and trying to impose taxes on all the necessities of the workingclasses. (Hear, hear.) The case for Fre() Trade was impregnable. It was the basis on which we had to build the structure of modern civilization which would reduce the disparities of life and spread, .on a much wider scale than had hitherto existed in England, a general level of well-being. (Applause.) It was mainly owing to the labours of John Bright and Richard Cobden that, after a tremendous struggle, Free Trade was carried. Speaking after the death of Cobden, Bright touchingly summed up the outcome of his efforts in the words : "There is not a homestead in the country in which there is not added comfort through his labours, not a cottage the dwellers in which have not steadier employment, higher wages and a more solid independence. (Applause.) Those were the facts which Free Trade had helped us to realize and even if they as Liberals had no other cause to work for, it was worthy of their highest and unremiting efforts. (Loud applause) Miss CROSFIELD proposed a vote ot thanks to the. artiste and also addressed a few words of encouaage- went to the association. The vote of thanks was heartily accorded.

WEALTHIEST TWINS. FORTUNES FROX GROUND RENTS.

Lady Howard de Walden gave birth to'ltwins, a boy and a girl, at Seaford House, Be'grave-square, London, on Wednesday. The twins will be two of the wealthiest babies in the country. Their fathers income is estinnted at between £200,000 and £300,000 a year, drawn mainly from his Mary lebone estate, which extends to Oxford-street and includes Cavendish-square. Lord Howard de Walden is also the owner of valuable property at Kilmarnock, Ayrshire, and recently bought Chick Castle, Denbigh, and the Island of Shona, on the West Coast of Scotland. Seaford House—he is also Lord Seaford—was remodelled by him a few years ago at a cost of some £200,000. Lady Howard de Walden is twenty-one, ten years younger than her husband. There is no record of boy and girl twins having been the first born of an aristocratic family in recent times.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A New Way with Ilouse-Flies.---For this year the house-fly has ceased from troubling, and if its disease - carrying habits are not very much exaggerated, sickness should he less prevalent in winter than in summer time. All authorities, however, are agreed that the house-IIY is a real danger, to which the Local Government Board is giving its serious attention. In a report published by that department in 1910, reference was made to the possibility of attacking the house-fly by spreadin Infection among the species. Similsr methods have been tried for exterminating rats, rabbits, and other pests, and they have generally failed. It may,however, be otherwise with the house-fly, which is peculiarly sub- ject to fungus disease. The dead flies one sees on glass, or walls, surrounded by a whitish patch, have all died of a fungus growth, which at death bursts from their bodies. Means have now been discovered for producing cultures of this fungi, and it is suggtsted that flies might be destroyed wholesale, if popular means were adopted to spread the fungus infection among them in the early summer. But possibly the fly might have its revenge, for it appears that when one dies millions of fungi spores are discharged into the air, and these,manY scientists declare, are a danger, albeit a remote one, to human beings.

Hard Times. for Cats.—The higher cost of living ig not only troubling the housewife, but, also her domestic pets. Motor traction hqs to a very large extent superseded the horse-drawn vehicle, and although it has greatly increased the number of accidents in the streets, the victims are mostly human beings and net horses. The result is, a considerable live in the price for cats meat, owing to shortage of supplies, and what poor pussy will do when there are no dLad horses at all to be marketed, one hardly knows. That however, 15 not the only danger, which threatens the domestic cat. With the great increase in the price of paltry generallY there has arisen a brisk demaad for cat skins, and in ell the great towns and cities, there are complaints of tbe depredations of the cat stealers, which account for the mysterious disappearance of many domestic pets. It is a heartless form of robbery, and often causes the greatest grief to the ownerootwithst inding Calverley's lines in 'Sad Memories." Should ever anything be missed—milk, coals, umbrellas, brandy—the cat's pitched into a ith a boot, or anything that's handy. The Popularity of the Sash.—The scarf scorns to have suddenly disappeared, a matter for regret, for it is an elegant Lod becoming accessory, capable moreover of biding the deficiencies of a dress that has seen its best days. Its plsce appears to be taken by the sash, which resumes shapes end forms hitherto unknown. The arrangement of this popular accessory is somewhat reminiscent of the Turkish harem, where the sash swathes the figure tightly, and covers the urper part of the skirt ; or again one is reminded of some Eastern easante model of draping the wide sash, which gives so picturesqne a finish to his costume. Even panniers rye draped and knotted to represents sash. No evening dress is complete without a sash of some sort, and nil kinds of handsome e broideries and fringes adorn the ends of these indispensable adjuncts of fashionable gowns,.

The Vogue of the Long Coat.—There is no doubt whatever about the suitability, and the popularity of this s-tason's long coats. To prove the truth of this . statement it is only necessary to attend any fashion- able function where well-dressed women congregate, and it is safe to say that every ether one will wear a long coat of some sort. All coats wrap over end fasten at the side, many have draped effects and others are pro- vided with trains, that happily may be looped up. new material used for these garments, is velours frapPe the surface of which is covered with tiny crescents, checks cc lines. This fabric is also used for coats and skirts with good &Lt. Many of the newest long coats are trimmed with a new fur, which be.nts a strong resemblance to sable, but is much less soft in colour, the hair being q lite wiry—It is an expensive pelt. The Zortave Coat.—The terrible war raging in the Balkan States, has probably drawn attention to Bulgarian and Hungarian fashions, and led to the re-appearance of the Zouave coat. In its present shaper which differs, of course, from that worn some yeara ago' it is becoming to any type of figure. The Zouave of to-day has a long elegant line, is rounded under the arms, and is moderate in length. It is suitable for theatre or afternoon wear, and in any case must be made of rich materials, richly embroidered, and gorgeous in colouring. The Bulgarian coat, from which the Zouave is copied, is of embroidered cloth, lined with sheepskin ; it is warm end handsome. Women and intellectual Interests.—The Actresses' Franchise League has taken steps to show that politics are not necessarily dissociated from beauty, or persons' charm. There is something like a general belief that this is the case. It was therefore arranged by the League nut some 40 actresses of undoubted beauty, Biad who are strenuous advocates of votes for women should take part in some artistic suffragist tableau at a matinee this week at the Lyceum Theatre. That has afforded proof positive that all suffragists do not look like prize' lighters. There is no doubt that athletics, business, sports, and politics, must create a certain tendency te a more robust woman, but it does not necessarily mean that the sex will lose its feminine attributes. The activities of the modern woman work to her physicist benefit ; and intellectual interests, whether in politica, art, literature, or business, do not detract from personal charm or beauty. A Beauty Map of the British Isles,—The °lain? advanced by Mr Dawson, of the Royal Nations' Literary Society of Ireland, that Dublin girls are the prettiest, would have been freely allowed by Qto'e: Victoria, who was struck with the beauty of Iris, women, when she first visited the Emerald Isle—lrist. , eyes, and a fine skin favoured by the soft wester?, climate, contlitute their special charm. In the Isle 01 Wight and West of England, women genarally hat good complexions, and Scottish lassies BB a all have regularity of features. Most artists, however: are of the opinion that Lonchn is • the Mead favoured spot in the British Isles, as regards goo looking women. This was the opinion of Sir Franco' Dalton, whose zeal for eugenics led him to impropriate a beauty ma of the British Isles. Ha walked the streets in many towns in all parts of the Kingdoca, carrying an instrument for ticking off and classifyiog all the women he met. iie labelled them as ettractiv?! indifferent, or repellent, and at the end of his investl. gations he declared that " London ranks highest 10. female beauty, and Aberdeen lowest." As confirmiOg Sir Francis Galton's opinion, respecting the metropolo:! it may be:mentioned that all the prizes at this yesr° Folkestone beauty show, were taken by Lou residents.

LOCAL WILL.—Tbe will of the late Mrs. Mary Warburton, of the Cross, Lymm, has been proved at 41,675. WEDDING.—The marriage took place at the Primitive Methodist Church, Lymm, on Wednesday morning, of Mr. Henry Appleton, of Rush Green, to Mrs. Elizabeth olleming, of Sandy-lane, widow of the late Mr. James Fleming. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. R. W. B. Whiteway, resident minister, The bride, who Was neatly attired in a navy blue costume, wore a fancy Straw hat vvitt. a black lancer plume, and was accom- Panied by her daughter, Miss Fleming, who was prettily dressed in green. Mr. H. Proffitt, the brother of the bride, performed the duties of best man. Later on the bridal pair left for Blackpool, where the honeymoon is being spent. Additional interest was attached to the wedding owing to it being the first one under the ,

newly appointed Lymm registrar, Mr. H. T. Mercer. PARISH CHURCH TEA PARTY.—One of the great annual events on the Lymm calendar, namely, that of the " Parish Tea," with its attendant entertainment and dance' was brought to a successful conclusion in the Drill Hell on Wednesday night. There was an excellent muster at the tea tables, about 500 persons Partaking of the ample supply of edibles that had been Plovided. The material demands of the "inner man" having been attended to, the audience indulged in a /east of song and mirth, Miss Craggs and Mr William Gorman, of Altrincham being the artistic caterers. Prior to their programme the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, M.A., in a brief speech welcomed his guests and expressed his pleasure at seeing such a large company present, and hoped that the artistes aould be well received. Although the enter- tainment was limited to one hour the audience had a thoroughly enjoyable time provided for them by the following items :—Duets, "The rain came pitter patter down," • The keys of heaven " ; solos by Miss Craggs 'The lass with a delicate air," "The Brook," and "Dear Old England " ; contributions by Mr Gorman were : a musical monologue "The 11.69 Express," The Lady's Penny Paper," " Months and months and months," in which the audience played a prominent Part, imitation of a little girl giving an essay on the cow, two items in dumb show-1, "How different people cross the road," 2, "Stitching Buttons," and lastly an example of magnetism as demonstrated by the actions of a wooden table. Both artistes, who were . . .

Cooke, by the skilful accompaniments 'of Mr W F.R.C.0., made most of their opportunities,Miss Craggs' sweet singing being warmly applauded, as was Mr Garman for his amusing songs, patter and Puns. At the conclusion of the concert the room was cleared of forms chairs, tables, &c. Slid in a short time a large number of couples occupied the spacious floor of the Drill Hall and were tripping the light fantastic toe to the strains of music emanating from McDermott:s Quadrille Band. Messrs Evans and Hillier carried out the duties of ALCs. The following ladies and gentlemen proved to be excellent workers Under the control of the Rector :—Mesdames P A Ardern, Burrowes, A W Callender, W Cooke, Ditchfield, Druce, Hill, Hillier, Lathom, Lowe, Moulds- Worth, Odber, Omar, H Pearson, Richardson, ,Richards, Saville, S Scragg and Watkin. The Misses trazendale, Fanny Cadman, Callender, Maud Darby- shire, Gartoo, Goffin, Hardwicke, Hill, Innes, Kirk, Minnie Mothers, Mills, Mouldswortb, Vorris, Annie Owen, Winnie Owen, Eva Richards, M Saville, Watkins and Wilson. Messrs Druce, Hillier, }Emote, Hodgson Odber, H Pearson, Rishardson, Richards and Woodhead, PRIMITIVE METHODIST ANNIVERSARY.— Last week- end the anniversary of the Primitive Methodist Church was celebrated. The preacher on Sunday was Mr J Sivil, of Sheffield (ex-vice-president of Conference) who delivered striking sermons at the morning and evening services. His subject for the former service was that " The dew of God," Hosea xiv, 5. He prefaced his remarks on the " dew " by giving a description of Israel's relation to God at the time and said that the estranged people had just returned to their God and that amongst the joys of the return were God's promised ?leasing:, as illustrated in the characteristics of the dew, I.e. That the dew was 1, a refresher; 2, a fertiliser; 0:! _composed of the common or surrounding atmosphere. Alt Sivil's text in the evening was from Luke xii., 20, But God said unto him, Thou fool." After deaiing With the capabilities of the farmer referred to in the Shove chapter,the preacher commended his industry and said that the failing or sin lay in the decision " Soul take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." The follow- ing were given as the reasons for God calling the man tool. Firstly, because in his plan of life the man left out the most important thing—God. Secondly, when .lats said to his soul" take thine ease '&c he made a 4lttal mistake for in each person there is a continual Warfare between right and wrong, which must go OD nntil the end of this life, and so by telling his soul to ease this struggle the farmer was giving way in his lower nature. The soul that gets ntrong is the one that continues the "good aght." Thirdly, when he thought to feed his Soul with "Corn." Material things, said Mr Sivil, Would not satisfy the needs of the soul as Esau had found out. He urged those present to include God in ',nu plan of their life, and to fight their battle with God's help and they would find that life would be lull of nobility, happiness, and prosperity. At this service the choir gave a spirited interpretation of Dr .1 Clarke- nhitfleld's "In Jewry is God known."—A choral service Was held on Sunday afternoon when Mr a L Welford Ir,t4ad " The hymn and the crisis," by J Morley Adams; he choir, under the leadership of Mr J Edwards, sing- ;Pß the various hymns referred to, and the anthems God is a spirit " (Sir William Bennett) ; " Cross and Crown " (J it Thomas), solo sung by lisS Esther Appleton ; "Rock of Ages " (Dudley Duck), solo by Miss M J Appletou and "Jerusalem, r3l3' glorious home" (Lowell Mason) ; Miss Shore 81ng the organist.—On Monday evening there was a 81.69 assembly to partake of a choice and excellently ilerved tea, provided by Mesdames H Champ, a W C'ross, J Edwards, W Moss, E Moss, and G L Welford ; and the Misses Goodwin, Hallam, Smith, and Welford. Ater in the evening Mr 3 Sivil presided over a eeture, and opened the proceedings with an ideal 14,11 d witty, if brief, address. After expressing 18 pleasure at a renewal of his acquaintance Zl;th the Lyrnm friends, the lectiaer, the Rev „ Cooper, of Warriogton, spoke on the topic of the hate.' Alter a humorous reference to 'ne broad-brimmed hats that ladies were wearing he 41ticl that his subject dealt with the Quakers.He gave an csnutline history of George Fox, the founder of ,Inakerism. This was followed by a description of the Znaracteristics of the Quakers :—The origin of the -4111° ; the peculiar mode of living and of dress (not c)ntitting the broad-brimmed hats); the growth of the 11:89vement ;the persecution it encountered, on stories of ;Non life and the judgemnts God infliclei on their per- nUtors ; their humour: and in conclusion, the high PS they essayed to achieve. A vote of thanks to Mr Rev W Cooper, and all the workers, was proposed Mr G L Welford,seconded by the Rev It W B White- '3', and carried unanimously. A DISPUTED ACCOrNT. WESLEYAN CHAPEL GAS SUPPLY.

At a meeting of the Gas Committee held on November 21st, a letter was read from the Rev Pawlyn (treasurer of the Wesleyan Church) declining to pay an account of £3 9s 9d, the cost of gas consumed during the past June quarter, The objection was on account of excessive consumption.—The Gas Manager reported a leakage from a pipe in the ceiling of the chapel. After a discussion the Clerk was instructed to write and ask for payment of the account and to state that the Council were not responsible for leakage.—All the minutes were approved,

div.head: PROPOSED INCREASE OF MEMBERS.
div.p: PROPOSED INCREASE OF MEMBERS.

The Clerk said he had received a letter from the County Offices at Chester in reference to the proposed increase of members. The letter stated that the County Council at its meeting held on November 14th decided that in their opinion a prima facie case had been made out for the proposal contained in the petition of the Urban Council. A local inquiry should be held into the subject matter thereof, and a committee had been appointed for that purpose. He proposed arranging for the inquiry to be held on the morning of Tuesday, the 17th proximo.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the above committee held on November 28th were approved. They stated that Mr Ridgway submitted a draft agreement for the purchase of waterworks as agreed to by Messrs Simpson North and Co., vendor's solicitors _ _
On the proposition of Mr Virelford, seconded by the Rev G B Thurston, it was unanimously decided to recommend the council to approve of the draft.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.
WESLRY G lIILD.—The usual weekly meeting was held on•Tnesday evening. The chair was ,occupied by

Mr J H Mason, literary secretary. Mr J Baligave most instructive and interesting paper on "William Morris." The poet's works were freely illustrated by suitable quotations, finely rendered. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer on the proposition of Mr Arthur Bennett seconded by Mr E C London.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

SANKEY CRICKET CLUE DANCE AND WHIST DRIVE. —The annual whist drive and dance of the above Club took place at Sankey schools on Friday last and right well did the members and friends gather together fully 130 being present. Dancing commenced at 8 p.m. and continued until early morning. The 111. C's for dancing were Messrs T Whitfield, B Wright and H Plumpton. The Bros W and J Ray were the accom- panists. The winners of the whist drive were :—Ladies: I,Miss Darlington ; Miss Bardsley,consolation. Gentle- men : 1, Mr T Owen; Mr W Lawton, consolation. The M.C. was Mr F Davies, who also distributed the prizes at the close. The hield of which the Sankey Club are holders of (belonging to the Warrington and Dis- trict Cricket League) for this year. was on view In the school. Mrs George Clarke supplied the refreshments.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.
FREE CHURCH SALE OF WORK.

A sale of work for the liquidation of the debt on the Winwick Free Church was held on Thursday and yester- day. The room had been very tastefully decorated and there was a great array of useful and fancy goods on the stalls. [he following is a list of the stallholders : Drapery Stall :—Mesdames Lawson, Holmes, Davies and Bate.
Fancy Stall :—Mesdames Ormiston, Carter & Hewitt. China Stall :—Mesdames Dodd and Hewitt. Dairy and Sweet Stall :—Misses Ormiston and Sballcross.

Refreshment Stall :—Miss Ormiston, Mesdames A Lawson, Milligan, Evans and Crompton. At the opening of the proceedings on Thursday. the chair was occupied by the Rev J Yonge, who, from the first, has had much part in the promotion of the cause. After singing, prayer was led by Mr C E Parker, J.P., of Penketh. Mr Yonge referred to the promotion of the Church, under the auspices of the Warrington Free Church Council several years ago. He stated that Nonconformist services had been held with consider- able success from that time to the present and the desire now is to reduce, or if possible, to extinguish the debt on this building of £4OO, still outstanding. The endeavour was stimulated by the recent generous challenge of Mr C E Parker to double any sum which might now be secured. Considerable and painstaking efforts have been made by the Winwick Nonconformists and the display of fancy and plain articles was taste- fully arranged.

M'rsArrn'tage, in opening the bazaar, expressed her pleasure in doing so in a brief but practical address. and also her sincere hope that it migbt prove a com- plete success. Mr Parker proposed, and Mr Ormiston, who has been the superintendent of the work from the beginning, cordially seconded a resolution of thanks to Mrs Armitage. which was carried with acclamation.

A further vote of thanks to Mr ParEer, op the motion of two of the members of the congregation, for all his constant and generous help; and the Chairman also was thanked for his services that day, and on fre- quent occasions in the past. There was a very good attendance, despite the storm of [WOW and rain which prevailed without. The assembly then commenced a raid upon the stalls. The sale was re-opened yesterday by Mrs Simpson, the chair being occupied by Mr T Griffiths. To-day further arrangements are to be carried out to dispose of the articles provided. It should be added that tea and refreshments were tastefully arranged under the care of Mrs Ormiston and her daughters assisted by other ladies.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

OLD BOYS' DINNER.—The Orford Old Boys' Associa tion held their tenth annual dinner on Friday the 22nd inst., in the schools. The dinner was a great success, everyone voting it as one of the best they had attended. There was a decrease in numbers compared with other years, due to various causes, some of the members having to work late, &c. The general meeting was held previous to the dinner. Mr T S Steel read the Secre- tary's report, which was approved of, and duly signed. Mr Steel said it gave him very great pleasure in proposing that Mr John Cann be re-elected as president. Although he agreed with Mr Cann that someone else should have a band in the working of the association, and not have the same officers year after year. Still they knew a good man when they had one, and he thought they would be I doing a very unwise thing if they did not re-elect Mr Cann. No other name was proposed and Mr Cann was 1 re-elected unanimously. In a brief reply Mr Cann said that as these gatherings came round year after year he kept protesting against being in office so long, and he was still of the same opinion that some new blood ought to be brought into the management. Still if they were determined to have no one else he would continue to serve them to the best of his ability. Mr Steel was unanimously re-elected hon treasurer, and Mr T Reddish was also unanimously re-elected bon secretary. The committee elected were Messrs W J Woods, I Thomas Attwell, G Higham, John Gilbert. Walter Povey, George Ball, Charier. B Woods, H G Williams, I Thomas Williams and J Whitham ; and Messrs H Criicbley and J Smith were elected in the place of Mr R AndreWs (resigned) and Mr G H W Steel, who has taken a business in Chorley and so cannot attend. Mr Chas B Woods was appointed hon treasurer of the ways and means fund in place of Mr R Andrews. The com- pany then sat down to an excellent dinner which was served up with the usual smartness of the Atkinson Cafe Ltd. Warrington. After dinner a social evening was spent with songs, toasts, and short .speeches. The president proposed the toast " The king, Queen and Royal Family. Mr T Reddish sang the first verse of the National Anthem, which was taken up very heartily by the company. " Past and present managers" was proposed by Mr H G Williams and very ably responded to by the Rev G Vale-Owen, who was the only manager able to attend. " The President," was submitted by Mr T Reddish, and received with musical honours. Other toasts were " The Old Boys" proposed by Mr Steel, and responded 'to by Mr Charles B Woods, " Present scholars ' pro- posed by Mr IV Povey. responded to by Mr J Swinton, sen. A very enjoyable musical programme bad been arranged by Mr 'l' Attwell. Messrs J Sephton and W Dutton were in good trim and were loudly applauded for their several items, duets, " Battle Eve "I, and "Watchman " ; songs " Jolly old cavelier," W Dutton, and " Good company" and "Sailor's grave " by Mr J Sephton. Mr T Attwell sang "Monach of the storm," "0 hear the wild winds blow.'"' Down in the deep," and in response to an encore" Drinking," Mr J Gibson sang" Bombedier "and "True till death?! The duties of accompanist were in the very capable hands of Mr F Banner,

div.head: SCENE OF THE FINAL GREAT BATTLE.
div.p: SCENE OF THE FINAL GREAT BATTLE.

The above sketch map shows the scene of final great battle which the Bulgarians have commenced. In the foreground is shown the position of the Bulgarians. Immediately on the right are the Turkish warships which have shelled the bridge at Bijuk Chekmeje and stopped the Bulgarian advance along the road to Constantinople. The Turkish trenches in the low ground below the forts are indicated by short black lines. Those to the left of Tchatalja village are Bulgarian trenches. The famous Tchatalja forts are shown in their correct position, and on the extreme left can be seen the Turkish warships shelling the Bulgar left from the Black Sea.

div.head: STOCKTON HEA rn.
div.p: STOCKTON HEA rn.

GARDEN SOCIETY AT WALTON HALL.—OR Sunday afternoon the members of this society had the privilege of visiting the greenhouses at Walton I Ball to view the magnificent display of chrysanthemums. A large number availed themselves of the kind invitation of Sir Gilbert Greenell, Bart., and were conducted through the gardens by Mr C Goves, the head gardener. The chrysanthemums grown at Walton Hall have during the past few weeks been shown with great success at all the principal shows in Lancashire and Cheshire, and those who took advan- tage of the visit to the gardens on Sunday were delighted with the exceptionally fine display of blooms

div.head: GRA P PENHA LL.
div.p: GRA P PENHA LL.

A DANGEROUS CORNER—The dangerous corner opposite the Dog and Dart Inn, which has been the scene of several recent motor accidents is now very much improved. Corners have been taken off and levelled and it is now hoped that the danger to fast traffic have been removed.

LECTURES ON HORTICULTURE, Mr J R James (Holmes Chapel College) concluded his series of lectures on Monday evening last in the Council Scboollls His subject was "Apples and Pears." The leoturer gave a very lucid explanation of the subject. Altogether his lectures have been very interesting and very instructive. The Rector, Rev H V Pigott presided, and at the close proffered the thanks of the audience to Mr James. The lecturer responded and said that his duty as an horti- cultural lecturer was a pleasant one inasmuch as he loved the work. He hoped that some of the hearers would profit by his efforts. (Applause.) 'MOORE.

PAROCHIAL TEA.—The parochial tea in connection with the Daresbury Parish Church was held in the Milner Church Institute on Tuesday. At 6 o'clock a good number sat down to tea which was catered for by Mrs G Gandy. Afterwards a pleasant entertainment was given by local artistes. the programme including : —Dulcimer solos, Mr W Sleekly ; violin solo, Miss Hutchins ; Irish songs, Mr Gough ; recitations and songs, Mr Gilby ; pianoforte solo, Miss W Sloane; and sketches by Misses Partington, Lee Jones and Sloane. At the close the Vicar, who presided, proposed a vote of thanks, and, asked the audience to show their appre- ciation in the usual Cheshire fashion. _ _ _ _

WESLEY GUILD.—On Wednesday evening Mr R E O'Callaghan, of Manchester, gave one of his most interesting lectures entitled " Mutual aid amongst animals and co-operation in Nature,' which was illus- trated by excellent lantern slides. The lecture was presided over by Miss Dutton.

div.head: "MY MAYORALTY."
div.p: "MY MAYORALTY."

SOUTHPORT COUNCILLOR WHO SPENT £1,700. " My Mayoralty "was the subject of a remarkable lecture at the Southport Liberal Club on Thursday by the ex-Mayor (Mr F T Reynolds). He suggested that when an invitation was issued to anyone to accept the mayoralty he should be told what the probable cost would be over and above the salary voted by the Town Council. In Southport the salary was £5OO, and he himself had spent in all £1,700. Among the details he instanced the following items : Music and decorations £231 Refreshments Tobacco and Cigars ' 30 Wines and Mineral Waters Subscriptions to Bazaars,Sales of Work &ci 66 Subscriptions to Charities Carriages, Taxicab Bills &o l6B Subscriptions to Football Clubs, &c. Travelling Expenses to civic functions in other towns

Warrington Photographic Society. "Devonshire Cream" was the title of the Hon Treasurer's lecture on Tuesday to a very full audience. It dealt with the adventures and impressions of himself and wife in a cycle tour of 650 miles to Launceston through South Wales and back through the Shakespeare country. It was done in 17 days this summer, when the weather was fairly favourable, with only one puncture, and with2mt a railway ticket, and not "under the carriage seat" as a cruel friend suggested. The Bristol Channel was crossed from Swansea to Ilfracombe, and three days were spent at Appledore, Kingsley's "White Fisher Village," one of the few places unspoiled by the modern sea-side tripper. About 110 slides were shown. A hearty vote of thanks proposed by Mr E Seymour of Londbn, and seconded by Mr W Daintitb concluded a pleasant evening.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES MAN DROWNED..

The body of an old-age pensioner, named James Coyle (76), residing in Wellington-street, Winnes, was recovered from the Sankey and St. Helens Canal, near to Hutchinson's works abont noon on Sunday. He had been seen last alive about 7.30 on Saturday evening, when be seemed in his usual state of health. How the deceased got into the canal is at present unknown.

div.head: WIDNES BIRD CAGE SHOW.
div.p: WIDNES BIRD CAGE SHOW.

The sixteenth yearly show of the Widnes and District Cage Bird's Society was held in the Conservative Club on Saturday. There were 113 entries, and both for quality and quantity the exhibits were in advance of previous years. Borders and Norwich Greens were features of the show.

Mr R Porker Widnes, gained a special prize for the best bird in the show. Mr J Hampson, Warrington gained a similar award for the best British bird. The most notable prize-winners were IVIr NV Ridge, Wigan ; Mr S Andrews, Mr A Leycester, and Mr T Higham. Mr S Andrews scored the highest number of points with 127. RUNCORN LIBERALS' BALL. PRIZES FOR FANCY DRESSES. _

A fancy dress ball, promoted by the Runcorn Liberal Association, was held in the decorated drill hall on Wednesday evening. About 300 were present, fancy costumes and masks were generally worn, and a lengthy programme of dances was gone through. The judging took place at the interval, and the prizes were awarded as follows :-1, Miss Hind, " Eastern Princess " ; 2, Miss Grounds, huntress ; 3, Mrs Chenery, Welsh Disestablishment." Men : 1, J Charles,jockey ; 2, Mr G F Jones, cowboy; 2, Master H block, red Indian. Other prominent characters represented were " Duchess of Devonshire " (Mrs Corrin), " Folly" (Miss Aston), Indian squaws (Mrs Watson, Mrs Bulock, Miss Jones), and Irish colleen Miss Amy Gibson.

div.head: CHILDREN AND THE STAGE.
div.p: CHILDREN AND THE STAGE.

Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Alderman S Owens and Mr J B Aitken occupied the bench, when Madame Ada Mansell, of Leeds, applied for permission to allow her troop of nine boys and girls, whose ages ranged from fourteen to eleven years, to perform at the Co-operative Hall during the week. Applicant said all the children lived with her, and all attended school. They were finished by ten o'clock. The Clerk : Why didn't you make the application earlier ?

Miss Mansell : We only came in from Leeds last night. In answer to the Bench, applicant said several of the children were adopted because they had no parents. She had a written agreement, and was under an obliga- tion to consider their welfare to train them properly. Mr Aitkin : These children are being farmed for the purposes of money-making. Applicant : That is not so. Mr Aitken : We don't doubt you are very kind to these children, but the Bench can be no party to these children being used for this purpose, so that you can make money by it. The licences were refused.

div.head: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
div.p: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
COMMON SENSE ADVICE BY A. DISTINGUISHED SPECIALIST.

" Acid" stomachs are dangerous because acid irritates and inflames the delicate lining of the stomach, thus hindering and preventing the proper action of the stomach, and leading to nine-tenths of the cases of stomach trouble from which people suffer. Medicines and medicinal treatments are useless in such cases, for they leave the source of the trouble, the acid in the stomach, as dangerous as ever. The acid must be neutralised, and its formation prevented, and the best thing for this purpose is half a teaspoon- ful of bisurated magnesia, a simple antacid, taken in a little warm or cold water after eating, which not only neutralises the acid, but also prevents the fermentation from which acidity is developed. Foods which ordinarily cause greatest distress can be eaten with impunity if the meal is followed with a little bisurated magnesia, which can be obtained of any chemist, and should always be kept handy.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST HELENS HOMES. WHERE THE SUN NEVER SHINES.

At Wednesday's meeting of the St Helens Health Committee, Dr Buchan said he had very carefully pre- pared statistics as to the housing conditions in certain parts of the town, and there could be no doubt that overcrowding existed, such overcrowding as was bad for the health of the people. It was not necessary to bring up the forty-seven, as quite half of them were houses that had been reported on and closing orders made, but if desired he would lay before the committee the separate reports on all the forty-seven. He would be glad if the committee would take the whole question into consideration, because all the houses were those that the committee had been dealing with in a variety of ways. It was most interesting to find that the reports made by the police as to overcrowding and dirty houses were exactly the same as his staff had picked out. Mr W Bates said there were plenty of houses in the town, but a certain class of people would crowd together in one house in order to save rent. Mr Fox : That is so. I knew of a case of eight men sleeping in one room. Mr Forshaw said that dealing with the housing ques- tion would zertainly do something, but it would not do everything. Some people put the blame on the tenants and on the parents, but he thought as a fact some of the blame must attach to the landlords, while in some cases neither tenant nor landlord was to blame. If they closed every house in St. Helens that should not be inhabited they would cause a great deal more over- crowding than there was at present, or they would have the people in the streets. Mr Ellison: Best place for some of them. Mr Forshaw could not agree with that. He reminded the committee that they some time ago visited a place where there were twelve or fourteen houses with one common yard, the drainage of which was anything but satisfactory, and there was one water tap for all the houses. It was harder for those people to get clean water than it was for some people to get champagne. Then they went across the road from that place to a house that was entered from an alley, and when they got inside found that it was impossible to read a news- paper in the middle of the day without artificial light. People talked about an empire on which the sun never set. Why there were houses in St. Helens on which the sun never shone. The question was referred to the Housing Committee.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
A HOUSING REFORM BILL.

At the weekly meeting of the Parliamentary Debating Society on Thursday evening, a Bill for the better housing of the working classes was introduced by the President of the Local Government Board (Mr Norman Nield, member for Newton Division). The provisions of the Bill include :—The appoint- ment of three officers to be called the Housing Commissioners whose representations to a local authority shall be treated as official. The Local Government Board may make an order authorising a local authority to acquire an estate or land exceeding ten acres for the purpose of Part 111. of the 1890 Act. A local authority with the consent of the Local Government Board may release any bye-laws with respect to streets and buildings. A local authority shall have power to pay cornpensAtion to the owner of property demolished as unfit for habitation, where the owner agrees no buileinc,' shall be erected upon the cleared site except with the consent of the local authority. There shall be annually paid out of the Consolidated Fund a sum (to be called the housing grant) of £500,000, to be distributed as the Local Government Board may determine, among local authorities.

Mr NORMAN NIELD (Newton) in introducing the measure, said the present age had been called one of discontent, and he was inclined to think that the ques- tion of the proper housing of the working classes was the cause of more discontent than most of them imagined. Education had given man a broader outlook on life. He no longer looked through a black fog of ignorance but, on the contrary, his critical powers had been quickened, and he was beginning to use that faculty 1 which distinguished him from the dumb beast of burden. As a result, a deeper and more earnest interest was being taken in all those matters which affected the conditions under which the workers lived. There was a feeling that the price we paid in ugliness, crime, disease' filth, and physical and moral deterioration was far too high for our commercial prosperity The feeling was growing stronger that a lot of these evils might be remedied and avoided in the future with a little foresight and co-operation. Light and air were two of the great essentials for health and fitness, and in overcrowding our workers in small houses he thought we had made a terrible mistake. Far too long had we allowed the individual to gallop unbridled along the path of enter- prize, leaving a multitude of degraded and despairing I citizens behind him. The manufactuier had to con- tend in his business with scores of Factory Acts which had been passed to prevent him from coo- ducting hie business in a way which would have a harmful effect on the health and lives of the citizens,butl there had been nothing resembling the Factory Acts to prevent the frightful and rapacious work of the Jerry builder. The Imperial Parliament had attempted during the last fifty years to do some- thing in that respect for they had passed no less than I 28 Acts similar to the one they were considering, yet in 1 spite of that the progress made was very small indeed. In the memorandum just 'published to Mr Burns's ' Housing and Town Planning Act, it was stated that the number of repairing orders which bad been made by the mass of local authorities in the country had increased by 128 per cent and also that orders for the closing of unhealthy and unfit buildings for human habitation bad increased largely. They pointed out the greatest difficulty ' with which they had to contend was that hen a row of houses or section of the town was condemned as heieg unfit for human beings to live in, they found that in those houses generally condemned the poorest of the poor lived. The difficulty was to provide other accom- modation for that class of citizen. The Bill had been devised to remedy many of those obstacles. Reviewing the details of the Bill, Mr NIELD said the most important f clauses related to the by-laws. One of the greatest causes of the present day evils lay in the absence of co-operation between laud owners and local authorities. Town dwellers had to suffer from the mis- takes and had to pay more in rent and rates. Under the present regulations the land owners were compelled to overcrowd with houses. Under the clause the local authority could reduce cost of estates development and I reduce the number of houses per acre. There was one thing ceitain—until the wages received by the poorest classes of the workers could be made to square with the rents, such e scheme was imperative. Mr F R ISHERWOOD (Midlothian) formally seconded the Bill.

Mr. J. JARMAN (Leader of the Opposition) said be did not propose to move the usual resolution to defer the passing of the Bill. Such a question be hoped could be treated on non-party lines In order that they might get the best out of the measure. He would like to draw attention to one serious blot which referred to tne appointment of three officers as Housing Com- missioners. Their opponents must have forgotten the nice things they said about the Insurance Act with regard to the appointment of officials. The question cf housing reform was bcund up with the land question and the introducer of the measure would find himself faced with it all through. The clause which dealt with the power of authorities to acquire an estate or land was already in a measure passed through Parliament. But in this Bill they were met by the fact that there was no limitation as to the price or value to be put upon the land. They were left in the awkward position of bartering with the land owner, with no other court of appeal, and they would have to pay the price of the landowner or leave it alone. They already had an experience under the Small Holdings Act. Estates could not be acquired unless at prohibitive prices, and here were no means of ascertainin•r, the fair vain,. He suggested that they might do worse than prohibit the payment of an amount which exceeded the valuation which had been made by the valuers, or failing that,not more than 20 years Purchase. With regard to the housing grant of £500,000 to local authorities it was overlooked by the promoters that they were subsidising property which was going to compete with the local landlord and they were leaving out altogether the erector of properties. Mr J DALBY (Soc., E Bradford), said that the Bill at the best was a measure to patch up a system which in the opinion of his party was radically wrong. The question arose ;whither were they going ?—to save life or property? It appeared to him that the Government had their main interest in property. On the other hand the Bill did not go far enough because it simply scraped the problem In our large towns families were living in rooms which were totally inadequate, and the conditions in the country districts were no better. He hoped there was no-one present who advocated the attacking of the evils of inadequate housing by moral methods. nerwere often told that if they removed the working classes to better conditions they would in a short time return to exactly the same condition as they were before. but it was absurd to expect at once a marvellous change in a man of forty years of age with a wife and family. Dealing with the question of compensation he said he was at a loss to understand how anyone could propose , that a man who had let out for hire habitations should receive compensation forlthose dwellings at when they were razed to the ground. Such statements went to prove that property was the thing which they were out to save and that human life was only a secondary con- sideration. He would fight such a Bill with the last breath of his body if he thought it was going to diminish one jot the discontent of the workers. (Socialist applause). Mr W FURNESS (Foreign Secretary) contended that the methods of the Imperial Parliament in dealing with the land question had been to hamper the development of land. They had put on taxes, increased the cost of transfer and how could it be expected if they restricted the transfer that land would become cheaper ? If they

wanted to make land cheap and to give the workers cheaper and better conditions in which to live, they must make land as saleable as they would a pound of sugar. If they did that they would do more to improve the environment and adequate accommodation for the cottager than any scheme they could posbibly devise. Mr J HELSDY (SOO , Comae Valley), contended that the composition of the local authority under the Bill should not include any property owneis. They had found that many of our housing schemes were lett in the hands of property owners and the working classes generally did not come out at all favourably under them. He objected to any compensation being paid to owners of property. He was of the opinion that the Leal authority ought to penalise the owner of shun dwellings. Mr CHARLES E PARKER (L. Dundee), said he did not quite follow the loreign Secretary in his argu- ment in regard to the tax on unoccupied land making it dearer. Supposing they had an acre of unoccupied land for building purposed. At present the tax was one halfpenny ; and if they were to tax such land valued at. £lOO to the extent of £5 how much would that tax increase the value of the land? In his opinion it would reduce it, if anything. Mr FURNESS : Sly point is that by imposing the tax on land you are making it difficult to acquire or transfer land for building property. Mr PARKER: If you put a tax on land you depreci- ate the value of that land. The greater tax you put on land and you necessarily make it of less value. Dealing with the Bill, Mr Parker said he was sorry the Govern- ment did not start a Bill on their own. It seemed they had followed on the lines of the one Sir Griffith Boscawen brought before the Imperial House. He thought they could have devised a better measure if they had started afresh and it appeared to be one of the projects of the new Tory democracy. With regard to the clause which gave power to a local authority, with the consent of the Local Government Board, to release any bye laws with respect to streets and build- ings, he thought it a most unfair system which gave the local authority special privileges. The ordinary builder was to compete against the municipal authority. Mr NEILD: The clause applies also to the private builder.

Mr PARKER : If the byelaws are to be put aside then the better way would be to improve the byelaw% In the matter of compensation why should an authority have to pay for a thing which was worth nothing ? Under an old Act the conditions were that when pro- perty was demolished the materials were sold, and if then there was any surplus, over and above the cost of demolition, it should be handed over to the owner. If an owner of property, after repeated warnings, allowed it to get in such a condition that it was not habitable why should ratepayers be expected to pay compPnsa- Hon ? With regard to the grant of £500,000 out of the Consolidated Fund, he would like to know how it was to be repaid ? _ . _

Mr NEILD : It is not to be repaid at all. Mr PARKER : A gift. (Laughter). Then every local authority will apply for a grant. Mr FURNESS : The principle is in operation in Ireland, and if it is good for Ireland it is good for us. Mr PARKER : But the £500,000 will go nowhere. There will be a perfect. scramble to got it. In conclu- sion he said the Bill was about the worst that could ever be introduced in that House. It was bad business bad finance and bad charity. (Applause). Mr C D PARKINSON then moved the adjournment of the House.
