div.head: CALEDONIAN DINNER. SIR JAMES BITIIICON SCOTLAND AND SCOTSMEN.
div.p: CALEDONIAN DINNER. SIR JAMES BITIIICON SCOTLAND AND SCOTSMEN.
MORE ABOUT POLITICS IN MUNICIPAL LIFE.

To-day is St Andrew's Day, but the community of Scots in Warrington anticipated the feast of their patron saint by holding their annual dinner on Thurs- day evening. The function was the twenty-fourth promoted by the Warrington Caledonian Association and was characterized by that feeling of cordial good fellowship which is alwas so pleasing a feature of these gatherings of the clans. The sons of Scotia were once more carried back in imagination to the impressive natural glories of their native land and had also the pleasure of listening to shrewd estimates of Scottish qualities both from kinsmen of their own and from the mere Sassenach who was also represented on this occasion. The association was honoured in having as its principal guest Sir James Barr, M.D., President of the British Medical Association, to whom was entrusted the principal toast "Scotland." A splendid welcome was accorded to this distinguished leader of a great profession and, in an interesting and homely speech, Sir James dwelt upon the history of Scotland and, in particular, upon the migratory tendencies of its inhabitants. Incidentally he cheerily described the Englishman as the donkey who bore the whole of the burdens of the United Kingdom and allowed the Scots and Irish to rule him. As -usual, every effort was made to impart a distinctively Scottish air to tho prccoedings. The guests assembled to the .skirl of the bag-pipes and each was presented with a buttonhole in the shape of a sprig of heather. Behind the cross-table was displayed the Scottish national ensign (" Scotland's ruddy lion in its field of gold ") and the blue and white banner of St. Andrew. That indispensable national dish, haggis —"the chieftain of the puddin' race," was borne into the room, with due comp and solemnity, to the strains of " Bannocks o barley meal" played on the pipes by Sergeant J Stoddart, of the Liverpool Scottish Territorial Battalion, who was clad in the full "garb of old Gaul." A delightful programme was submitted, the vocalists being Mr J W Willett, Mr B Poole, Lieutenant Westbrook, and Mr J Robertson. Miss Lockerbie, a young and promising violinist, received a warm encore for her skilful playing of a couple of solos. Mr II M Ashton's humorous recitals were, o! course, a very popular feature. Mr T Ford was an able accompanist. Mr J FULTON Smtrit presided and amongst others present were :—The Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph), Mr A 11 Crosfield, Lieut.-Colonel Brereton Fairclotigh, Mr F A Frost (President of the Chamber of Commerce), Mr J L Davenport (the indefatigable vice-president of the association who contributes so largely to 'its success), Mr G Bowman (hon. treasurer), and Mr J Tennant (the bard-working hon. secretary). Apologies for non-attenuance had been received from Bishop Welldon, Sir Peter Carlaw Walker, Bart. (patron). Lord Wolmer, M.P., sir George Douglas Bart . sir Gilbert Greenall, IBart., Sir Edward Missed, Mr Ilgrold Smith, M.P., Colonel John held Walker, Colnnel W Hall Walker, M.P., Mr R Hutton, Mr E J Hall, end Mr M Nicholls (Chief Constable.) The Norwich Scots sent the following apt greeti:tg:— Altho' the flood has swept the toon, We Scots hue met thogither, To celebrate St. Andrew's nicht And toast onr Sainted Brithert The Banker's in the chair the year, And fills it like a king, Wl' cheery smile and jo.ial laugh He makes the rafters ring, We send a greeting tea the friens Noo scattered far and wide, For Norwich stands where she has been, The toon that stayed the tide. THE KING AND THE CRISIS.

--- --- The PRESIDENT, in submitting the health of "The King," said that never had the responsibility which faced his Majesty been more serious that a the present moment, in view of the unrest which prevailed in Europe. It was to be hoped that in this great crisis, his Majesty's advisers would have that stability and consistency of policy that would at least keep this country out of the terrible turmoil which threatened us at this juncture. (Applause.) THE TERRITORIALS AND COMPULSORY SERVICE.

Mr J C COPPOCK proposed "The Navy, Army and Reserve Forces." Referring to the recent speech of that distinguished and grand old fighting man Lord Roberts, he said that whether they agreed with him or not, they must concede that Lord Roberts had no axe of his own to grind, and that whatever he had said was uttered with the sole intention of promoting the welfare of the country. The Territorial Force deserved every encouragement, for it was labouring under many disadvantages. It was still considerably short of its establishment strength, and it rested with the public and with the Government to make it a real force. If we made it clear to the Territorials that we were pre- pared to support them, there would not be the apathy that had been experienced in the past, and the day of compulsion in military matters would be far distant. If, however, the apathy continued, we should have no alternative before us but to resort to conscription or compulsory service. Lieut.-Colonel BEE RETON FAIRCLOUGH responded. , Having referred to the marked development of the scientific side of the navy's work— pointing out that England was taking the lead in aviation and wireless telegraphy— and to the stupendous work which the army was doing, he passed on to that branch of the services in which be was specially interested, lie declared that as a Terri- torial officer he was getting absolutely " fed up," because one was living in a most precarious kind of position. On the one hand they bad an extremely good soldier like Lord Roberts making one statement—and he was perfectly right—and on the other hand they had an extremely good soldier like General Bethune snaking another statement—and he, too, was perfectly right. It was perhaps calculated to make the public mistrustful to see such a paradoxical situation. How- ever, the fundamental principle of arbitration was that they must have a standard by which to judge. What were the respective standards of Lord Roberts and General Bethune ? Lord Roberts did not give them a standard at all ;he simply made the statement that they were not fit. General Bethune said they were perfectly fit to carry out the duties for which they were organised. There they had the whole thing in a nutshell. Dealing with promiscuous criticisms of the force, the speaker said he had been " spoiling for a row " for a long time. There had been a great deal of mud slinging on the part of the public. The Colonel went on to argue that the official conditions of servi.,e in the Territorials were not such as to make it possible to produce an efficient soldier, but he pointed out that in their desire to be a really useful force, the men did vastly more than the minimum service asked of them. Their feelings at the criticism constantly directed at them could therefore be readily understood. It was not the Territorials who were at fault, but the reason why things were in their present state was to be found in the manner in which the force was organised and in the apathy of the public. The Territorials had done more than their duty and it was for the people to insist that the force should be put on a proper footing. Unfortunately, however,patriotism was at a low ebb in England sad one evidence of that fact was that charit- able institutions lacked workers and Town Councils and other authorities were not attracting the right type of men. If we could not find sufficient men to work in the Territorials at the price we were at present offir- ing, we must he prepared to pay more. It was his firm belief that, owing to the lack of patriotism, we should never do any good until we bad some compulsory method of dealing with the question. The chaos which existed in many people's minds was due to the political aspect of the question, because no party felt strong enough to go to the country and say " We must have compulsory service, because you beggars will not serve voluntarily." (Applause.) In introducing bir James Barr, the PRKSIDENT said the position which the British Medical Association had taken up with regard to the working of the Insurance Act was most justifiable. SIR JAMES BARR AND SCOTLAND.

Sir JAMBS BARR, who bad a very enthusiastic greet- ing, then proposed the toast of" Scotland." He dealt largely with the history of the country. It had, he I said, been tr;laimed that Scotland existed before the Flood and that it was one of the Mc Gregor's or Mc Pherson's who got a boat of his own and did not bother about old Noah and his ark. (Laughter.) Unfortun- ately for that story, history showed Scotland to be a comparatively young nation, dating back to about the end of the tilth or the beginning of the sixth century. Prior to that we knew practically nothing about Scotland. The peculiarity about it was that the Scots actually came from Ireland. (Laughter.) Sir James then dealt with the Christianising efforts of St. Columba and St. Aidan and to the gradual evolution of Scotland into a nation. The battle of Bannockburn was something of which Scotsmen had reason to be proud but, in one sense, it was a most unfortunate thing, because, having defeated the English, the Scots had*nothing to do but to fight among themselves— laughtor)—and the result was a great many feuds between the different clans. Coming down to the reigns of the James, Sir James said the corruption and immorality of the clergy in Scotland at that time was about the worst in Europe, and that was probably the reason why, at the Reformation, Scotland went to the other extreme. They thought they would put an end to the clergy and consequently they over- threw episcopacy and the Presbyterian religion had ruled Scotland ever since. He thought it was a religion which suited Scotland and the North of Ireland and he was very proud to belong to it. (Applause.) The Scots had always been, as far as he could make out, fairly religious, but, as many of theta were perhaps aware, religion and morality did not often go together.

(Laughter.) He did not know whether that was a mis- fortune or not, but it was a matter of observation. It was a great advantage to England that Scotsmen did migrate south, because if it were not for Scottish and ' Irish blood, what would become of England ? (Laughter). They had heard a great deal that night about the army and navy, hut if it were not for Scottish and Irish soldiers he did not know where the British Aimy would be. It was a great misfortune that the Englishman was so deeply engrossed in making money—(laughter)—that he had not time for anything else, and the result was that be allowed the Irishmen and the Scotsmen to govern. (Laughter.) England was not governed by Englishmen, but by Irishmen and Scotsmen—the Welshmen were also coming in now (Laughter.) That was entirely the fauit of the English. There was plenty of ability among them, if they were not so keen on money making. (Laughter.) The English- man did not stop at a bluoee ; he wanted a sovereign. (Laughter.) It was often said of the Scotsman that he kept the Sabbath end everything else he could lay his hands on. The Englishman, however, kept everything but tae Sabbath. (I.,aughter.) He (Sir James) never cared much for saying that the Eaglish- man loved his Bible and his beer. He might love his beer, but he certainly did not know very much about his Bible. (Laughter.) The Englishman was 00 State donkey who bore his own and other people's burdens without a grumble. (Laughter.) He used to be called a land grabber, but now he was prepared to give a slice of his territory to anyone who would acknowledge hini as the ground landlord. He proposed to give Erin's . Isle to the Irishmen, with a few millions a year to keep it ',float. (Laughter.) I always like to prod the animal " added Sir James "and hope some day he will kick out. Perhaps be will when like Baalam's ' ass, he sees a sword hanging iii front of him, ready to dismember." Sir James further expressed the view that the Scotsmen retained their original virility; in , spite of their migration south ; at any rate it took . many generations of living in England to change s Scotsman into an Englishman. ; Laughter). POLITICS IN MUNICIPAL LIFE.

Mr F A Frost proposed The teen and trade of Warrington." He said they were proud of the town and of the way in which it. was governed. They niiot, in fact, wonder that it was governed as well as it. was Colonel Fair°lough had expressed the view that they did not always get the best men in the Council and had asked how they got there. They got there on party lines. If a man was a really good Horne Ruler for. Ireland, he knew all about building bridges for War- rington. (Laughter.) If be happened to ye a thorough tariff reformer—taxing Manchester goods coming into . Warrington and so living on 4anchester—(lBl[odt er)— he was qualified to work the insurance Act in Warring- ton. (Laughter.) That was how they were elected. They got their line from a so-called leader—a man, he (Mr Frost) presumed, who could think and who became a sort of hell wether to be followed by the others. Whether that resulted in the right man being put in t he place, he (Mr Frost) left them to judge. However, they could not deny that the town was well governed and he thought a great deal of the credit for that was undoubtedly cue to the Mayor. (Applause.) Having described his 11'srship as a "record Mayor," Mr Frost said Warrington wits also fortunate in having a record Mayoress. (Applause.) It was the only town that could boast of two future Mayors having been born at the barite time to the same mother. (Laughter and applause.) They all joined in congratulating the Mayoress and in wishing her a speedy recovery and long life in which to enjoy the benefits she had got. (Applause.) Having pleased for a greater interest on the part of the manufacturers in the work of the Chamber of WI-amerce, Mr Frost said the trade of Warrington was never better than it was to-day. (applause.) He attributed our commercial prosperity to the grit industry,integrity and perseverance of the English ye q;le and be believed that if we could only have peace in the labour world and in the international field, our trade would 'continue to flourish as it had done in the past. (Applause ) The MAYOR, having thanked 2fr Frost I r his kindly allusion to the Mayoress, said the trade of Warrington was as likely to be good as that of any town in the king- dom. No manufact rihng town could be beautiful but Warrington compared very tavournbly in that respect with the majority of to wss engaged in similar trades, particularly in Lancashire. Ile wits sorry Ill Ore War- ringtouitins did not bring their local patriotism to the test of living in the town' instead of migrating to the ! suburbs. It. has said that no man could serve two masters, and he thought no man could be loyal to two municipalities or atanorities. Those who were naturally situated under the sway 'of a given munioipality should cordially and loyally support it. He did nct think it seas absolutely necessary to live in the country to obtain health and enjoyment. One could be quite healthy in the town if one lived a proper and regular life and indulged in country walks and recrea- tion. The fact that a large proportion of people lived out of the town made the town dull and dreary at night, and he could not help thinking that order in the streets would be better maintained if there were more residents in the heart of the to wu. Referring to War- rington Bridge, his worship said be was sorry that with their 80ft. bridge, which would he one of the widest in England, they would be blocked by that wretched crossing at Wilderspool. If they could only devise some other meat s of crossing the line, it would add to the trade ad comfort of the town to a greater extent than many supposed. Alluding to his civic dirties, his Worship said the office of Mayor was an education in itself, be knew about 100 per cent, more of men and affairs now than he did two years ago. He had often thought there ought to be some previous education before a man entered upon the duties. Tat-re ought to be a Royal College of Mayors —(laughters)—for such preparation would save the Mayor a great many fears and heart-burnings. It was a pity that the hest men in the Council were often taken from it by the cruel operation of the party political system. Politics were, of course, the real life, the very breath of the nostrils of the Imperial Parliament. but in a Town Council they were not only not required but were actually a hindrance. (Applause.) He could mention two members on both sides of politics—excellent men who had been driven out of the Council by that agency. When he was asked " Why don't you get better men ?" his answer was " Why don't you let us Keep them when we have got them ? " (Applause). AIR. A. H. (31.108 FIELD'S SPEECEL

- - Mr A 11 CROSPIELD proposed "The Warrington Caledonian Assoc.ation." lie said that about the middle of last May he bad the pleasure of forsaking "The crowd, the hum the shock of men " in London and renewing his acquaintance With the banks and braes of Bonnie Scotland. He was addicted to mountain climbing, and had long had an ambition to ,1 scale the heights of old Loch Nagar. Mr Crosfield then I gave a vivid description of his climb and added that, ,1 basing seen something of those precipices in the Tyrol, I the Alps and the Pyrenees, which were apt to give one a rather nasty feeling—(laughter)—he had seldom encountered a more splendid piece of steep rook work I than he found on old Nagar. A projected expedition to Ben Mao Dhui had to he abandoned, because the weather proved to be " kin a wee salt." (Laughter.) Mr. Crostleld referred to a five miles tramp over the heather in a snowstorm in the heart of the Highlands j and, comparing the West of Scotland with the East, I he unhesitatingly gave the palm for impressive scenery to the West. Passing on to speak of St. Andrews and its golfing associations, Mr. Oros- ft.dd said he did not know any place where they got a better sample of Scotsmen and more varieties than were to be met at the autumn gathering in the grey old city. As to the Scottish characteristics, he particularly singled out the sarcasm and riry irony which was the peculiar gift of many who hailed from over the Border. He had always thought that the insinuation that Scotsmen were deficient in humour was one of the grossest 'Discharges that could be made against any set of them. Humour, however, WEIS not, their strongest , point, for caution Was one of the finest, attributes of I the Scot. Having related several Scottish anecdotes, which were much relished by theassembly, Mr Crosfield said the cheerfulness and good spirits which the Cale- donians in Warrington manifested was wonderful, considering the fact that under this misguided, mis- chievous and foolish fiscal system of ours, we were, as it were, under the hammer and all our industries either going to the dogs or gone. (Laughter.) He was surprised that they were bearing up so well—(laughter) —and must congratulate them upon their pluck and optimism. (Laughter.) Commenting upon the way in which men of different views fraternised at those gatherings, Mr Crosfield instanced the Chairman and himself who were hardly the closest of politicAl allies. (Lau)ihter.) On the contrary, he believed Mr Fulton Smith was one of the most active men in helping to upset his apple cart. (Laughter.) "I am sorry, of course " added Mr CroOeld " that he should do any- thing so misguided. Laughter.) On the other hand, what a testimony it is to the afflatus, the mellifluous influence of your Ciledonian gatherings—which I have now attended for thirty years, going back to those good old days of John Dun at Hoylake—that your honoured President, his Worship the oe.yor—who is also, I am sorry to say. on the wrong side—laughter)—and myself can fraternise, just as we should do on the links of St. Andrews, as if no politics existed." (Applause)' Dr MaNsos responded. He said that in these days of cosmopolitanism, national societies tended to ke,,p alive national customs and traditions. All nations with a distinct histor - should be preserved and associations like theirs helped, in a small way, to protect small nationalities from the levelling and destructive forces of social evolution. (Applause). The health of " Our patron " was proposed in felicitous terms by Mr G Bowman and honoured in true Scottish fashion. Mr J L Davenport proposed "The visitors "and Mr A Bottomiey responded. Mr :1 Bennett submitted " Health of the lasses and Mr P H Brown replied. "The president, vice-presidents and officers" were honoured on the proposition of Mr W Skinner.

div.head: ChOSFIELD ON CARSON.
div.p: ChOSFIELD ON CARSON.
TRENCHANT CRITICISM.
[To Tim EDITOR OF TIIE EXAMINER.] Patten Arms Hotel, Warrington?
November 28th, 1912.

Sir,—Sir Edward Carson's visit to Warrington on Saturday is announced legibly enough on vari- ous posting stations in the town, and it is only a pity that these announCements do not tell us whether he is to be received, as on other recent occasions, with military hononrs. No mention is • made, so far as I have seen, of wooden cannon, though I suppose we may take it they will be imported for the occasion. Nor are we told whe- ther spectators will have a unique opportunity for assisting at a coronation. However, that may be, I have no doubt that not a few members of -the Liberal Party will be on hand on the chance of enjoying comic opera proceedings of that charac- ter; and if they are present, then our friends will be able to give Sir Edward a lesson in political order and decency of which he, in common, with other Tory leaders, Stand in very great need just now. If his open-air meeting was interrupted and made impossible by continued uproar, Sir :Edward is about the last man who would have one vestige of right to complain; but he may be taught on Saturday that Lancashire men do not hold with the methods of hooligans, do not believe that an- archy promotes political progress, and do not admit that a minority is entitled to indulge in disorderly ruffianism the moment it fails to over- rule- the majority. In the meantime may I venture to draw special attention to criticism in the Colonies of these pro- ceedings. div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The Courtiers in original musical comedy numbers assuredly carry off the palm at the Hippodrome this week. The troupe consists of four ladies and four gentlemen who are possessed of excellent voices which they use to advantage in well chosen numbers. Each member acquits herself or himself in a highly creditable wanner and whether it be in solos or con- certed items their singing affords delight. Lam ies Wylie and Co. appear in an excruciatingly funny sketch entitled " Early Morning lieflsctions." Three persons are involved and the theme deals with the adventures of a dissipated actor who arrives home in an advanced stage of inebriation and, although during his absence a large mirror has been broken by his servant and a policeman, when the actor looks at where the glass should be he sees a reflection of a man which in reality is the policeman, in the pereou of Mr Laurie W 3 lie, but who mimics the actor's actions in so realistic a manner that eventually when the actor falls through the frame of the mirror he is saddled with the blame Camp and Critic create much boisterous laughter in a rollicking absurdity " Waxworks ; " the farce is one , which cannot fall to appeal to all lovers of genuine clean and witty comedy. Charles Denman is a clever, light comedian who scores with a catchy song rendered in an infectious manner. Fields and Mansell are dexterous lightning painters and produce some capital work. A great achievement is the painting of a bouquet on a rapidly revolving canvas. As a diver- sion the gentleman introduces some smart juggling feats. The brothers Bernhart as "the university man and the other chap" are fairly successful as crosstalk- big comedians. The Nelson Trio show us what can be done in the way of trick comedy and skating within the circumscribed area of the stage ; the antics of "father " on the occasion of his first visit to the rink cause toars of laughter. Laurie Wylie presents his toy theatre marionnettes with a large amount of success. His chief and most appreciated " turn " is that in which the "doll " gives a capital ventriloqual per- formance. Molly Wynn,. is a dainty and attractive comedienne and dancer. As usual the pictures shown on the bioscope deal with interesting subjects. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. The bill for next week is headed by Alice Raymond and her players in "A night in Egypt." other terns are ilson Hallett, comedian in his humorous and pathetic studies of children ; Ma,cot the educated horse ; Clara Coverdale'a Eight Boston Boys and Girls in vocal and dancing act; Queenie May, star chorus vocalist; Julian Ross, light comedian and actoz ; Gordon Brown, the boy tenor.
From

of the Dominions strongly. Their press, on the strength of it, seems to be forming a habit of calling the Unionist Party the 'Gentlemen of England' in inverted commas, apparently iron- ical. The Montreal Gazette asks whether they have been taking lesson; from the more villent section of the militant suffragettes? The Montreal Herald congratulates Mr. As- quith. 'There is,' it says, 'something very at- tractive after all, in the picture the cables show us of the strong-faced man sitting with arms folded while his enemies in their anger made themselves ridiculous.'

'The Montreal Daily Star draws a contrast between the calmness of English public opinion about Home Rule and the 'civil war' which Mr. Wyndham proclaimed in the House of Commons. The Daily Star goes on to explain what 'the Colonies' generally are likely to think of party men who choose a time like this for the practice of violent disorder. `lf,' it says, 'the cables do not mislead us, and if the action of the military and naval authorities of Great Britain have not been wantonly wasteful and provocative, there is a serious European crisis at this moment, and the Empire is within 'measurable distance of war Under such conditions BritiSla Min- isters ought to have something better to think of than how to quell a riot in the House of Com- mons and keep the First Lord of the Admiralty out of the hospital." . .

There we have sufficiently significant examples of the stream of derision and contempt which is being poured out in the Colonial press on these methods of political hooligans. It would be very interesting to hear, when Sir Edwarrl' Carscn comes to Warrington. what he thinks about it; and, further, how he likes a reference in a London Conservative paper to these "methods of the pot- house brawler,"—and perhaps somebody will invite him to tell us.—Yours, etc., _
A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: WYCLIFFE CHURCH. Invitation to a—S-hef field Minister.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CHURCH. Invitation to a—S-hef field Minister.

The Rev T T James, M.A., of Wycliffe Congre- gational Church, Sheffield, has been invited to accept the pistorate of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, rendered vacant by the resignation of the Rev John Yonge, after a pastorate extending over thirty-six years. The decision to invite Mr James to Warrington was arrived at at a meeting of the members of Wycliffe Church on Thursday night. Mr James was a student at Lancashire Independent College, Manchester, and was a warden of the college' settlement from 1901 to 1906. Since then he has been pastor of Wycliffe Congregational Church Sheffield. Two of Mr. James's brothers are also in the Con- gregational ministry, one being assistant to the Rev J D Jones. M A.,of I3ournemouth, and the other pastor of a church in Gloucester.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDING.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDING.

Richardson---Crowther. The credding of Mr. James Richardson, jun. elder son of Mr. Wm. Richardson, J.P., of Holly Bank, Walton, Warrington, and Mrs. Richard- son, to Miss Marjory Heron .Crowther, younger daughter of Mr. George Hy. Crowther, M.lnst.- C.E., and Mrs. Crowther, of Thorn Hill, Eger- ton, Huddersfield, took place on Thursday afternoon at Hudderfield Parish Church. The bride, who was given away by her father, looked charming in an ivory satin charrneuse gown, trimme with Maltese lace, with lovers' knots in silver galon, the separate train being sus- 'pended from the shoulder. She carried a very handsome shower bouquet of orchids and whitt roses. The bridesmaids were Miss Hilda Whiteley, Miss Dora Richardson, Miss Helen Crowther, and Master James Cormack Robin- son (godson of the bridegroom) acted as page. The dresses of the ladies were cream shadow lace draped with cherry-coloured charmeuse, and their black hats were trimmed with cherry. coloured ostrich feathers. They carried shower bouquets of carnations to match. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. C. H. Holt (vicar), who was assisted by the Rev. James Collins (vicar of St. Thomas's, Stockton Heath). Mr. Wm. Richardson, jun. (brother of the bridegroom), was the best man. Dr. Hull presided at the organ. Following the wedding a reception was held at the residence of the bride's father, a large number of guests being present. The happy couple received the hearty congratulations of their friends. The honeymoon is being spent in London and Devonshire. The bride travelled in a golden. brown coat and skirt, with touches of black panne, a hat of black plush, with feathers to- match the costume, and a travelling wrap af light blue cloth with black collar. SOCIETY. Mr James Richardson, jun, is one of the hon. secretaries of the Warrington Society and on MondaY evening the members took the opportunity of express- ing their goodwill by presenting him with a wedding present in the form of a handsome solid silver inkstand/ suitably inscribed. Mr JOHN FAIRHURST presided and made the pre- sentation. He said he had known Mr Richardson for 3 long time and he even remembered his grandfather. Be and Mr Richardson's father had been intimate friends for many years. lie could say of Mr James Richardson, jun, that whatever work he undertook he did well, and if anyone had earned the good withes of the society be had earned them. (Hear, hear). Speeches were also made by Alderman Bennett, Mr J Longland and ADD D Parkinson. Alderman Bennett said he owed a great deal to the Academy, certainly more than he could ever repay, as he was indebted to it for some of the hest friends he had, and the more he saw of them within those hallowed walls the more were the old friendships;endeared and made the sweeter. He had had the pleasure of making many friends since the society was formed, and he did not think he should het invidious if he placed Mr Richardson tint. (Hoare'' hear and applause.) He had shown them how with their serious aims they might couple friendly inter; course and mutual enjoyment, and be felt sure tbat health and strength were continued to him they might'; look forward to him taking a still more prominent pert in local life. (Applause.) Mr RicHannsom who was warmly cheered on rising to reply, said he had always been proud or being - their secretary. When he mentioned to the lady wb was about to be his wife what his work, interests ad' hobbies were, and informed her that he was one of o_l' hon. secretaries of the Warrington society, she esler. him to show her over the building, and he did so Wit'. great pleasure ; and he should be prouder still of tb? position be held when be took that beautiful inkstand to her, and showed it to her people ass token that tht men with whom be associated—who were as capable oL- sizing up and criticizing as anybody—had such a deeP affection and regard for him. (Applause). ANOTHER PRESENTATION. On Tuesday morning Mr Richardson was presentea.. by the staff and employees of the Vernou-streeD' fanning Co., Ltd., of which he is the managing director, with a handsome silver salver. The preseots; Hon was made by Mr Joseph Forster, director an', manager.

Day of weekly Half- holiday. All trades, other than those Wednesday (or at option exempted by Section 4, sub- of Shopkeeper, Saturday) section 6 of the Shops Act. I Communications relating to the (working of thifl Order should be addressed to the Chief Inspector of Weights and Measures, .he Castle, Chester. Dated this 15th day of November, 1912. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. NOTE -It is provided by Section 4 (5) of the Act that if a Shop is closed throughout the whole of a Bank Holiday, and the Bank Holiday does not fall on the day fixed for the Weekly Half-Holiday, the Shopkeeper may keep his shop open either on the half-holiday before or, the half-holiday after the Bank Holiday.

"Wool was threatened," but the advance in our exports during the eight years has increased from £24,500,000 to £37,500,000; while similar Exports from France have increased from £10,000,000 to £11,500,000; and from Germany they have only increased from £15,000,000 to £17,000,000. More significant still is the fact that since the introduction of the last German Tariff the rate of increase of exports has, in Germany, become slower than previously. When, however, we compare the imports of fully manufactured woollen goods of the two countries the contrast of the effects of the two policies becomes still more marked. Germany has doubled her imports while we have reduced ours by a full third--see diagram. It will be noticed that to bring the lines in contrast we have had to use two indexes, Million Marks for the German, and Million Pounds for the British. The move- ment of the lines when compared does not therefore exactly correspond with actual figures because the indexes are different, but each is correct by its own index. A further striking point in connection with the woollen industry is the individual trade ' between the three countries named. Our exports to Germany and France have both 1 increased during late years, while German and French exports to this country have both I gone down.

GENERAL BETHUEN AND THE TERITORIALS. Major-General Bethune, Director-General of the Territorial Force, on Wednesday, addressing the Birmingham employers, said some people discouraged the system because thoy favoured conscription. He urged the employers to set aside prejudice and make the best of the present system. He did not wish to inconvenience them. It the men could not be spared let them remain at work. Thousands who could attend camp and drills did not join. If they could get these he would be satisfied.
